reviews.text: The September 2012 attacks on the U.S. diplomatic compounds in Benghazi may have occurred less than four years ago, but 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi is the movie that Michael Bay has been waiting his entire life to make. He wanted to direct Black Hawk Down, but Ridley Scott got there first. (Bay has begrudgingly approved of the movie that resulted.) He then wanted to direct Lone Survivor, but Peter Berg snatched it out from under him. And just when it seemed like we’d never again strand American personnel in a FUBAR situation on the soil of a distant country (pause for bitter laughter), Bay was finally able to acquire the rights to one of recent history’s most violent wrongs.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Ridley Scott's "1492: Conquest of Paradise" stands as a sort of training exercise for a director priming himself for later, more successful epics. An already-accomplished filmmaker, Scott's retelling of Christopher Columbus's discovery of the Americas finds him expanding his vision, canvas, and narrative scope in comparison to his previous and smaller yet iconic films. While the film lacks the potent politics of "Kingdom of Heaven" or the grand, entertaining spectacle of "Gladiator," it is a lushly visualized piece of work. Its humanity is communicated in overly broad strokes that suit the effectiveness of the film less than deeper, more textured portrayals would, but it still makes for an engaging first stab in classically epic cinema.

The film presents the Cliff Notes version of the Xinhai Revolution, which overthrew the last imperial dynasty in China in, you guessed it, 1911. The story is told from the perspectives of many different characters, wherein lies its first problem. Clocking it at barely over 90 minutes, the film condenses a lot of history into a short amount of time and throws characters at us rapid fire with nothing but a text based name and position, no back-stories. This makes it really hard to care about any one person, or the general…

This is one of those borderline-likable early 2000s movies, and strictly because of the fun practical effects and Robert Englund and Lin Shaye clearly having a ball in their respective roles. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Ramin Bahrani's 2nd Chance is a fascinating departure from his earlier immigrant-centred dramas. This time, Bahrani chooses to tell an all-American story through a documentary format, with businessman and entrepreneur Richard Davis as the focal point. Davis is the inventor of the concealable bulletproof vest and a real showman filmmaker who used female models in his catalogue to promote the vests and produced hyperkinetic shootout videos that were shown to police departments across the United States in an effort to promote the vests. Police departments bought the vests, hook, line and sinker, and that led Davis to open a vest factory in a small Michigan town where 80% of the town worked for him.

reviews.author: Bilge Ebiri
reviews.text: Bahrani's first feature doc, and his power over his craft really comes through in the way he edits the pre-existing footage and the newer footage. The Herzog influence is strong, too, particularly in the interviews. Maybe too strong? There's a lot here that aligns with Bahrani's fascination with hustlers, hucksters, and dreamers, and with his fascination with the American Dream, but at times it feels like maybe he's going for that inevitable metaphysical Herzogian lift -- one that never quite comes. I didn't experience this film as an exploration of America, or society, or the human condition, but rather as a more intimate and odd tale of betrayal among friends and colleagues. And it totally works that way. Looking forward to seeing it again at some point.

Amazing how sad the sound of a bird chirping can sound. Ah, empathy.

Not because they are bad people, but because suddenly they enter a system that tracks them, brands them, incarcerates them, and adds hundreds of stipulations for when (if) they get their freedom back. Easy to take this for granted.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: The snail can never hide where he’s been. As soon as he is born and makes his first moves forward, a residuum trails him, hard to clean, even harder to hide—he cannot outrun it, for wherever he goes, it follows him—that indelible substance of life traces his path like a prophecy etched in stone, a track of tactility and history that spans a lifetime. Does the snail deserve to be punished for his mucin? Surely we cannot allow for him to slither across places in which he is not welcome and cause harm to those surfaces he defaces. But it is in his nature. Should we kill the snail? Lock him away? Does he deserve our empathy? Is the lowly, slippery snail worthy of redemption? Maybe the more important question is: what does the snail think?

reviews.author: Chris
reviews.text: The way this so seamlessly flows from a leisurely, absurdist dark comedy following the exploits of 9 escaped convicts to a poignant, deeply melancholic rumination on their near impossible task of making amends for past misdeeds is simply outstanding. The inability to find solace haunts everything so vividly; these souls can leave their physical prison far behind, but that means very little once the vibrancy brought about by freedom succumbs to the despondency at realising that the cages placed upon them by their own mindsets and by society itself are much harder to break. Disorder is the only outlet they have to mask the unbearable pain of leading a life where rejection is an ever-present, their callousness and aggression gradually…

reviews.text: Denmark’s highest-grossing film ever (to date) is the third of the Department Q crime dramas based on the novels of Jussi Adler-Olsen. After two successful entries directed by Mikkel Nørgaard, Hans Petter Moland takes the helm, and the result is a brighter, more action-oriented film that helps balance its bleak storyline and sometimes shocking violence. Aided by their red-haired secretary Rose (Johanne Louise Schmidt, who provides some levity), detectives Carl Mørck (Nikolaj Lie Kaas) and Assad (Fares Fares) are in pursuit of Johannes (Pål Sverre Hagen), a serial killer of children taken from religious families. While the previous film stayed mostly within the dark, wet streets and alleys of Copenhagen, Moland takes A CONSPIRACY OF FAITH out of the city…

reviews.author: JakubM
reviews.text: By design, A Constant Forge is more about John Cassavetes the filmmaker than it is about John Cassavetes the man, but it makes a strong case for the two being inseparable. For him, filmmaking was a way of seeing the world and processing its joys and challenges. The work was more vital than the end result. Entertainment was secondary to emotional response. At just over 200 minutes, it has the structural looseness and emotional depth of an actual Cassavetes film, building its narrative by bouncing an actor's reading of the filmmaker's words off of interviews featuring countless regulars and collaborators. It's one of the richest and most engaging filmmaker-centric documentaries I've ever seen. The biggest compliment I can give it is that I immediately felt an urge to dive back into Cassavetes' filmography, now equipped with context and perspective I lacked the first time around.

reviews.text: La hagiografía es mal vista, y con razón, por su renuencia a desnudar a los héroes. Por ejemplo, en A Constant Forge, Charles Kiselyak se olvida del alcoholismo de Cassavetes y se ciñe a anécdotas donde encuentran al gran autor reparando un retrete o fingiendo ser un pollo muerto en un ensayo. No son imágenes de un hombre ridículo sino de un artista comprometido. Sin embargo la unción interminable y un estilo simple que combina entrevistas con metraje de las películas, se compensan gracias a un ejercicio de crítica colectiva donde colaboradores y especialistas diseccionan la obra de Cassavetes como un botánico a una flor: en sus subjetividades nutridas por la experiencia o el estudio, las películas se abren y la mirada del espectador se alimenta.

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: Shoddy in conception and construction, this adaptation of the 1973 Broadway musical—based on Ingmar Bergman’s Smiles of a Summer Night and featuring music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim—is most interesting for the presence of Elizabeth Taylor, who is at once sorely out of place and somehow the movie’s centripetal force. (I guess that’s star power?) She plays Desiree Armfeldt, a stage actress, circa 1900 Vienna, and the hub of an ever-expanding array of interconnected mistresses, wives, husbands, sons, daughters, and others. Taylor may not have the singing chops Sondheim’s material requires, but there’s a brash attitude and eventual vulnerability to her performance that nevertheless charms, culminating in a surprisingly moving rendition of “Send in the Clowns.” Otherwise, A Little Night Music is a supposedly scandalous sex comedy undone by an endless array of uninteresting medium shots and storeroom lighting, the latter of which makes poor Taylor look 30 in some scenes and 70 in others.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Suzuki's first foray back into filmmaking after a 10-year blacklisting is about as bitter about the exploitative, machinelike politics of entertainment industries as you'd expect. Taking a manga about the world of professional golf and advertising companies in Japan and turning it into a Play Misty For Me-esque psycho-fan thriller about a woman being transformed into an unrecognizable sex object by the bureaucratic men who profit off her only to be projected on and abused by a ravenous, celebrity-obsessed consumer culture of women's bodies and television screens. In typical Suzuki fashion every opportunity to highlight the artificiality of this world (ridiculous sets, overwhelming color, surreal bursts of subjective expression) is taken and then some; and the only way out is of course a complete, destructive breakdown.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Hiring Seijun Suzuki to direct an adaptation of a melodramatic manga set in the world of female professional golfers was a real "someone put Chris Farley in charge of the bees" moment for Shochiku Studios. Kinda doubt the acidic stuff about celebrity, television, image and marketing was in the source material, and probably nobody at the time imagined he would break with traditional structure and form and go gonzo surrealist nightmare with the piece (double mustached Joe Shishido is one of the funniest prankster filmmaker gags I've seen in awhile). Benefit of hindsight, Suzuki is known for being the guy who does exactly that. Footnotes aside, his visual creativity here is bristling, with barely a shot left without eye-popping color or complex lighting tricks. His flourishes may make it obtuse at times, but imagine how forgettable this would be were it straight-forward.

The performances are similarly top tier with both Katrine Greis-Rosenthal and Nikolaj Coster-Waldau bringing their all. It is in the narrative construction and the editing that I feel the piece ends up falling apart. With more than a month of distance from it I can not even begin to explain why exactly but I do know it still feels grating to me.

Adoption is a curious work of loneliness, centering on women caught in relationships that do not fulfill them. These women have their lives limited by the world of men, whether through uncaring parents with demands about marriage or facing accusations of being a whore. Adoption is a film of life's mundanity, with plenty of close-ups of hands working in manual jobs. This is cinema of the working…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Márta Mészáros has always objected to being referred to as a "feminist filmmaker." In her view, she's simply a director who happens to be a woman, a reality which affects the world her camera sees, and the stories she chooses to tell. And, always, those stories are about women who refuse to conform. Whether they're rebellious teens or adults taking a stand (both are central to the film under consideration here), Mészáros' lead characters are fiercely their own, refusing to sacrifice any of who they are or what they believe for an easier life, or to win the approval of those around them.

reviews.author: J
reviews.text: the hum of machinery. pieces of wood turned over and polished repeatedly on its belts. middle aged women with bandana’s over their heads. dust is inhaled, dispersed; it clung to their clothes. a woman’s work*; humdrum, routine work. Kata is in the midst of it all. but she’s also isolated from the “ordinary woman”, not only in distance or address, she’s also without a child or a husband. tethered to the ground of her emptiness, surrounded by the illusionary void made up by the patriarchy, the thought of motherhood is believed to be an existential panacea / a validation of womanhood. so when Kata meets a troubled teenage girl, Anna, from a boarding school, she wants to be Anna's carer…

They travel the countryside through poor villages meeting people of various cultures and economic background. The dialogue can be crude & offensive but I would be lying if I said I didn’t laugh a lot. The fact that a lot of these stereotypes are still around highlights how…

I was strongly reminded about both Mizoguchi film Sansho the Bailiff and Mika Waltari's epic and great novel "The Egyptian".…

reviews.text: devoting time to preserving someone’s memory — not the memory of them, but within them. loss, even when processed internally, can feel very selfish. our grief is limited to the memories we hold, or at least it seems that way. what kogonada achieved with after yang is so precious, because it reaches beyond our own limitations. i think loss feels so endless because it’s that separation of putting your own pieces together when what you really want is so much more. you grieve for your own loss, you grieve for the memories that were stopped mid sentence, you grieve for the people that you never met but lost something too, you grieve for everything that hadn’t happened yet. i think that’s why we can feel loss over someone we didn’t know. the knowing of everything that was left in them. and would it be intrusive to extract all that was left? maybe. and maybe it’s just the beginning.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: What renders this film so much of its effortless moments of beauty is exactly how practical it is, such a simple, straightforward formal construction, a narrative so fulfilling with its intelligent simplicity and rhythmic blooming of events. The drama isn't strained, but smoothly delivered through sophisticated dramaturgy, things happen within a cohesive structure of naturalism that is easily modulated in current arthouse cinema but hardly rendered this effective. The private bruises are healed through public well being, we are never alone, there is so much beauty everywhere. A lesson for life.

reviews.author: Christina
reviews.text: I’ve watched numerous onscreen interpretations of the Tudor period-with its tales of sex, murder and intrigue, no wonder it’s one of the most popular periods of English history to explore. Consequently, that means it becomes harder for films to have fresh or interesting takes on the historical record. Anne of the Thousand Days is hardly revolutionary in its retelling of Anne Boleyn’s ascension to (and fall from) the throne, but the action moves along steadily enough and the sets and costumes are pleasingly lavish. The main attraction here is Genevieve Bujold’s Oscar-nominated performance as Anne: sharp-tongued, intelligent, and fully determined to be her own woman. Watching her defy Henry openly and make her own political machinations, you think “Elizabeth is definitely her mother’s child.”

reviews.author: Gabe Klinger
reviews.text: Stunning present-day 35mm and 65mm (!) images of the phantom mining hub of the title, inactive since the Great Depression. Long hypnotic takes of desolate landscapes are interspersed with shots from a microfilm viewer lens showing various documents -- newspaper reports, land surveys -- related to Anyox and its miners' labor activities. Reminisces from South Slavic immigrant miner and striker Marko P. Hećimović -- who had been emboldened by organizers in Chicago's Slavic community and was oppressed by the Canadian government for his allegiance to labor movements -- are heard in voiceover (read by Zoran Konjević, presumably an actor). reviews.text: the first feature-length from British Columbia’s finest landscape-slash-labour documentarian duo does not disappoint. Anyox tells the story of a suppressed labor strike at a mine in the titular “company town” in northern BC during the early 20th century, through a combination of voice-overs and archival documents. the visual backdrop for most of the film consists of stunning 65mm landscape cinematography shot on location in present-day Anyox (the town now has what appears to be 2 inhabitants, an old couple who lead a solitary life of silent, dignified work). while the “ambient” approach taken—long shots of nature, vast stretches of time vibing to the thrum of a microfiche machine as it scrolls through an archive—is quite immersive and effective, i couldn’t help but…

reviews.author: Julian Doove
reviews.text: The stunning large format photography beautifully conveys the atmospheric environment of a once bustling mining town. It’s both sad and beautiful to see how the remnants of men’s concentrated actions can leave such a clear afterimage just lingering in the air. Places like this become haunted—or scarred, rather. The historic sequences adequately contextualizes the location and its now slightly apocalyptic air with gorgeous blueprints, newspaper clippings and archival documentation about the location itself and specifics on the working conditions during the active period of the mine, and the environmental impact that it had. Lots of respect to the brutalist stubbornness of using the mostly illegible archival documentation sequences! I love choices like that, where confidence in ones intention completely tramples logic.

reviews.text: I've yet to really understand the label that Feng Xiaogang has acquired as "China's Spielberg", the two have little in common outside, I guess, the financial success fo their movies. But here at least Feng is quite obviously imitating Saving Private Ryan, and so it kind of makes sense. The first half is a war movie, largely one long battle as a depleted PLA company holds out against thousands of approaching Nationalists. The camera shakes a lot, there's blood and dirt and snow flying everywhere, standard post-SPR stuff. The second half though is something different: the lone survivor of the battle, the Captain played by Zhang Hanyu, is discovered sometime after the Civil War in a POW hospital, mistaken for…

reviews.author: Andrew Stasiulis
reviews.text: In the early 2000’s, it was all the rage in national cinemas to produce home grown answers to Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan. Following in the muddy, bloody boot prints of Russia’s The Star and South Korea’s Tae Guk Gi, The People’s Republic of China offered their own resurrection of past military spirit with Assembly. While a lot of these movies simply attempt to recreate the new standard in the aesthetics of combat set by Spielberg’s wildly successful campaign, Assembly is much more interesting than mere shaky, high shutter speed, handheld images of battlefield carnage.

reviews.text: This must have seemed like a major Oscar-contender, taking a well-regarded novel and crafting a three-hour epic on faith and fanaticism, filmed on glorious Amazonian locations, with a then hot cast and a previously lauded director. Alas, this is a slog to sit through, with only occasional stirring moments. The actors seem uncomfortable in their roles - Kathy Bates, so often wonderful, is almost unbearably shrill, hamming to the rafters - and only Lithgow, always good value when portraying self-righteous assholes, retains some dignity. There is beauty in Zbigniew Preisner’s score, and there are some striking aerial shots of the rainforest.

reviews.text: In the New Zealand of 1941, impoverished farmer Stanley Graham went on a killing spree that became one of the darkest chapters in the history of the country. Bad Blood is a shocking, bloody, relatively faithful and matter of fact dramatisation of those events, originally made for British television, directed by Mike Newell and starring Jack Thompson in one of his finest roles.

reviews.author: jrhovind
reviews.text: One New Zealand farmer’s boozy, violent crack-up during the Second World War rendered as a slow-burn study of paranoia and resentment. Amid the war-time deprivations and austerities, and his world crashing down on him thanks to economic depression, Graham’s sense of loss feels total, his grievances so vast and insurmountable, already before the authorities come asking for his rifle to aid the war effort. “Oh, I know what goes on behind my back!” And once his spleen erupts in a series of shocking acts of violence, the film never tries to either sensationalize or condemn his actions, but rather simply tries to imagine what it’s like to inhabit this particular kind of headspace in this particular time and place. A climactic couple of casually cruel gestures suggest his world was already eager to forget people like him, long before he decided the entire world was his enemy.

reviews.text: Radu Jude’s latest is a playful yet biting piece of social satire. It’s a film that grapples with the mess of hypocrisies and contradictory morals of contemporary culture, with Jude exploring this in a wonderfully absurd but incredibly thoughtful manner. It’s definitely a strange endeavor with all of its many meta, unhinged moments but it’s undoubtedly unlike anything out there. Plus, that ending might take the crown for the most bonkers ending of the entire year.

The filmmakers have fun with this and arguably it only proves many of the points I believe this film is making, but it feels like why even bother on Hulu’s behalf. As a society we are so quick to label a select few things immoral or degenerate, while giving the pass to all the actual immorality thrusted upon us on a daily basis by degenerates. reviews.text: "Between Two Worlds" is quite a ruminating examination of the thin line between exploitation and exposé. The method of immersive reportage laid bare, where the writer conceals herself within fictitious identities in exchange for factual figures, real life stories. But personal involvement often complicates the situation. In soaking herself up with other people's experiences, even forming intimate relationships with them, her non-consensual use of their lives is navigated by the film as it unhurriedly hangs the dirty and stained laundries of the cleaning industry. These workers, with their calloused hands and aching backs, paid by the hour without any benefit, without any compensation, the impermanence of their jobs, the series of job-hops, emphasise the prevalent and persistent disregard and abuse…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Justin Chon’s overcranked but achingly heartfelt “Blue Bayou” is a case-study in how issue-driven melodramas are a double-edged sword. If done well, these tear-jerkers can emotionally galvanize audiences into grappling with the sort of social injustice that people tend to cry over in the dark of a theater and then leave behind when they re-emerge into the light of day. If done poorly, they risk glazing an urgent problem with a gloss of untruth, and making an all-too-real tragedy from our own backyard feel like the kind of thing that only happens in the movies. An eye-opening sob-fest that eventually loses sight of its everyday tragedy behind a thick veil of tears, “Blue Bayou” is such an uncommonly lucid example…

reviews.author: Brian Formo
reviews.text: There is no denying that the final 2-3 minutes of Blue Bayou are heartbreaking. The stills at the end of the film, however, make me wish it was a documentary instead. What could've been an effective movie about an adoption loophole law written in the year 2000, which has opened up deportations of individuals who've lived in the US for decades, is instead an over-plotted drama. Each new "everything falls apart" moment stacked on top of each other dulls the narrative overall until basically the only part that works is the epilogue of stats and faces. It's information that people need to know, and if it's effective for people in that way, great. As a movie, however, it moves from quiet introspection to a grab bag of trauma. And, unfortunately, 10 different items are pulled from that bag when two or three would've been more effective and still achieved the same message but allowed more character space.

reviews.text: “Boy Erased” is neither the first, nor the best, of this year’s films about the crucible of gay conversion therapy, but Joel Edgerton’s adaptation of Garrard Conley’s memoir is most interesting for the ways that it differs from “The Miseducation of Cameron Post.” Although it’s fortunate we have both, and tragic that we need either, “The Miseducation of Cameron Post” leveraged the awful and dehumanizing evangelical practice into a coming-of-age saga about a teenage girl’s hard-won self-acceptance; “Boy Erased” uses a similar premise to deflect that burden outward — to put the onus for change and understanding on the misguided people who surround its traumatized young protagonist.

reviews.author: Four Winds Movie Reviews
reviews.text: A father travels from Georgia to the United States to find himself caught in the throes of his son's invariable and impetuous gambling addiction. Finding a temporary community during his visit, we experience an up close and personal look at the immigrant experience through community, sacrifice, and the unwavering stoical reserve and forbearance of unconditional love. Evoking a keen self-awareness through depicting hardships and unorthodox allegiances placated by common struggles, Levan Koguashvili blends incongruous humor into this slice-of-life drama that gains its rhythm and finds empathy where there is traditionally conflict and animosity. This was Georgian's entry for best international feature at the 2021 Oscars. An exceptional work from the far reaches of Georgia using mostly non-actors that made for quite an impressionable film.

reviews.text: This movie projects so much British nationalism into Ancient Rome it might as well be called Churchill and Cleopatra. Not only does Shaw's dialogue feel like poor Shakespeare emulation, but he even put an ancient British denizen, a druid with a Victorian attitude, in the story and made him nearly as sophisticated as Julius Caesar, himself ludicrously modern in his value system. I'm not knocking the film for being inaccurate, historical films always are. However the changes here all feel like propaganda in nature, and never in service of a good story. The Romans, as English historical stand ins, are portrayed as the unquestionably superior culture. Julius Caesar and his advisors are constantly bemused or shocked at Egypt's quaint ways.…

reviews.text: "Candy Mountain" is a 1987 drama directed by Robert Frank and Rudy Wurlitzer. A presented road movie that hinges on the energetic mythos of rock and roll, the film follows a down and out personality of Julius as he goes on a patronage to find a legendary guitar craftsman named Elmore Silk. Leaving the hustle and bustle of New York City behind, Julius volunteers to find Silk at the bequest of a rock star whom Julius tells a lie that he has known him previously. Thinking that journey might hold some difficulty but having nothing else to lose, Julius surprisingly finds himself lost and wandering within Canada. The only thing he has to go on is incremental selections of information…

reviews.text: despite a god tier, eclectic, cast this is rather conservative in structure and story, much less freewheeling and antagonistic than Two Lane Blacktop or Walker (both also written by Wurlitzer) but, like those, is still a potent time capsule of a singularly weird time in American culture — tbh, probably plays best when stoned

reviews.author: orson houellebecq
reviews.text: Low-key sort of revelatory. Borderline so-hip-it-hurts (just look at that cast!) but gets right at that vulnerable beating heart of dorkiness lying just beneath the surface of every hipster pose. In a sense the perfect missing link between Local Hero and Hal Hartley. It's easy to forget, but probably shouldn't be overlooked, that this was co-directed by two guys old enough to have been a part of the original Beat Generation, despite feeling unmistakably like the product of the post-Jarmusch, pre-Tarantino '80s indie film scene. Kind of makes me want to move to Nova Scotia?

reviews.text: A meandering, cheerfully morose road movie exploring the pleasures and virtues of going nowhere much at all. With legendary photographer Frank as co-director, the mood is more Beat-era hangover than post-Jarmusch hipsterdom; not seeking a pose of resistance within consumer capitalism, but an actual escape route from it. Book’s search for Silk’s legendary guitar maker ends up a nearly Beckettian kind of breakdown; vehicles that keep on stalling out, cars traded and lost and given away, perpetual motion even in the eventual absence of all the usual ways of getting from one place to another. “Don’t take it so hard. Life ain’t no candy mountain, you know?” So many eccentrics met along the way, many of them trapped in their…

reviews.text: Radu Jude is always interesting. This short takes 19th century Lithographs and is built on the premise that the suggestion of movement in them integrated Eisenstein. They are then presented one after another, with nothing else, as a kind of filmic flip book to engage with this idea of potential movement in the still image.

reviews.author: Christof
reviews.text: Can we even consider this a short film in its own right? After all, more than half of it is just a series of pre-existing caricatures without any additional context or commentary. It really only starts to get interesting when Radu Jude adds something of his own to it. And only in the final minute did he finally succeed at making me laugh.

reviews.author: Edwin Davies
reviews.text: A fun formalist experiment inspired by Sergei Eisenstein in which French lithographs from the 19th century are presented to the audience first without context, then with their original captions, and finally presented as memetic reactions to a contemporary news story. Each repetition reveals new meaning for the images, and ultimately serves as a funny and instructive account of how our understanding of an image can be so easily changed by the context around it.

reviews.author: Corwyn
reviews.text: Almost remarkably bland and substanceless. It opens with a brief intro talking about the lithographs, and for what feels like much longer than it possibly could have, simply presents a flat, silent slideshow of many many still images. After awhile, it adds voiceover to a few, imagining what the characters might be saying - this provides little to nothing in the way of entertainment or intellectual value. Then, he presents a headline about Gwyneth Paltrow's vagina-scented candles exploding, and repeats this headline a few times, using the lithographs as reaction images. This final minute is at least moderately amusing, but despite the contrast between old-timey lithographs and wacky modern headline, there's really nothing there of substance.

reviews.author: Jeremy Herbert
reviews.text: Look, am I saying the George Carlin that made punchlines out of disgusted wails at weirdly named food is a greater artist than the one who railed against The Forever War like a loon on the street years before the first shot was even fired? Not necessarily. But I am saying I know which George makes me laugh harder. Pretty obviously loses his groove in the middle of this before finding his way back into the dog bits, which is more curious than destructive. Given how adamant he is that farts aren't allowed on TV, this special must've been recorded at the last cultural moment before gross-out comedy became an eternally viable subgenre. They should've cut out the few close-ups on giddy audience members to maintain the illusion that Carlin was playing for the approval of a void.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Located somewhere between a classic opera, a modern dance piece, and a deadly fever dream — between the timeless beauty of ancient myth and the modern nightmare of America’s current immigration policies — Benjamin Millepied’s “Carmen” is stretched across a few too many borders to ever feel like it’s standing on solid ground. And yet, it’s undeniably exhilarating to watch one of the world’s most accomplished choreographers team up with one of its most virtuosic composers (Nicolas Britell) for the kind of aggressively unclassifiable movie that would never exist if not for these two artists reaching beyond their disciplines to create it themselves.

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: CARMEN is a singular & hypnotic vision from Benjamin Millepied. Nicholas Britell’s grand operatic score is a jaw-dropping stunner. The angelic & overpowering soundscape functions as a third character alongside Melissa Barrera & Paul Mescal in this bold & mystifying experimental musical. Could’ve used a more fleshed-out screenplay but this was not at all what I was expecting.

reviews.text: "Cash Cow" is a 2023 film directed by Matt Barats. Starring Barats just the same, the film follows his time experienced during the 2020 pandemic. Thinking that he has hit a big score by starring in a Domino's pizza commercial, life comes to a complete stop with Covid-19. Now questioning if his commercial will even air, he wanders off into the wilderness and randomly starts venturing onto the trail of Mormonism from a historical standpoint. He does all this by living in the elements with his microphone and his blue tent.

reviews.author: Ella Kemp
reviews.text: Cooper Raiff has this rare quality when it comes to making movies about young people figuring themselves out in that he’s so thoughtful and generous about other people across all periods of life. Coming-of-agers (at any age) are so often selfish to the point of excruciating obsession but Cooper looks out for little brothers and old friends and party guests and new loves and his mum, oh how he loves his mum. He’s a party starter! A people pleaser! An impossibly kind and big-hearted filmmaker and human who listens to others and tells them exactly how he feels (how dare he!) while also stubbornly continuing to make movies like this, so sincere, so unprovocative, when everybody else rolls their eyes and tells you it’s all too much. Maybe it is, but sometimes I think that’s vital. I loved it!

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: Set during the interwar period in the Netherlands, Karakter is the story of an ambitious young man trying to make his way through life whilst breaking out of the shadow of his father. The premise itself isn't novel but it's interesting enough, and the film has strong production values but suffers from a melodramatic tone, certain theatricality, a justified but excessive use of voice-over. Mike van Diem also tries to cover so many episodes about the life of the protagonist that he doesn't give the viewer enough time to get involved or even interested. The end result is a visually appealing but frankly heavy, dull and a bit sappy work that resembles more a run-of-the-mill Hollywood production than a film with a personality of its own.

reviews.author: Cinemonster
reviews.text: This film from Dutch director Mike van Diem is simply one of the best of the ‘90s. Set in The Netherlands in the ‘20s, it follows the life of Jacob Willem Katadreuffe prior to his arrest for the murder of Dreverhaven, a bailiff who had antagonized him as he clawed his way up from destitution as a young lawyer. We learn that Dreverhaven is Jacob’s pops, and we endure the contentious and miserable relationship between the two that led us here. Jacob’s mother is on the hook here too, as the illegitimacy of the pregnancy (and implied sexual assault) impacts her interactions with her son. Lead performances are outstanding and design and photography are sumptuous.

reviews.author: ‮وسيم‬
reviews.text: One of Masri’s most sensitive and powerful works I’ve seen so far. Granted, her subjects in this film are so uniquely precocious and multi-dimensional; the children articulate their fantasies, their dreams, their and their family’s histories and hardships with a really heartbreaking maturity and wistfulness. But I still believe this stands out in her oeuvre (and much of the catalogue of this Palestine/Lebanon war genre) as a film that translates the glimmering humanity of the downtrodden in a way that I really can’t describe. The children are hopeful, their parents are enterprising and patient, there is an elusive but also intensely omnipresent Palestine that finds them all in communion. Beautiful film ❤️❤️

reviews.text: TWO ORIGINAL ENDINGS. When "Chilly Scenes of Winter" was eleased in 1979 it had an upbeat ending. When the response was lackluster, the film was recut and retitled "Head over Heels" with a downbeat ending--more in sync with the ending of Anne Beattie's novel. Criterion has now released both. The Chilly Scenes upbeat ending and Head over Heels with the downbeat Beattie ending. So which is it? Two films, two titles, two endings? Or one film, two titles, one ending?

reviews.text: My preferred version of (500) Days of Summer: a completely scathing indictment of the way that men perceive themselves in seemingly romantic stories and ultimately how it damages the women in their own worlds. But it's interesting to see how this movie starts off feeling like it could turn itself into another ordinary romantic comedy, and that layer slowly comes undone minute by minute as John Heard's Charles first shows himself as a shy young man slowly turning into a sociopathic stalker. Ultimately, it's the fact that he manages to sell you in on him being a completely pathetic loser that makes Chilly Scenes of Winter work so brilliantly.

reviews.text: Documentary about a man who was in charge of one of the greatest comic book runs in comics history ,that lasted almost 17 years. The way Claremont talks about these characters and people he worked with on their stories is so heartwarming. X-men as we know them today would not exists without Claremont and his dedication to make those characters as real as possible and to focus on their personal struggles and drama more than just big action and adventures. It's awful that he had to leave the series the way he did ,but he will be remembered as someone who made X-men the highest selling title at Mavrel for a good while and defined those characters and comics for many future generations.

reviews.author: Dominic Griffin
reviews.text: A much better documentary than I expected, tbh. Sure, there’s some John Byrne erasure but that’s fine. Really highlights a lot about the double edged sword of corporate comics and some of the psychology behind the intricacies of long form serialized storytelling.

reviews.author: Deaner50
reviews.text: This is a another review on the run. Happy Canadian Easter! Chris Claremont defined the X men for a entire generation. He didn't create them but the characters that people know are his creation. He took over the comic when it almost was canceled. Stan Lee wasn't writing for it anymore. He created iconic story lines like the Days of Future Past and The Phoenix Saga. He helped define characters like Wolverine and Storm. I read his run in the 80's. It was excellent. He worked on it for about 15 years. This documentary is pretty interesting and has some creative touches like having cosplayers standing in as the characters inbetween the talking heads. If you find comic history interesting or the X men then this is for you.

reviews.author: Jay
reviews.text: Aside from the Justice League, the X men are some of my favorite superhero teams. It is great hearing about how the classic runs of X men by Chris Claremont had so much thought out into them. Writing characters in ways that made people able to either identify with the characters or analyzing the content of the stories. I wish his name was as known as Stan Lee’s. Claremont paved the way for more writers to have dense and complex stories in their comics. Comics that will challenge audiences expectations on what to expect from superhero stories. I have been reading a lot of the recent X men stories since they remind me so much of what the Claremont era did for the X men. Timeless stories that will continue to inspire writers for years to come.

reviews.text: I'm not really sure how this even came about-- did Claremont's mom commission it?-- but it's a pretty informative run-down of his 17 years piloting the X-Men (and later New Mutants) and how, under his aegis, they went from being the cancelled red-headed stepchild of Lee and Kirby's Silver Age output, to being Marvel's bestselling signature franchise. Since I was reading the title all along, I didn't learn too much new, but it's a good primer if you're not up on your X-history. Welcome input from Jim Shooter, Len Wein, Ann Nocenti and especially Weezie Simonson who I always find delightful. Not surprisingly, John Byrne does not appear in this. Most likely when he heard it was being made he became outraged "That hack Claremont? Everyone knows I'M the reason X-Men became huge! It was ME ME ME!!!"

reviews.author: Scott Rice
reviews.text: Even though this Aldo Lado film wasn't released until 1992, it easily has the same feel as a classic Giallo from the 60s or 70s. A police detective and his partner, with whom he has become romantically involved, begin investigating the murder of his ex-wife who was gunned down by a group of unknown assailants. Though initially her death is chalked up to the mafia case the detective is investigating, the clues soon lead to a deserted house, a mummified head, a psychotic countess, and all the smooth jazz you could ever want from a motion picture soundtrack. Though not as nuanced as Lado's previous efforts, Short Night of Glass Dolls and Who Saw Her Die, it's still nice to see that he could still put out effective thrillers even as the genre itself seemed to be overtaken by the American slasher.

reviews.text: Clara Sola is an incredibly understanding and strangely beautiful film. The lead character of Clara clearly has an intellectual disability, and her mother has kept her repressed for many years, unable to truly explore herself or her world. Clara is also a faith healer, and an element of mysticism underlies the entire film. Clara Sola is about Clara's sexual awakening, and through that she is able to begin to heal herself. She finds it hard to understand her desires and feelings, but she acts on them with a combination of sincerity and self-interest. Wendy Chinchilla Araya gives an incredible central performance, derived from physicality and uncertainty, which is one of the year's finest feats of acting. The film emphasises nature…

reviews.author: Jeff Light
reviews.text: This is a documentary included for the big DVD restoration of the 1963 epic "Cleopatra", but it's really a fascinating story in its own right. What at first blush looks like a Making-Of extra turns out to be a chronicle of the time when the Hollywood studio system was failing and producers were flailing, trying to find any way to save flagging studios that struggled to compete with TV. In the case of Cleopatra, the solution was "Go bigger! Make it a massive production, a can't-miss, star-studded event!" Hmm.... sound familiar? You can watch this on its own here.

reviews.author: 8BeanSoup
reviews.text: Cleopatra: The Film That Changed Hollywood is a documentary that came with the DVD of Cleopatra (1963). It's an interesting look at a production that got out of control. If you've never heard of the sunk-cost fallacy/phenomenon, the making of Cleopatra is a good example of that idea. Twentieth Century-Fox got so involved in the making of the film—spending so much money—that they couldn't stop, even when all good sense said they should. Too much money and too many egos were involved.

From choosing to recreate Rome and Egypt on the backlot at Pinewood Studios, where the weather is decidedly un-Mediterranean, and immediately incurring the wrath of the hairdressers, to the constant ill health of the star which lead to her nearly dying, holding up production, losing her co-stars because of the delays, abandoning England for Italy, and starting again, a script that was being written as the film went along, and a studio that was near bankruptcy.

And when you do see it yourself you think omg this film has so much potential. It was interesting to hear the background. The onset drama with Elizabeth, as she almost died and her somewhat iconic affair with Richard Burton became one of the world's most publicised and sensational love affairs and news stories. And like the grandness of the film is often discussed. I will rewatch the film sometime soon so there…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Attaining the status of being both touching and humorous, Closely Watched Trains is one of the pinnacles of the Czech New Wave film movement. It's the minor moments within a variety of scenes that director Jiří Menzel employs to deliver some profound meaning in this coming-of-age tale based on Bohumil Hrabal’s novel about an apprentice railway signalman working at a station, with a strange collection of co-workers, in German-occupied Czechoslovakia during WWII.

Ostre Sledované Vlaky puts a new standard in adolescent awkwardness in the most inappropriate chaotic setting, among drastic decisions and subtle and sexy hilarity. A unique project.

She got a little beat up herself in the bargain, but her eyes are all intense determination, with a little bit of fear mixed in. This kind of attention to character detail is miles ahead of what usually goes into an exploitation action-revenge joint, even the great ones, and to the extent that this works it works in large part thanks to the face in question, belonging to one of the truly great film stars of her own or any other era.

There's no need for it; the focus is on the strangeness, mostly supplied by Tom Waits (who made me laugh quite a bit). However, one aspect of his career that remains a truism, throughout this, is that there is not a soft-rock song that he does not love. This glib attention to musical detail does not really impact most of his films, apart from Coming Home, where Ashby barely lets the drama get five minutes before cranking up The Beatles, The Stones, Jefferson Airplane, Simon & Garfunkel, Buffalo Springfield et al. reviews.author: Maria
reviews.text: Such a moving documentary. One where people aren't just talking heads, but rather storytellers and keepers of memory & history, sharing the memory of their loved ones who died of AIDS-related illnesses. The film weaves their stories with the AIDS Memorial Quilt project beautifully, constantly reminding the viewers how many more stories, how many more people, how many more tragedies there are. And the quilt itself is one of the most stunning pieces of community folk art and manifestations of shared grief.

This is a whirlwind of murder and Giallo tropes occurring during a busy day at a TV studio where a ton of variety shows and dramas are being filmed. People get shot, stuffed in film closets, hidden in scenery, steam cleaned, encased in carbonite, impaled, axed, waxed, and left in stacks... This has a dwarf, some clowns, and a camel. But I felt the most disorienting aspect was the "borrowed" soundtrack to Fulci's City of the Living Dead; I kept waiting for Italian Shelly Duvall to start horking up her internal organs at any second.

Many great chases and deaths (even though it's for television) with a lovably silly conclusion which we've come to expect, my 2.5 is merely how I feel when it all settles. It's really something to seek out, and at 60 minutes it'll fly by. Also it's Aldo Lado so obviously it's shot nice.

reviews.author: Georg Frank
reviews.text: Ursprünglich als Mehrteiler mit sehr kurzen Folgen konzipierter TV-Giallo, der mit extrem vielen wechselnden Protagonisten (schließlich wird, wohl aufgrund der kurzen Folgen, gefühlt alle paar Minuten eine ermittelnde Person umgebracht) und überraschenden Wendungen auftrumpfen kann. Der Clou ist, dass die Handlung im RAI-Gebäude spielt und stetig irgendwelche TV-Szenen auftauchen, die wir dann in der Gegenperspektive sehen (z.B. ein Auftritt der Kessler-Zwillinge). So ergibt sich eine Hetzjagd durchs Ganze Gebäude und in gefühlt jede Abteilung. Da verzeiht man die absurde und an den Haaren herbeigezogene Begründung und Auflösung.Keine Ahnung wie die Serien-Fassung war (angeblich gab es mehr Morde, aber mit Logikfehlern, so dass man diese Gründe Filmfassung entfernte) - der Zusammenschnitt (bei YouTube zu finden z.B. im Kanal GialloRealm) ist wirklich flott und atmosphärisch, wenn auch durch die stetigen Wechsel der Protagonisten etwas holprig - aber echt entdeckenswert.

reviews.author: Hill Wigga
reviews.text: An undiscovered treat for any giallo fan: an hour-long TV movie packs in kill set pieces, wall to wall Fabio Frizzi music, and nipples galore in a sort of semi reality behind the scenes whodunnit on a tv set A precursor to 1987 fare like Stagefright Aquarius or Delirium: Photos Of Gioia.

reviews.text: Crime Story is an unbalance blend of the standard Jackie Chan flick with the style of a John Woo/Chow Yun-Fat collaboration. I give director Kirk Wong credit for mixing it up a bit, but Chan’s never been known for ultra-violent squib work, which is sorely missed in Crime Story’s shootouts, of which there are many. Still, there’s some great action beats sprinkled throughout and Chan is able to sneak a couple moments of comedy into an otherwise dour and supremely serious script. The finale contains some truly insane explosions too, probably the biggest and most dangerous in Chan’s career, which is saying something.

She serves as a sober outside to the intersubjective aura of desire and youthful vigor into which Colin, Angela, and Lane fall. Confronted with capital-D Death, the others' ego struggles seem especially feeble and foolish. In addition, Christina's refusal to exit the story shifts emphasis toward (and lends a more sinister edge to) Lane's primal betrayal of her. It's like watching Lane's narcissistic vision of herself crumble from external pressure.

reviews.author: Wes
reviews.text: I think my main takeaway from looking into Aotearoa's late-20th century cinema so far is just how petrified we were about what America is doing to us. I don't think that fear's been resolved, but at some point we stopped articulating it. Here we've got an erotic thriller with an almost unguessable American lead; sexually voracious in a way which reminded me of the empty sensuality of Johansson's character in Under the Skin. She's the snake in our national Eden, and everyone drawn into her orbit is wrenched out of virginal Kiwi androgyneity into new knowledge of themselves as existing within interplays of gender and sexuality which had been invisible to them before. All the time though that's suspended in the laconic distance of the tourists' cameras; the surface of the place apprehended in flat pastoral tones which only barely suggest the geothermal motions of lust and performance roiling beneath.

reviews.text: An obscure revisionist western from the early 70s that's quite bleak but also not as downbeat and brutal as I was lead to believe. It's got a gritty and realistic mood to it, but even with the violence that's happening it feels closer to something like 'The Hired Hand' than it does to the more violent and shocking 70s westerns like 'Soldier Blue' or 'The Hunting Party'. It's still a good one, but I was hoping and expecting for the (rape &) revenge part to be more of the main focus of the movie. Harry Dean Stanton really shines in his supporting role, and as Quentin Tarantino points out in the Video Archives podcast, this might be the first real Harry Dean Stanton performance in any movie.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: It’s no Gun Crazy or The Big Combo, but any genre film directed by Joseph H. Lewis is worth checking out. As several critics and film noir aficionados have pointed out, this crime drama basically reimagines Les Misérables, adding an obvious gay subtext to its policeman’s (Barry Sullivan) obsessive pursuit of an escaped criminal (Vittorio Gassman). Also of note is its critique of its own genre’s investment in hardboiled masculinity; all that posturing is a projection that masks the male characters’ underlying anxieties.

Also, this movie has serious issues with Meatloaf. I love meatloaf!

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: A lieutenant in charge of a prison's maximum security section pursues an escaped convict from the section into the Louisiana swamps. Before that there was a fistfight in his cell between them after which the two men shared a cigarette indicating either a gay subtext or a mutual admiration in a kind of subtext of prison reform and second chances. I think the second subtext is probably what the film was going for although they both seem to be pursuing each other, too. With Barry Sullivan as the lieutenant married to his adoring wife played by Polly Bergen who has a pitcher of Martinis in the fridge and Vittorio Gassman reconnecting with his Cajun roots and wife played by Mary Zavian passionately making out in their sweaty shack on the Bayou the real star is snidely William Conrad as next in line for Sullivan's job.

reviews.text: Not a movie without its interesting elements, redeeming qualities, but for all that's attempted here, none completely worked for me. We get a 2 hour and 20 minute, Lawrence of Arabia influenced biopic of General George Armstrong Custer (Robert Shaw), beginning with the end of the Civil War, through the Battle of the Little Bighorn, while trying to deal with race, and this somewhat contradictory character at its center.

Definitely a time for a resurgence I think?This has all the attributes of a sixties Western, but without most of the charm. It's a rather dodgy biopic that tries desperately hard to make a controversial figure less of an enigma. General George Armstrong Custer finished bottom of his class at West Point and without the outbreak of the…

reviews.author: C.A. DeStefanis
reviews.text: I think George Armstrong Custer is one of the more interesting figures in US history - an arrogant glory boy who ultimately bit off more than he could chew and paid the ultimate price in fairly spectacular fashion. You would think that alone would be a pretty strong basis for a historically accurate western, yet we have this highly fictionalized feature that does zero justice to the actual story. Custer Of The West is an awful film, aside from some nifty camera shots of calvary charges there is literally nothing here. Plus, the film seems to be trying to re-contextualize Custer in a way to make him more sympathetic of the Indian's plight and less culpable for the disaster of…

reviews.author: Luscious Johnny V
reviews.text: Chronologically and ideologically situated halfway between Cheyenne Autumn and Little Big Man, this is every bit as schizophrenic as you might expect a Custer biopic made at the height of the Vietnam era to be and then some, with Custer and Phil Sheridan denouncing Washington's venal, duplicitous, and racist Indian policies in one breath, and expounding on the need to exterminate the brutes in the next. At least it gives Lawrence Tierney's Brooklyn-gorilla rendition of Sheridan a chance to walk back his too-often-repeated "only good Indian is a dead Indian" line. Much appreciated.

reviews.author: jack
reviews.text: I hate to use the word “bloated” when describing cinema because I feel it often discredits what the filmmakers were trying to convey. The idea that something is bloated may be accurate, but the term feels a bit disingenuous and malicious towards the filmmaker. Yet with Custer of the West, I cannot find a better word to describe this film than that word. It’s evident that there’s a conflict of interest between Siodmak, whose style can easily be described as interrogative and intense, but also experimental and honest. While the film seems to beat in a similar fashion to what Siodmak was fascinated with, the film seems to evolve beyond his comprehension. Robert Shaw, one of the great actors, took…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Rigid gender norms push those of us who don't fit into them. Often that push is small, a nudge here or there, a little rebellion. Wearing pants to this, earrings to that, makeup here, not cooking this, not doing that job, not taking that shit. Sometimes, it's a bigger push, and those of us far outside the rigid norms suffer for it. Depression and anxiety and the trauma of the closet can take hold. Some of us break free to varying degrees. Dandy Dust is actually transgressive. A clique of creative European perverts got together and figured out how to assault the senses through as many mediums as possible on a prop budget of around 50 dollars: claymation, stop-motion miniatures, crude video editor effects, bursts of cacaphonous industrial noise. But all this obnoxiousness delivers a joyous message: join us and shed your shame, your self-awareness, your insistence on logic…

reviews.text: A little danish treat. Stylistically it borrows some from the likes of Pusher and Drive, as it blends the gritty, criminal underworld of Copenhagen with social commentary, a cool synthesized score, and good looking visuals with saturated colors and neon lights. It's a pretty brutal, tense and entertaining albeit clichéd revenge tale that also contains its own touching little moments, and somewhat patiently builds characters and relationships. The opening scene throws you right into the criminal world in a shot or two, and the last 30 minutes are preeeetty darn tense. It has some credibility issues and never really reaches the same level of quality as its influences, but fuck that; it's really enjoyable, so if you get the chance, you should definitely check it out.

reviews.text: Even in an era when rock shows were all about orgiastic excess, former Talking Heads frontman David Byrne made a warm and inviting spectacle out of his own smallness. The signature image from Jonathan Demme’s totemic concert documentary “Stop Making Sense” finds Byrne getting lost inside his own comically large silver business suit; maybe it was a Kabuki-like expression of a man being swallowed alive by runaway capitalism, or maybe — as Byrne maintains — he just wanted to make it look like his head had shrunken down to a funny size.

reviews.text: No one gets it like David Byrne gets it, an artist who somehow translates alienation and disenfranchisement into positivity, decency, inclusion, and shameless dancing. A genuinely inspiring person with more good songs than just about anyone who started after 1975. I felt my heart pause and grow a little when "Slippery People" started. Spike Lee does a lot that Jonathan Demme didn't do in STOP MAKING SENSE—overhead cinematography, pitiless closeups on faces and feet, an acknowledgement of the audience. It's with purpose—it's not a surrealist exercise, it's a communal jubilee. What a bookend.

reviews.author: Dylan van Frankfoort
reviews.text: "Horror" not only being an intense feeling of fear, but also of disgust (according to Oxford Languages), this is undoubtedly one of the most horrific movies I've ever seen, Bassett using the flooded trenches of WWI to create a Poltergeist (1982) nightmare pool purgatory where angels fear to tread, but a dozen ill-fated sods will wind up—to be bludgeoned; bound and threaded with barbed wire; feasted upon; or shot, if they're lucky. Caught myself slack-jawed several times, completely aghast at how grim and bleak Bassett was willing to make this, on her debut, no less. Well worth tracking down if you want to feel the absence of god this Halloween.

reviews.text: "Deathwatch" comparada con las películas que salen hoy en día en el género de terror, resulta un film muy decente y enérgico. Una tropa británica que se encuentra perdida en la trinchera enemiga, esperan ser rescatados por sus aliados.Cadáveres, sangre, suciedad harán que los personajes se sumerjan en la locura y desesperación por sobrevivir en un ambiente bastante hóstil. Gracias a una ambientación tan bien conseguida, que genera tensión y claustrofobia a base de escenarios oscuros con el contexto terrorífico de encontrarse en guerra, hacen de este film de corta duración una noche muy llevadera y entretenida.

reviews.text: This film suffers from the same problem that not only all non-fiction films have that I'm aware of about the psychedelic question, but it also suffers from the same fundamental issue that plagues most USA-based non-fiction films. They are not documentaries, simply because they do not allow other perspectives to speak. They have no moral journalistic code. They are just based in pure capitalism. Which film will sell better to its audience? A film about DMT with only people that speak well of it, or a differentiated version where people get to speak, that aren't part of the projected audience of the film (mainly other stoners)?

reviews.text: I tried to approach this with the kindest eyes possible but it is what it is: a filmed version of a student drama production. Richard Burton's voice is endlessly listenable but I can't say that he is good here, producing an uninspired, laboured performance. He is surrounded by young male students, none of them destined to become known actors, who declaim their parts and fail to breathe life into them. Elizabeth Taylor appears throughout wordlessly as a representation of the epitome of beauty, which she admittedly manages well.

reviews.author: Niall Urquhart
reviews.text: If you want to see Elizabeth Taylor made up as a beautiful Star Trek alien then this is the film for you. If you want to see her actually speak then it's best to avoid. She's allowed to laugh late on but otherwise this is all about Richard Burton listening to himself recite line after line after line. Visually this is very good and is at its best when letting the visuals do the talking. Sadly, this isn't very often. I was probably expecting too much because of Murnau's silent version of Goethe's Faust which is far superior.

reviews.author: DKW_Skidoo
reviews.text: That classic tragedy, of a hubristic blowhard who sold his soul for a schnozzle at the epic bosom of Liz Taylor. Richard Burton directing this himself, after it flopping on stage, suggests this was a very personal story for him. One wonders if there's been a stage version where booze plays a big part. Burton directs like he acts, having some striking moments but getting too monotonously ripe after a while. I'm guessing it was pitched as Marlowe being the Stones to Shakespeare's Beatles (there was always that edgy Eng-Lit student insisting the former was better, dying as he did young and violently like a bad-boy rocker). It has some effective faerie folk-horror moments. Other times it resembles the interiors…

reviews.text: A Full Moon production by Charles Band about living toys that kill people. Sound familiar? He did a few with Full Moon. This is surely one of the lesser-known Band iterations of killer toys. While these Full Moon features may be ultra-low budget I almost always prefer them over other popular low-budget production companies such as The Asylum as Full Moon features typically always have this creative flavor that seems to ooze from all of their films. This one is no different with Band's killer dolls creating tons of bloody fun in a teen party turned house of horrors. It certainly entertained me more than it really should have as nothing in it is really special or unique, but it's surely one of those Full Moon features that just keeps you watching regardless of how bad it really is.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Don't Torture a Duckling is one of the truly great Giallo films and maybe Lucio Fulci's most accomplished work. This is a confrontational and shocking film; mainly for the fact that the central plot is the murder of young boys. We focus on a small village in rural Italy. Boys are turning up dead and the police are scrambling for answers, limited by the fears and superstitions of the local people. The ensemble cast is great, with Florinda Bolkan standing out in particular. The mystery is constantly intriguing and doesn't ever fall into genre tropes. Fulci instead prefers to explore the characters, situations and themes such as innocence, religion and black magic. It's surprisingly tame in terms of gore; but…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Fulci’s most angry and hysterical movie and his strongest one outside his Fulvia period. Part of what makes it successful is its constant shift between propulsive punk horror and doomed pastoral. It is a movie about a damned place that represents a large section of Italy itself. The set pieces are gruesome and brutally effective (there’s probably no more Italian moment than when during the lynching scene the soundtrack suddenly goes from loud to melodramatic), and then the movie keeps returning to that sense of a small town going on looking the other way.

reviews.author: kat🕷
reviews.text: "Don't Torture a Duckling" is a melodramatic study of people and their individual, rural religiosity, mostly far from offers of identification and sympathy: The movie caresses and plows through the genre foam without relying on superficial, (village) sensuality that would veil the tragedy. It‘s precisely in this certain absence of the usual and the deliberate used visual brutality that Lucio Fulcio finds his unique expression. A fairytale drama in the mountains.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: “Eight Postcards from Utopia,” co-directed by Jude and Christian Ferencz-Flatz, is a 71-minute long montage of Romanian television commercials. Broken into eight parts with titles like “Money Talks,” “Found Poetry,” and “Masculine/Feminine” (an obvious nod to Jean-Luc Godard) the commercials are situated in the edit with varying intentions. Sometimes it’s simply hilarious to look at the kitschy ads promoting Pepsi, photocopiers, the lottery, hamburgers and more. At one point ABBA’s The Winner Takes it All provides the soundtrack to a toothpaste commercial. Jude even includes clips of sex hotlines, just to give you a full range of everything that could've been hitting tv at every hour of the day. These commercials, despite their clunky acting and obvious low budget, however, aren’t too dissimilar in their intent from commercials seen in any other country. [full capsule review via RogerEbert]

reviews.text: 70 Minuten lang bekommt man hier die völlige Reizüberflutung – irgendwo zwischen Waschmitteln, Bier, Wohlstandsversprechungen und technischen Errungenschaften.Grob in acht Kapitel geordnet, werden rumänische Werbespots der 90er Jahre aneinander geschnitten, ihrer eigentlichen Suggestion beraubt und neu kontextualisiert. Durch die Magie des Filmschnitts zahlen sie aufeinander ein, sie kommunizieren miteinander, vervollständigen sich gegenseitig in ihren ästhetischen Gemeinsamkeiten und Unterschieden, und entblößen damit den Kapitalismus der westlichen Konsumgesellschaft in die sich Rumänien Ende der 80er Jahre eingliedert, als utopische Traumwelt.Das ist sicherlich keine große Erkenntnis, aber doch sehr unterhaltsam, wenn Grenzen verschwimmen und man in dieser unglaublichen Schnelllebigkeit der Bilder, in der ideologischen Gleichförmigkeit, gar nicht merkt wann von einem Spot zum nächsten geschnitten wird und daraus ganze Gag-Straßen entstehen.…

reviews.text: Last night I dreamt I went to Elephant Walk again.The set-up is pure Rebecca. A beautiful young bride comes back to the family home of her new husband, where she encounters a recalcitrant servant still loyal to a deceased master. There is a locked room kept as a shrine to this master whose spirit still lingers malevolently, an obstacle to the happiness of the newlyweds. No spoilers but the parallels don't end there, and what's more, the film was originally conceived as a vehicle for Maxim de Winter himself, Laurence Olivier, and his wife Vivien Leigh. Olivier dropped out due to theatrical commitments while Leigh started location filming in Ceylon but dropped out due to her mental health.

One of the animation studio’s stronger offerings in recent years, it’s visually radiant, backed by an emotional score & filled with likable characters. reviews.text: Quite possibly the most thoughtless movie I have ever seen, not in the sense of it being super-dumb and offensive in nearly every expected way and more, which it so totally is, but in being pitched so manically and heedlessly into action, any action, that it does not have time to think, regarding it as a process so expendable as to be treated with contempt if ever deemed worthy of notice. The late 70's of the Emmanuelle movies are a world in which appetite has been wholly liberated, where consumption of what is desired is the only recognizable good. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Europa Europa possesses an extraordinary narrative which is an adaption of Solomon Perel’s 1989 autobiography, who was a German Jewish boy who escaped persecution during the Holocaust by impersonating a Nazi. The direction by Agnieszka Holland (The Secret Garden) manages to transform an incredible and historical memoir of intolerance into a gripping film complemented with a couple of strikingly absurdist dream segments; one of them encompassing Hitler and Stalin engaging in a waltz! reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: The tricky subject of a person's right to die is addressed thoughtfully, compassionately and with some humour in François Ozon's low-key, restrained yet heartfelt Everything Went Fine. The film, based on a novel of the same name by the late Emmanuèle Bernheim, who also wrote the screenplays for several films directed by Ozon, is an introspective, empathetic depiction of a family facing a difficult situation. Through his accomplished and sophisticated approach, the director manages to craft a profoundly moving drama that avoids melodrama or judgment. His light hand and calm eye allow us to focus on the characters' day-to-day lives, as well as its thorny central question.

reviews.text: Everything Went Fine has two sisters (Sophie Marceau and Géraldine Pailhas) navigating their comfort and discomfort that their father (André Dussollier) wants them to arrange an assisted suicide for him after suffering a stroke. Assisted suicide is illegal in France but it is legal in nearby Switzerland. It’s the type of drama that slowly reveals the characters and then the last act lets them loosen up and levity enters the picture. It helps immensely that Marceau is absolutely astounding as the main caretaking sister. And there are delicate little touches from Francois Ozon to not only show her suffering with the weight of this decision but also the immense love that she has for husband, her respect for her sister, and her complicated relationship with both of her parents. She radiates warmth and animosity with deft precision.

reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: A chillingly plausible picture of an authoritarian world that doesn’t feel far removed from where we might actually be heading. The story’s premise on how people willingly trade knowledge for comfort, truth for entertainment, and thought for obedience hits even harder now than it probably did when Truffaut made the film. The thing that makes it so unsettling is how familiar it all feels, a society that slowly stops thinking for itself, that begins to fear complexity, and that starts to see ideas as threats. You can already glimpse shades of it today where ignorance is indulged, curiosity is mocked, and those in power quietly benefit from keeping the public distracted and compliant.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: The gentlest of light scrapes crowd in on Spencer Tracy when his daughter Elizabeth Taylor announces she's having a baby. Father's Little Dividend is a TV sitcom in embryo, the happiness of its well-heeled family never in doubt for a single second, and very soon (if not already) audiences would stop going to the cinema for such mild family goings-on and sit and watch them on the box in the living room instead. Vincente Minnelli directs the weak script invisibly and anonymously and it's only the star power of Tracy, Taylor, Bennett and Burke that makes the affair remotely memorable.

reviews.author: Euan
reviews.text: One of the lazier sequels I can think of. Not that it's bad mind. The family dynamic between Spencer Tracy, Joan Bennett, Liz Taylor and co. is still easily charming. Their hijinks are remarkably droll, and the overall atmosphere is one of warmth and kindness, if leaning a touch into hokum. No, the main issue is that it's essentially a carbon copy of it's predecessor, Father of the Bride. From the opening scene, pretty much every narrative beat is lifted from Minnelli's prior melodrama, with matrimony swapped out for childbirth. Despite how likeable the main characters can be, it just made it hard to truly care about the plot mechanics. I guess this is the 1950s equivalent of a cash-grab sequel - the Jurassic World of its day.

reviews.text: Jackie Chan's directorial debut. The Fearless Hyena is an entertaining mix of kung fu and comedy. Jackie plays a young maetial artist trained in a secret fighting style by his grandfather. However, he winds up attracting the attention of his elderly relative's old enemies after using the style in public. The plot is really pretty thin, but where the movie excels is in its star's physicality and charisma. This is still early in Chan's career but its clear he was always going to be a star. There's some creative use of kung fu in the choreography with numerous scenes that see Jackie fighting alongside props like tables, chairs and chopsticks, along with numerous weapons. It's fairly obvious from the start…

reviews.text: There's a brief interview at Cannes where Omar El-Zohairy talks about photography being his main source of inspiration here rather than anything cinematic, and I think it shows, not only in the specific look of the images—their colors and compositions—but in the narrative structure as well. Every shot feels like it's eliding normal convention in what you would expect it to inform you as a viewer, as if you're looking at a photograph or a painting and trying to construct the story in your head, fill in the blanks of where these people are or what they're going through. That looseness bleeds into the editing too, and it makes for one of the more disorienting films I've seen in recent…

reviews.author: Ayush
reviews.text: Lightning in a bottle is youth. It feels eternal but it passes us by in a hurry, and before we have the time to acknowledge that we have grown up, there we are: all grown up. Our friends, our family, our worries and hopes all feel less real the more we grow up. Our innocent tomfoolery gradually fades away as the heart grows harder and the face grows more stoic by the year. Like buildings subject to acid rain, the purity we once possessed starts to erode with the passage of time. On one of those days, do we look back on our childhood when things seemed just a little sweeter and brighter, and when we dared to hope? With a sort of bittersweet smile curling our lips, do we lose ourselves in remembrance of those few years of gleeful naïvete when we had the time to ask questions like "Do fireworks look round or flat from the side?"

reviews.text: It's quite embarrassing, really, how much more pleasing Shunji Iwai's original lo-fi Fireworks, Should We See It from the Side or the Bottom? is compared to the barely intelligible anime remake from 2017. Made on a shoestring budget for TV, Iwai constructed a soft pastel-coloured heart capturing the approaching end of innocent childhood, full of warm nostalgia and youth. It's an ageless tale for all the summers to come, without any excessive sci-fi absurdities ruining the wishful mood.

reviews.text: Directed by Jack Smith, Flaming Creatures is representational of a sexual subculture as well as helpful in building a vernacular of alternative cinema. Frequently and unfairly written off as an inexpensive sexploitation piece due to its graphic portrayals; which once involved police interrupting a screening in New York and confiscating a print of the film after decreeing to be transgressing the city’s obscenity regulations. It’s an accomplishment of a rough style attained through agile use of a handheld camera roaming about intertwined bodies at strange angles resulting in a flickering series of cloudy images, which influenced numerous underground artists to go on to make films in a comparable primitive style.

reviews.author: Mister All Sunday
reviews.text: One of the things I like about searching for older queer media is how they have to form and mold their own language in order to express forms of queerness that hadn't been given name yet. They don't feel shackled by the burden of respectability politics of a lot of modern gay media where the queer experience is sanded down and neatly falls into every politically correct box (#woke). A good example would be the short film I watched yesterday, Jeremiah, a film so boring in its theme, concept, and execution that the film practically peters out by the end. Flaming Ears by comparison is a queer utopia with its stop-motion pop art, miniature landscapes, and every character existing outside of the gender binary. The film is scatterbrained and incomprehensible for most of it's runtime, but the way it chooses to explore its ideas speak to me on an aesthetic level that most films don't.

reviews.text: Each segment in this Julien Duvivier-directed anthology has an ingenious visual conceit to recommend it. In the first, it's the disjunction between a woman's hushed voice and the Mardi Gras mask she wears; then, it's Edward G. Robinson's reflection taunting him into murder; and finally there's a repeated shot from a dream, with Charles Boyer's tightrope walker tumbling to his death, dissolving quickly into footage of his waking no-net routine. (The latter's such an effective representation of lingering anxiety that I'm half-surprised the technique isn't ubiquitous.)

reviews.text: There are enough tears here to fill a river. Freda is a portrait of a country, a film that captures Haiti through a few characters but allows broader topics to appear in the background. There is talk of corruption, revolution, and crime. Many characters want to leave, as their opportunities in Haiti are limited. Colonialism and capitalism have crushed them. The film presents a conflict between forging a national identity versus fighting for economic survival. To survive, people marry for wealth over love, abandon Creole to learn the languages of colonisers, and emigrate when they have nothing else. Freda presents the people, the culture, and the music of Haiti, but it also highlights turmoil, strife, and pain. The film is…
