reviews.author: komodoskar
reviews.text: Freda is a powerful and heartfelt exploration of the scars left by trauma, colonialism and the patriarchy at both a personal and a national scale. Director Gessica Généus gives the film an empathetic yet unflinching tone with her intimate and observational style of filmmaking, as she shows the struggles and challenges that her characters (and their real-life analogues) encounter in an authentic and unembellished manner. Excellent performances from all the lead actors, especially Néhémie Bastien, Fabiola Remy and Djanaïna François, blur the lines between character and actor and in combination with the use of documentary footage and the cast's many non-actors, this film becomes a brilliant and impactful example of docufiction. Freda is the first film from Haiti that I've seen and it is unabashedly Haitian - it wears its identity proudly, whilst also recognising the flaws and baggage that come with it.

reviews.text: Takes Ringo Lam's distinctly-uncontrollable third-act conflict and makes the whole movie like that. Such explosive energy prevents a coherent matrix of character motivations to build-up to one final spark, but unlike his other films that is not the goal here: he just wants to "make a film with a style no one could put a finger on." He succeeds. Full Contact escapes easy categorization precisely because it sometimes doesn't even feel like a film insomuch as it is: an incredibly-elaborate music video; an exercise in shooting prop guns; an excuse to blow up cars just laying around; an advertisement for butterfly knives. It becomes more an assemblage of moments glued together by the rule of cool than it does an actual narrative, and yet it somehow just works because no matter how ridiculously awesome the moment is now you know it'll somehow one-up it within fifteen minutes.

reviews.text: Deriving from a manga and anime television series of the same name, Galaxy Express 999 marked a noticeable transformative juncture for cinematic anime. Released the same year as Hayao Miyazaki’s debut Lupin III: The Castle of Cagliostro, together they proclaimed anime as a dominant cultural force. The planetary adventures continually subsist on the edge of the narrative as it explores themes of auctioning one's humanity for the opportunity for immortality and houses a poetic like mannerism birthed from insecurity.

reviews.author: William Cooper
reviews.text: Fascinating documentary about the late great director George Steven's - a man who brought us Shane, A Place in The Sun and Giant, to name a few - made by his son, George Steven's Jr. The film escapes certain traps of the documentary genre by not spending too much time on his personal life and instead solely focusing on his work. It does at times get mired in its inaction as it doesn't always have anything to say, so it just plays entire scenes from his filmography, which causes the movie to feel disjointed and disconnected from the audience. However, plenty of great interviews from legendary figures in Hollywood make this well worth watching if you, like me, are a fan of the work of George Steven's.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: When George Stevens Jr made this documentary about his father’s film career, such docus were still relatively new. As such, Jr deserves quite a bit of credit for pioneering the genre of films about filmmakers and proving that they could be so fascinating. It certainly didn’t hurt that he talked a number of stars who had worked with his father during the Golden Age of Hollywood, such as Katherine Hepburn and Fred Astaire, into giving interviews on camera. The result is a fairly good overview of Stevens the elder’s career, as well as some solid analysis of his approach to his medium, such as his slow-burning, observational treatment of rapidly escalating comical situations.

reviews.text: A well-made doc about one of the important directors of the 20th century. It was a treat to see and hear so many interviews with folks who had worked with him. Fred and Ginger, Katharine Hepburn, Douglas Fairbanks Jr and on and on. There’s amazing footage that he shot in color behind the scenes of Gunga Din, and from his WWII time covering D-Day and the liberation of Paris. Also some shocking footage from concentration camps, it helps to explain how and why his filmmaking changed after the war. And Joel Mc Crea talking about that scene on the steps in The More the Merrier, and Frank Capra saying that was the funniest and sexiest scene he’s ever seen… amazing!

reviews.text: Pretty straightforward documentary on George Stevens, but sometimes, that's all you need. Some movies (I Remember Mama, which they even interviewed Irene Dunne about, but we never see/hear her) definitely deserved more time to shine, but this was solid overview of his filmography, along with the Director's Guild controversy, and his time during WWII, which greatly impacted him and the types of films he made. Definitely see this is you are a fan of the director, as it's a loving tribute from a son to a father.

reviews.text: What does God's Country mean? I think it refers to a white man's arrogance. To the white man, ownership is a double standard. He simultaneously has the right to shoot one who enters his property without permission, and to enter another's property without permission, with no perceived punishment. That has been the basis for the United States of America for centuries. So when this film opens on a slide show of the people the white man took everything away from, one immediately knows what the film's title, God's Country means.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: In Julian Higgins’ arresting, slow-burn thriller “God’s Country,” systems and people in positions of power meant to protect are the ones causing the harshest harm. A former New Orleans cop turned college professor, the unflinchingly outspoken Sandra (Thandiwe Newton) is on the receiving end of a dangerous torrent, left unchecked by the local authorities, that begins when two white men in a red truck illegally park on her secluded Montana property to hunt deer. What erupts from this boundary breaching are bursts of lingering grief, hovering microaggressions and outright systematic racism — pushing an unmoored Sandra toward a haunting and cathartic confrontation with long-buried wounds.

reviews.text: En alternant brillamment plans rapprochés et d'ensembles, Hafsia Herzi fait dans Bonne Mère un portrait à la fois de Marseille et de ses habitant·es. Elle crée une nouvelle carte postale, une plus vraie, sur une ville magnifique où les gens les plus beaux ont des difficultés et des défauts. Le jeu naturaliste, la photo simple mais toujours belle donnent un film mélancolique qui ne joue jamais avec le pathos. La dernière réplique de Nora "Tant que je suis debout je resterai solide" est d'une monstrueuse simplicité et dès lors d'une force immense. Un très beau film d'une grande dame.

In his immersiveness, Kubrick gives you a sensory experience with 2001: A Space Odyssey, employing techniques that break film conventions. Kubrick neglects offering any proper exposition throughout the entirety of the film; most of the film's plot points and imagery are ambiguous, symbolic and profusely abstract. Instead, his unique and magnified use of form create the essence of the film, experience. His extreme attention to detail and perfectionism is displayed in each shot. reviews.text: Hammersmith is Out slides between being boring, scene devouringly interesting and hilariously odd. Richard Burton plays a master criminal who cons Beau Bridges to break him out of the asylum and he'll make them rich. In tow is Liz Taylor as Bridges' doofy girlfriend. Taylor whoops it up ALOT for better and worst at times. Bridges is 100% a Coen brother character. Just an absolute nitwit at the hands of the chilly Burton. Who is.... actually also very Coen-seque. It's like Nic Cage from Raising Arizona was paired up with Anton Chigurh from No Country and Bunny from Big Lebowski to take on the world. That might sound a little more fun than it plays. It feels longer than it is and is very uneven. Or maybe its just late. I can't deny the finale was pretty worth it though. If you love Liz's weird period or the Liz & Dick catalog then check it out for sure.

Liz and Dick had already flopped in a stagy version of DOCTOR FAUSTUS (67) but if at first they didn't succeed they'd try, try again, in obscure movies as in matrimony. From the pen of Stanford Whitmore, later the screenwriter of the wonky horror movie THE DARK (79), comes a contemporary version of the story, set in a hypocrisy-laden America (but filmed in Mexico, where the duo lived) and produced by…

Now on the run from the law, the pair are joined by a white trash waitress (Liz Taylor) for a satirical road trip across America, where Hammersmith's ability to make good on his promise sees Breedlove transported from stripclub owner, to big business tycoon to political office. Robert Knepper does a pretty convincing Lance Henriksen. One of the best DTV movies to come along in a while.

reviews.text: The idea of making a DTV sequel to/remake of Hard Target decades after that John Woo film isn't exactly something that would inspire much confidence in anyone but with Hard Target 2, this movie is almost exactly as good as it can reasonably be. This is no better and (thankfully) no worse than it needs to be, mostly because in Scott Adkins, it has a lead who elevates even the worse of these types of movies. He's solid here in the Van Damme role and the action generally is alright without being all that great, though it's with pretty much everything else that this movie is bad. The dialogue, characters, story, etc. are all expectedly shitty but since the only thing anyone is watching Hard Target 2 for is some good action, it just about fulfills that even with the massive downgrade from Woo to Roel Reiné.

reviews.text: Thankfully not a complete carbon copy of Hard Target but this sequel bogs itself down with stuff like character backstory and Southeast Asian politics instead of action. Scott Adkins is a disgraced ex-UFC fighter* conned into playing the Most Dangerous Game in Myanmar, believing it's just an underground match to reclaim his glory and lots of money. Meanwhile, villain Robert Knepper does another solid Lance Henriksen & Stephen McHattie impersonation. No Woo, no JCVD, no Mummy henchman; in fact, there's really no connection to the first movie except shots of doves. Best to ignore the title and pretend this is your everyday Adkins jam.

reviews.author: Jesse
reviews.text: For me, the number one ingredient for a successful slasher film is location, location, location. Give me a suburban neighborhood, a summer camp, a college campus, a hospital, or any place that offers so many places where a boogeyman could be lurking but also acts as a safe haven for characters to hide. Hell Night took this lesson with a sprawling abandoned mansion that is straight out of something like Resident Evil.

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: HELL NIGHT was one of those 80’s schlockers that would always be on Saturday afternoon on the local NY tv station so as a kid I watched it a bunch but clearly it was edited down for violence there so watching it again decades later uncut was eye-opening how solid the death scenes were, especially in the editing. It’s not great, kinda too long and Linda Blair looks bored but some quality kills and a fun atmosphere (but what’s with the castle? Did Charlie Band rent it out?) makes it more watchable.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: An eighties slasher that doesn't come with the best of reputations! Hell Night features a bunch of college kids who must spend a night in a mansion where the previous resident murdered his entire family. It's fairly boilerplate stuff that never really bothers to step outside of the common slasher tropes. This coupled with the fact that its a good fifteen minutes too long and severely drawn out in places means that it's never going to be the most exciting slasher flick. However, it's not all bad news. The mansion house where most of it takes place is really well utilised. While there's a lot of padding there's also a few well orchestrated kill scenes peppered in here and there.…

Kate Lyn Shiel, Sophia Takal, there’s even a Safdie brother in there. It’s all been covered before but it’s astute in its depiction of how anything can be passed off as some sort of postmodernist genius with the right angle or marketing. That’s passed off to audiences, but also to impresarios and other people who supposedly know what they’re talking about.

reviews.author: zandarthegreat
reviews.text: Kind of torn on this one. On one hand I admire a smaller film having the guts to tackle such a large subject like the meaninglessness of modern art and an artist trying to capture a subject far beyond his reach. It’s bold to make nearly every character unlikeable to show the narcissism that is “high art”. On the other hand, I have to ask myself, did I enjoy it? I don’t think I’ll look back and recommend Hellaware to anyone anytime soon, a voice of reason throughout this process would’ve really helped ease the viewing. Instead I just watched a photography graduate sink deeper and deeper into his own pride.

reviews.text: Hidden Strike is a passable venture that works more because of the Jackie and John combo rather than its script. Storywise it's cliched at many parts, so the twists don't really surprise us. The action sequences were good but most of the background sets for looks artificial due to poor CGI and green screen use. The pacing also feels uneven, as sometimes it drags and sometimes it rushes. However, The performance and chemistry between Jackie and John helps to overcome these negativea to a certain extent. The comedy scenes were good, though in some scenes it feels forced. Overall, it's a time pass flick that can be enjoyed by those who likes predictable buddy action movies.

I like both actors, and their pairing had some charm, but that's about where the positives end. While the action scenes were decent, the camera work, green screen effects, and CGI were inconsistent, often pulling me out of the experience. The film is a co-production between Hollywood and Chinese cinema, but it felt like a clash of styles rather than a cohesive vision. It probably would have been better if they’d stuck to one production style. The story was weak, and the dialogue was painfully bad, leading to an overall disappointing experience.

It emphasizes how black actors are still typecast as thugs, illiterates, and the like. In fact, the protagonist of my upcoming miniseries told me how he even has to face this himself, which is all the more tragic when you realize such discrimination has even crept into industries in predominantly black countries such as the Dominican Republic.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Nothing has changed, because the only way the issues this film tackles will irrevocably change is if everything changes radically. The film has a simple enough message: Hollywood offers little for black people beyond stereotypical roles that fit a narrow band of categories, each of them a different kind of harmful. Though you can cite examples now (and you could cite examples in 1987, too) of decent roles for black people, they are relatively rare compared (a) to the number of stereotypical roles and (b) to the number of non-stereotypical roles available to white people. Even popular films with significant black presence feature stereotyped roles, now and then and long before.

And most of the sketches shine, too. The exception for me was the overlong film noir aside which has aged pretty poorly for its fear of muscle-bound effeminate black men. reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Like trying to watch a movie serial and read a comic book at the same time while also simultaneously chugging Jolt Cola and watching a fireworks display through diffraction glasses. Overwhelming, exhausting, (increasingly coherent the more I see it, though), and digressive, but also hilarious, imaginative, and irresistibly fun. Shaw Brothers productions always make the most with tiny budgets, and here silent film tricks, B-movie wire suspension, and rotating platters are used to such great effect that you'll forget about the existence of computers. The part of your brain that keeps track of bank accounts and grocery lists will kindly step out of the way to let child-like joy take over. Step through that door, and you'll never wanna go back.

reviews.text: Throughout the sixties, Shaw Brothers spectactular Mandarin-language color movies competed with a scattered array of Cantonese-language movie studios making low budget black-and-white movies with their own stars and stylistic conventions. But the Shaw Studios production values won out, and Cantonese Cinema as a whole collapsed. In the eighties, the opposite happened. Shaw Brothers was rapidly losing market share to Golden Harvest and other more authentically Hong Kong production companies, with Cantonese language movies once more in ascendance. Shaw Brothers would essentially shutter its movie division to focus on television, but not before one last cycle of wuxia films, a cycle that looked to their competitors from the sixties as inspiration. Dusting off those old Cantonese series from nearly twenty years…

reviews.text: It’s not just that these type of films devalue animation (which they do, despite also relying on it heavily), it’s that they’re also actively devaluing the experiences that audiences deserve. Recycling the same stories over and over and over again puts us in a cultural feedback loop where the deeper political themes of the art we engage with grows increasingly stale and pushed to the background. Studios don’t need to continue to push the boundaries of storytelling when they can just reheat something we’ve already had. It’s disingenuous, even when it tries its best to capture the emotions of its source material.

reviews.author: sarah
reviews.text: Humoresque has glimmers of real passion, but it’s just so bogged down by the weight of its overblown story. The film can’t escape its own seriousness. I’m a big fan of both John Garfield and Joan Crawford— they’re enticing on screen together, when the film allows them the chance. However, beyond the performances, an aspect of the film I did enjoy is the unique editing and gorgeous cinematography. Unlike a lot of music-centered movies, the music here is not a separate entity from the action of the plot. It melts Garfield’s violin performances with close-ups of Joan Crawford’s face, and the film crescendos so beautifully to a magnificent climax. I wish I liked this film more, but it could have really benefited from a tighter runtime (and more Joan Crawford).

reviews.author: Krommedijk
reviews.text: More consistent than Game of Thrones - with a far more decent ending, I, Claudius is another 1970s landmark of BBC television. The series is based on Robert Graves' novels I, Claudius and Claudius the God, novels about the life and times of Emperor Claudius (10 BC - AD 54). Claudius was a stammerer, nicknamed 'Clau-Clau-Claudius'. His family - now called the Julio-Claudian Dynasty - would never have expected him to sit on the throne of Rome. He survived the madness of the reigns by Tiberius and Caligula just by not being murdered. Robert Graves’s brilliant idea was to reinvent him as a clever historian: the novels are his autobiography and just about possible. Murder, intrigue, sex and plain madness. Brilliant cast, so you can expect excellent acting.

It does Game of Thrones better than Game of Thrones and on a tiny fraction of the budget (and the inspiration for Martin’s novels is very clear). How completely refreshing to watch self-confident performance-based television made by and for adults during the relative wasteland of the streaming era. All you need to make thrilling historical cinema are a handful of solid sets, classically trained actors, and a competent hand behind the camera who understands how to block a scene. Bravo!

All the ingredients are there; he's a pitiless observer of human nature at a time of political extremism, his character comedy is always on point, and he is interested in challenging the actual ideology of fascism rather than using it as a symbol of Bad Things, which is exactly what more directors should be doing now. Unfortunately he has that Romanian director's tic of letting every scenes lag on for longer than any other country's film-makers would, which sometimes hits a real payload of awkward comedy or discomfort. And sometimes it just goes on.

The circumstances are different - Carice van Houten plays a criminal psychologist evaluating whether a serial rapist (Marwan Kenzari) has ‘recovered’ enough to begin reentering society after 5 years in prison* - but the exploration of gender & power dynamics is a constant theme. Swap the age-gap / BDSM fantasy for patient-therapist / rape fantasy. Van Houten is the only therapist who can see through Kenzari’s manipulative bullshit & opposes his release -- if he’s a psychopath, can he really recover?

What it means to be good in an age in which doing good mostly involves throwing gofundme abstractions at unseen disasters or offering bags of consumer society’s scraps to the less fortunate. These high-minded city dwellers off to the impoverished Romanian hinterlands in their four-wheel SUVS like it it’s some especially noble kind of weekend hobby; a trio whose cheerful sense of purpose comes undone with just one solitary man, a person whose corporeal thereness can’t be ignored no matter how many cheese puffs and Xanax they stuff him with. The fact that the…

reviews.author: Avirup
reviews.text: Muntean's genre work once again is quite good especially with the use of woods backdrop to create tension and to suggest something far more sinister and teases of it becoming something else, obviously that never was the intention so it naturally doesn't. Though it doesn't fully come together but utilizing the getting lost in the woods and turning the claustrophobia of the situation into a morality play was nice — so while this doesn't become anything truly sinister, it displays a certain level of darkness with its human elements. New wave's realism and dry mundanity typically are the highlights, as well as the social and human observations, character interactions, the look of the film and the touches of humour. It definitely could've been lot sharper overall but the general anticipation and peek into morals here work more effectively than it did in One Floor Below.

reviews.text: Watching this felt like Godard's Histoire(s) du cinéma with a personal cinematic narrative not only with his films but his life. It's very esoteric like much of Leos Carax material. I felt at times like I was watching a modern version of Man with a Movie Camera as we race through all these images. I felt he was keenly aware that this is meaningless in context but meaningful in abstract detail for anyone to fill in their own narrative as time moves by us and we sometimes slowdown and speed up in our lives. As much as it's challenging with all it's smattering of images and dry narrative I found myself engaged with it for the most part and it's circling around the human condition on this mortal coil.

At a time when I feel like we are really at the end of the world and everyone is going crazy, he channels cinema into the current world, essence of politics, and images of human beings from the films and history.

Je déteste comment il reprend Dans le noir du temps pour en faire son autoportrait à lui de manière si superficielle. Je déteste son humour, son amour de lui-même, sa posture renfermé, quasiment misanthrope et je ne comprend pas comment cet humain peut cacher autant de passion, de manière si transcendante. J'ai longtemps pensé que c'était un des pires films que j'ai vu de Cannes, je n'arrive pas à aimer un film dont je sens que l'humain derrière m'insupporte mais pourtant Carax est un génie. Je peux renier qu'au milieu de ce bouillon insupportable se cache des idées à la hauteur…

reviews.text: As many reviewers here point out, this suffers from its similarity, in genre and color scheme, to the 1938 Adventures of Robin Hood. Overall the talent involved here is a couple of notches below that more famous movie—Richard Thorpe is no Michael Curtiz, and Robert Taylor is definitely no Errol Flynn. But even if it’s no timeless classic it’s still pretty fun, and serves as a reminder of a time when “knights in shining armor“ were still a fixture in American pop culture. Although the success of HBO’s A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, which I coincidentally finished right before putting on Ivanhoe, suggests that these moribund tropes might be getting ready to stage a comeback.

reviews.text: Ivanhoe was released at a time when Hollywood was adapting every great literary classic they could get their hands on. It is far from being the best film of 1952, let alone the best of the decade but I still rather enjoyed it.

I thought the battle scenes towards the end were really cool and well orchestrated. Some of the production design came off a bit cheesy looking though. Ivanhoe has a strong cast, but most of their performances aren’t memorable and many of their characters come off too one dimensional. The execution of this medieval epic comes off flat and uninspired. It’s mildly entertaining at times, but a lot of it, particularly in the first half, is a bit of a slog.

reviews.text: Jack is the story of a boy about 10 and his younger brother who must fend for themselves as their young neglectful mother completely ignores them. An incident in the house separates the kids into a group home and a foster home. After Jack escapes from the group home, he retrieves his little brother and they spend the rest of the movie searching for their mom. Most of the film is taken up of images of the boys wandering the city streets, running up stairs, and sleeping in cars and benches. Director Edward Berger tried to put the audience in the kids’ shoes, but fails because there is never enough sense of fear and danger. Given the sparse dialogue and repetitiveness of the scenes, the runtime could have been cut in half with no ill effects. An OK low budget movie about child neglect that pales in comparison to Hirokazu Kore-eda’s moving Nobody Knows.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: This evening, while I was fueling my body with the refreshing coldness of a glass of water to break the fast, one simple thought brought me back to the film I had watched this morning: Claude Berri’s Jean de Florette, adapted from the novel by writer, director, and Academician Marcel Pagnol. You see, I always drink water to break the fast, but for the first time I truly valued it — it even tasted much better. Water, and subsequently land, suddenly became the stuff dreams were made of, or nightmares in their absence, echoing Pagnol’s story: their apparent yet no less agonizing absence.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Jean de Florette is an absolutely stunning film that captures the French countryside in a mesmerizing fashion, being so absolutely beautiful while containing a moral tragedy that is excellent to watch unfold. The film reveals the cruelty that lies beneath greed and rural traditions and is told in a great, slow-burning story. It allows all the beautiful landscapes of the film to seep to the surface and is a great, sharp contrast to the ugly morality of the story. It's a masterclass in tragic storytelling, and just about every aspect here works, especially Gérard Depardieu, who brings such strength to his character even if obviously the actor is a terrible person in real life.

reviews.author: alewatchesfilms
reviews.text: Jean de Florette is a masterful exploration of human nature, one that refuses to simplify morality into black and white. It presents a world where avarice, pride, and desperation intertwine, making it difficult to decide what—or whom—to support. For much of the film, I found myself torn, unable to fully condemn or sympathize with any one character. That’s the brilliance of it—it captures the nuances of human behavior, the way self-interest can quietly turn into cruelty, and how conviction can drive people to unthinkable extremes.

reviews.author: Ford H
reviews.text: In my previous review, I mentioned that Jean de Florette reminded me of Killers of the Flower Moon. Next time I see Marty, I’ll have to ask if he’s seen this backstabbing, two-faced masterpiece; I’ve never heard him talk about it, and the parallels are striking. While Killers targets an entire community, Jean de Florette is more personal and observational. It’s about two farmers who covet their neighbor’s spring water. To get it, they simply wait for him to fail by keeping the existence of the spring a secret and letting nature do the dirty work.

It’s well worth a watch, particularly because of its unusual shifts and masterful performances, but if you’re sensitive to knowing anything, like me, please exit the building now.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: It doesn’t feel like a big ask for a movie called Jungle Cruise to occasionally look like it takes place in an actual jungle on an actual river cruise. That seems like the bare minimum a movie called Jungle Cruise should provide. As a matter of fact, the old Jungle Cruise attraction at Disneyland occasionally pulled off a more convincing simulation of a river cruise through a jungle than this film inspired by it, and the ride’s technology dates back to Disneyland’s opening day in 1955. There are all kinds of elaborate effects in this film: Monsters, CGI jaguars, magical trees. And yet it never pulls off the simple illusion of its heroes floating down the middle of the Amazon. It always seems like everyone is standing on a set in a big green room.

The films are very cryptically presented, so those who didn't pay attention are weeded out by their vagueness, while others can't even agree on which film is harder to understand than the other, let alone whether or not they're about anything. reviews.text: Lots about this movie is very technically impressive, the grand, lavish sets, the costumes, the epic scale of set pieces with hundreds of choreographed extras. If nothing else it’s a spectacle. But that only does so much when the fundamentals are this shallow and the story is this heavy handed and dated. Charles Huston’s Charles Gordon is presented as this Christ-like saviour whose influence the locals would fall apart without, while Lawrence Oliver’s Mahdi, aside from…y’know, is played like a cartoon villain. Every character in this is a caricature, and between the big epic battle scenes, we’re treated to nothing but dry, patronizing, expository filler. I see a lot of comparison to Lawrence of Arabia among this film’s discourse, but…

reviews.text: When you consider the political landscape of today and the furore that surrounds the accusations of "whitewashing" in movies, then this ill-advised choice from United Artists to "blackface" Laurence Olivier to play a Sudanese Arab who believes he's the prophesied Mahdi would have seen protests in the street if it were made in the current climate. Back in 1966 however, Larry was the greatest actor of his generation, some would say any generation, but it's the only aspect of Basil Dearden's film that doesn't quite work.

reviews.author: Jakub Flasz
reviews.text: It is utterly impossible to see a film like Khartoum as anything but a product of its time. Between the Panavision presentation (by the way it was the last picture shot this way until Tarantino's The Hateful Eight), lavish sets, lots of extras, big set pieces with hundreds of people in full costume on horseback, overwhelming pathos and a browned-up Laurence Olivier in one of the lead roles, this was a textbook example of big budget filmmaking. And seeing how little it had beneath its glossy demeanour one should not doubt that the era of such movies was not only well into its Lebensabend but hooked up to a respirator waiting for the plug to be pulled.

reviews.author: Jim Beaver
reviews.text: Charlton Heston portrays British general Charles "Chinese" Gordon, the near-mythical hero of the Sudan with most of the general's vaunted stubbornness, self-righteousness, bravery, and insubordination fully displayed. While the portrait leaves out some of Gordon's psychological quirks and (latterly) his emotional deterioration, the film provides a not-especially hagiographic look at the man who refused to abandon the people under his care and died for it. As the Sudanese holy man who opposed Gordon, the self-appointed Mahdi, Mohammed Ahmad, Laurence Olivier gives a strong (though controversial) performance, and the (fictional) meetings between the two men are depicted with enormous gravity and quite panache. Heston allows himself to be more unlikable than expected, an honesty in portrayal which nevertheless leaves the viewer…

reviews.text: I’ll admit my woke ass was initially pretty turned off by this, what with Larry Olivier in blackface and stunt falls where horses’ necks bent in ways they definitely shouldn’t — but it pretty quickly won me over. Clearly Stephen Sommers used this as a key visual reference in The Mummy 1999, and the desert warfare vibes are impeccable, the Nile Valley in the 1880s brought to life in a tactile and gripping way (gorgeous costumes — chainmail epaulettes!!!) It’s truly transportive adventure cinema. I am not a fan of Charleston Heston but here he gives a charismatic and effective performance. Olivier is fine.

Learned the movie was called Khartoum and it is one of the best war films I've ever seen in my life. Gordon pasha vs the Mahdi out in the desert sands of the Sudan. Both men of honor. Only one can survive. The battle scenes I'm willing to bet Mel Gibson saw them here and incorporated a lot of the same shots in Braveheart. For 1966 this must've been the most violent movie ever made. Bloody, merciless even. The final siege left me in awe. Never knew this movie existed. An epic masterpiece.

You’ve barely kept up with the gnarly plot and you get distracted by his cool bad boy greatness. Kilmer and (then wife) Joanne Whalley are decent as an updated Bonnie and Clyde type, though with some exceptions. Character decisions begin to get questionable halfway through. Dahl’s hand in the script shows his deep affection for the complicated noir web of intrigue and deception…

KILL OR BE KILLED is amateurish and goofy, with a lot of ill-timed humor and bad acting, but it succeeds in…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Given Parajanov's abstract nature, this collection of fragments of lost films could just as easily pass for one of his other shorts. But the inherently political subtext of these mostly poetic, semi-erotic images being culled from work repressed by authorities is reworked into a more expansive series of windows into strange, beautiful images of art, sensuality, and a surrealist depiction of living history. In its own way, it's the ultimate summary of its maker, the cutting-room floor arranged not into a coherent sense of meaning but a flamboyant embrace of all possible meanings.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: A unique coming-of-age story. Rather than the traditional loss of innocence amidst harsh lessons about adulthood’s moral compromises, La Promesse’s young protagonist must instead come to recognize his complicity in his family’s immoral deeds, and to strive to do better than the previous generation. Instead of filling the viewer with nostalgia for a simpler and more idyllic past, it encourages you to take action in the present — while simultaneously showing how hard (and how expensive!) it is to do the right thing.

reviews.text: l’enfant du temps - the films of the Dardenne brothers look very carefully into the mechanisms of our times. the „education“ into competition, status orientation, fixation on money and materialism. symbolism meets ideology meets vivid life stories. after the pretty unknown (and hard to get) Falsch and Je pense à vous from documentary crossing over to fictional private tragedies La Promesse feels like the ultimate starting point into their award winning, palm heavy careers.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: I read that in the mid-90s, Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne had an unpleasant collective experience that encouraged them to trim the workforce and be as minimal as efficient. You don't win audiences by just taking a camera and “shooting,” but for all their innovative directing, storytelling is the siblings’ strongest suit, and seldom have directors provided such rich palettes of humanity’s struggles through globalized economic crises as the Dardennes have.

reviews.author: J
reviews.text: the hardheaded realism in La Promesse vets an experiential view of (colonial) capitalism and its lasting consequences through a coming-of-age lens. without pullulating itself with pornographic poverty or acute violence, it is the severest of normalised circumstances and the often disregarded exploitation of people that unfold in its social clarity. undocumented immigrants are transported in a vehicle and brought to a place where they are given shelter and work. the sight of tiny rooms, the complaint about a foul smell, the repeated mention of a malfunctioning heater, the continuous avoidance of authorities inspecting the workplace for illegals render harsh living and abusive working conditions. employers hire these people because it’s cheaper. without the need for bestowing benefits and bonuses, they…

reviews.text: A dark and ultimately disturbing watch. But a powerful and surpassingly faithful adaptation of Hugh Selby's 1964 cult classic novel that many deemed unfilmable. Set in 1952 in Sunset Park, a poverty-ridden section of Brooklyn, Selby's novel was broken up into six different stories about the underclass residents. Director Uli Edel manages to tie them together, in a multi-character film about the desperate and violent ways marginalized people survive and die.

reviews.text: It's not a movie for everyone. You need to have left the matrix to be able to watch it — Or just not be an idiot — It is an emotional film, and full of poetic meanings that to understand them you must humanize the Germans (why wouldn't you?). The story of the protagonist can be identified by any soldier of any nation, that makes the film more special. Ludwig Herckel loves his country, culture, nation, family and he has a reason to fight, to keep his country whole, because his wife is waiting for him at home. The German soldiers weren't monsters but citizens with a common commitment. This film does not sanctify the SS because there were war crimes in all wars; but the Director, Alessandro Pepe dared to show us what cowards do not, the humanity in that people that Hollywood bastardized.10/10.

El protagonista relata su vida como soldado SS desde 1943 donde todo es retroceder pero que lucha por su patria. Nada de doctrina nazi (son las SS no es la Wemacht algo tenían que decir). Las batallas patéticas, sin ningún sentido, con efectos fatales. El montaje con unos cortes que te sorprenden de lo absurdos. Los uniformes todos nuevos. reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: A slice of pure corn-fed Americana, set in a glossy Warner Bros version of 1880s New York City. Its success lies mainly in the typically skilful performances of William Powell and Irene Dunne as overbearing patriarch and dizzily wily matriarch of four sons. The script would appear to be closely based on a Broadway hit, broad characterisations and all, but I did laugh frequently and Michael Curtiz does his usual professional job at wielding the megaphone. The nineteenth century was never as pretty and mannered as this - in fact life never has been - but Hollywood is the world master at myth creation. It's breezy, frothy and delightfully performed with strong supporting work from Edmund Gwenn, Zasu Pitts and especially the teenage Elizabeth Taylor, as the apple of the eldest son's eye.

reviews.text: The ironic thing about Limelight is that it’s very clearly (and upfront about this) motivated by Chaplin’s own fear of going irrelevant and the world moving on from him. Of course, this never really ended up being the case - just two weeks ago a viral Instagram post with around 500 thousand likes used a long clip from Chaplin’s A King in New York (not even close to one of his most famous films) - this guy might actually have more legs than any artist much less filmmaker in the last two centuries. But what’s so incredible about Limelight is that he knows he’s self-conscious at this point, he can’t help it - so he leans into it, putting the…

reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: The opening scene of Limelight screams "drama," ushering in an entirely new side of Charlie Chaplin that had been all but invisible beforehand. Gone is the adorable little tramp of old, now a mere shadow, traces of him left to be found in Calvero, a stage performer well past his prime. Limelight is at once Chaplin's most humanistic experience and his touching goodbye letter- although this wasn't his last film, it's clear that he poured every ounce of his expressive talent into this production. Chaplin was many things. A comedian, a writer, a musician, a director, an artist. His versatility is put on full display here, giving a complete deconstruction of the man and his massive aptitude.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Built not on humour but nostalgia, sadness and personal ruin, Limelight was, in many ways, Charlie Chaplin's swan song. He wrote, directed, starred and composed the soundtrack—for which he won his only Academy Award—and was based on his novella Footlights. It served as a vehicle for the actor and filmmaker to present his opinions about how complex and ungrateful the entertainment world could be, along with broader commentary about life in general. The narrative observes Calvero (Chaplin), a vaudeville comedian who is already destined to be forgotten, when he finds Thereza "Terry" Embrose (Claire Bloom), a young ballet dancer about to commit suicide. Terry is aching with psychosomatic paralysis, and Calvero helps her heal with his observations and words of encouragement. Like Calvero,…

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: So as I’ve pointed out on my review yesterday, I am a Batman diehard fan. When it comes to Superman, I always religiously watched Smallville all Sundays or Tuesday (depending on the channel) as a kid, but I’ve never been that really interested in the “grandaddy” of Superheroes. Despite this, as I went through the free docs on Youtube I decided to give this a try and the fact I went in and bought the 80th Anniversary comic book should give you an idea of how much I was into Kal-El and his adventures.

reviews.author: Mark Mooney
reviews.text: Look, Up in the Sky! The Amazing Story of Superman is a 2006 documentary that serves as a love letter to the Man of Steel, chronicling his evolution from comic book icon to cultural phenomenon. Directed by Kevin Burns and narrated by Kevin Spacey, this 110-minute feature is a breezy yet engaging overview of Superman’s legacy, perfect for fans seeking a nostalgic celebration rather than an exhaustive academic analysis.

reviews.author: HAL
reviews.text: Aside from having appearances of people no longer in the public’s good graces (Kevin Spacey, Dean Cain, Bryan Singer) this is one really interesting documentary.It was a ton of fun seeing all the different portrayals of the character, all the unique media he’s been a part of that I DESPERATELY wanna watch now. I felt it could’ve gone a tiny bit more in depth with some things but I guess there’s a lot of ground to cover seeing as Superman has been around since the 30s. Still though, very enjoyable. Had me excited when Superman 1978 was a huge success and devastated when George Reeves died (yes I’m familiar with the story but it’s still fucking sad). But like any good piece of Superman media, it makes me hopeful for the future and excited for what’s yet to come.

reviews.author: K Gray
reviews.text: A behind the scenes look at one of the most infamous and disastrous film shoots ever. Crew members give candid interviews on the chaotic unraveling of Richard Stanley’s brainchild, originally adapted out of the bizarre premise from brilliant author H.G. Wells, into a full blown catastrophe orchestrated by the likes of Marlon Brando, Val Kilmer, and a toxic Hollywood system. It’s a surreal fever dream of interconnected stories from various people in different departments giving their own firsthand account on the absolutely wild experiences they endured on set, with some being shocking, others hilarious, but all entertaining. A fun, ferocious, and fascinating documentary on filmmaking filled with witchcraft, dogpeople, ice bucket hats, the smallest man in the world, and everything else in between.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: A making-of documentary about what happens when a small, aspiring studio takes on a small, aspiring director and forces him to make something bigger than he or the studio could handle.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: The infamous late-90s film adaptation of The Island of Dr. Moreau is a textbook example of what happens when you combine way too much money with way too little artistic passion. My reaction when I heard they were making a documentary about it was similar to what I imagine most people in the general populace's would be: "Why?" But that question gets cleared up within minutes of the beginning of this, as it becomes abundantly evident that Richard Stanley wasn't just some director who got fired off of a movie, but a guy whose career, maybe even his entire life had been leading up to his chance to tell this story, to capture violent dog-person births onscreen and to lick the blood up afterwards. He lost the job, but he also lost a lot more than that - I'm reminded of the Sturgill Simpson lyric: "Some say you might go crazy, but then again it might make you go sane."

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr. Moreau" is a 2014 documentary directed by David Gregory. Focusing on the development of "The Island of Dr. Moreau" (1996), the documentary is a fascinating look of what was originally intended and what was the end result of one of the most notoriously mishandled films ever to be completed for the big screen. I obviously want to highlight the word "completed" as even though there were probably worse production efforts that never made it, the fact that some iteration of this film even saw the light of day is a complete story of insanity within itself.

reviews.text: A very entertaining screwball. Not a lost classic, but this shows you just how good the average film was back in the late 1930s. Tyrone Power is a reporter who wants to get a scoop on the wealthy Loretta Young. She turns the tables on him and tells every other paper in town that she and Ty are engaged. This makes him big news and he is constantly hounded by the press and salesmen. Through a series of manipulations and misunderstandings they end up together. Don Ameche is Tyrone's boss and they have a love-hate relationship. Ty keeps getting fired and re-hired. I had a good time watching.

reviews.author: Jack Russo
reviews.text: Love preserved in letters and tears frozen in snow. The durational brevity necessitates currents of effervescent melodrama, two years apart reuniting in recurring passages of emotional ellipsis. Footsteps trail through the mountains by day and piano melodies drift into the night, actions sustained in anticipation of words which never seem to transpire until a felled tree brings with the collapse of the winter dream. This should be a matter of devastating heartbreak but it is hard not to be enveloped within the wall of roses; a shimmering romanticism by which all these lovelorn confessions can be read in a new light.

reviews.author: martamcfly
reviews.text: What a pleasant surprise this was! Included as a bonus 40-minute flick on Radiance Films' release of Underworld Beauty, Love Letter offers yet another glimpse into the early works of Seijun Suzuki — an exciting preview of the auteur he would become. As Suzuki expert William Carroll notes in the audio commentary, Suzuki's crime films understandably dominate discussions of his career. Still, Love Letter stands out, offering glimpses of the surrealist touches he would later perfect and a softness that’s hard not to get swept up in.

reviews.author: David Robson
reviews.text: Other features don't pack as much loveliness in as Suzuki manages here in 40 minutes. It's pure winter melodrama and one of the most elegantly shot movies I've ever seen (delightful that they sprung for 'Scope for a novella-length drama), its lovelorn characters as one with the wintry forest that frames them. Between the deep writerly longing and the hepcat milieu two of our characters live in it feels like it's sketching out Haruki Murakami's whole deal. And holy shit, the roses. THE ROSES

reviews.text: Talvez seja o filme mais abertamente melodramático de Suzuki, e certamente um dos mais belos da primeira fase. Por ser melodrama, lembra Mizoguchi, diretor que os modernos gostavam de negar com o intuito de matar o pai. O estilo de Suzuki é mais diretamente sentimental que o de Mizoguchi, que não chegou a filmar em scope, como Suzuki o fez a partir de 1958. Talvez se aproxime de um David Lean, embora de um Lean anterior ao scope. Outra referência é Noites Brancas, de Dostoievski. O principal é que em 40 minutos deste seu 11º longa já sentimos a mão de mestre.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A biblical desire. Diluvian flood and wrathful fires; widespread pestilence—well laced with poison. To a soul simmering and boiling like a cauldron, each object of permanence becomes transitory, a thing to be eschewed—chopped down in the manner of wood, but this is not how we are meant to be. God made us hungry not for to starve, but to feast. The snake that tempted Eve persists, slithering in your hand, and the rain falling harder with every ardent breath soaks through to the skin and down deeper still, revealing what seems to be a symbiosis in the wreathing but is really a kind of mutual parasitism, and in this dynamic set against a backdrop forged on hierarchies, there always has to be a sacrificial lamb. Living and dying in silence. It could’ve been either.

reviews.text: An absolute triumph of neo-pulp thrills without an ounce of irony. From end to end, it’s nothing but hair-raising action, gigantic landscapes punctured by explosions, and stuntmen (seemingly) dying. Michelle Yeoh is at maximum charm as an adventurer who fancies a rope dart (*cough*notawhip*cough*), and while she sometimes gets pushed aside to make way for a growing cast of characters, each of them get something to do - evev Richard Ng’s goofy thief gets a fun little arc that ends with him carrying around a hundred guns on his back. I understand the non-stop set-pieces can be exhausting to some, but not me!

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: This was I rewatch that I enjoyed so much it felt like a first time watch all over again; in fact, I think this cements "Magnificent Warriors" as my favorite Michelle Yeoh film. A film that asks the question, 'What if Indiana Jones but Michelle Yeoh?' and to that I reply, 'Two tickets, please.' Yeoh dives into the film's (numerous) action sequences with athleticism and moxie to spare; her co-star Derek Yee is a capable enough hero but wisely never attempts to upstage his leading lady—and how could he? And "Magnificent Warriors" is almost as hilarious as a Stephen Chow flick, thanks in large part to the supporting efforts of Richard Ng.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: A self-consciously Hollywood-esque period adventure with Michelle Yeoh as an Indiana Jones-inspired hero who helps a small Inner Mongolian town resist the Japanese with the help of Richard Ng and Derek Yee. Relentlessly-paced, with a series of show-stopping action scenes (including a mid-film highlight where Yeoh takes on seemingly the whole Japanese Army single-handed), a light touch with the comic elements (a well-modulated performance from Richard Ng, which is something I didn't think I'd ever see, much as I love the guy) and maybe the prettiest cinematography I've seen from an 80s Hong Kong action film (director David Chung was a star DP of the Hong Kong New Wave, and that experience is much more in evidence here than his previous collaboration with Yeoh, Royal Warriors). The only real problem is the score, which features a nice martial trumpet fanfare that gets repeated again and again and again. I can still hear it.

reviews.text: An Indiana Jones style adventure come kung fu movie starring the great Michelle Yeoh. Magnificent Warriors features Yeoh as an airplane pilot tasked to rescue the ruler of a city where the invading Japanese forces plan to build a poison gas factory. The film nicely sets the tone in the opening - showcasing the 1930s period setting and then delivering an explosive action sequence that sees Yeoh whipping and kicking a load of men into submission. The film keeps up a heady pace with a mix of well choreographed action scenes and goofy hijinks, along with some inventive use of weapons. The tone is kept generally light and breezy, but the body count in this is still off the charts.…

reviews.text: This Indiana Jones inspired action adventure is even better then I remember it. A fun and lighthearted 90 minutes non-stop action thrill ride with plenty of gunfights, explosions and excellent choreographed hard-hitting fights. And the lovely Michelle Yeoh, in her absolute prime, right in the middle of it all. A Hong Kong action movie fan can’t ask for much more. The cast, cinematography and production values show, that Magnificent Warriors had a considerable budget behind it. It’s now out on Blu-ray in the US and the UK. Buy, watch, enjoy!

reviews.text: Goddamn, this is one of the most violent films ever made. The documentary-like shooting makes it all the more gripping, and the black humor even more disturbing. Man Bites Dog doesn't reach the level of violence of Cannibal Holocaust, but it’s more intense and powerful because the setting and atmosphere are ordinary: an everyday life in an average town that could be mine or yours. In fact, the literal translation of the original title is “It Happened in Your Neighborhood.” Basically, whatever happens in this film could happen to you. It unfolds in such a random way that fear is useless, and with such ruthlessness that it feels scarily democratic.

reviews.text: Manon des Sources continues the profound exploration of human nature that Jean de Florette began, shifting its focus toward revenge and the moral ambiguity that comes with it. What makes these films so powerful is their refusal to paint anything in black and white. Every character exists in a moral gray area, no one is entirely right or wrong. Even Manon, whose vengeance is completely justified, ends up hurting people who had no hand in the past injustices. How far can revenge go before it becomes its own kind of cruelty? At what point does justice blur into something else? And yet, she has every right to do what she does. That tension, that complexity, is what makes the film…

Through the anger and desperate frustration displayed by the farmers, I was reminded of the scene in Chinatown where Nicholson is amusingly looking at the sheep invading the L.A. council while farmers protest the absence of water. Watching Berri's films before Chinatown would be recommended, if only to give you an idea of how precious water is, which makes Manon's vengeance even more delicious.

reviews.author: James (Schaffrillas)
reviews.text: Manos: The Hands of Fate was praised for its visual effects, performances, production values, direction, score, cinematography, story and emotional depth. Among other awards, it was nominated for 14 Academy Awards and won 11, including Best Picture and Best Director, tying Ben-Hur (1959) for the most Academy Awards won by a film. With an initial worldwide gross of over $1.84 billion, Manos: The Hands of Fate was the first film to reach the billion-dollar mark. It was the highest-grossing film of all time until Avatar (2009) surpassed it in 2010. A number of re-releases have pushed the film's worldwide total to $2.257 billion, making it the second film to gross more than $2 billion worldwide after Avatar. It was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry in 2017.

Awkward shot lengths and jump cuts, blurred focus, and stilted out-of-sync dialogue merge into this sustained, ugly seepage of dread, inadvertently conjured by sheer ineptitude and a spring-wound 16mm camera's operational idiosyncrasies.

reviews.text: "Mark of the Devil" is a 1970 exploitation folk horror directed by Michael Armstrong. The film makes for an interesting blend, as every bit of it is a colonialism-based witch-hunting film but holds embellished torture exploitation elements in completely over the top design. Many folklore laden films often display a naturalism element in their delivery, not necessarily deterring from some scenes of violence, but still not exerting itself to over-the-top shock gore to go counter the organic element it has already set up. "Mark of the Devil" throws any candor of that build right out the window, simply doing a balancing act of naturalism and almost schlock. reviews.text: Trippy little slice of 70s electro funkadelic New York sleaze. More of procedural than proto slasher, was sort of surprised how tame this was compared to other titles of the era. Muzak for the exploitation crowd, makes some pretty wild choices narratively. Goofy at times, drags its ass at others, has a silly aimlessness to it to keep you groovin' along. Randomly weaves needle drops of Grieg, Tchaikovsky, and some Atari 64 new wave 8 bit synth pop into this juicy tapestry of kitschy psychotronic wallpapers, leisure suit Larrys, organ solos, shag carpet and dirty New York City landscapes. Really bizarre stuff. Barely vulgar, hardly shocking, but captivating enough to not regret my purchase. Is it just me or does George Dzundza not look like he should be in a Meatloaf cover band?

reviews.text: ​In some ways, Meadowland reminds me a lot of Rabbit Hole from five years ago, since both films wrestle with spouses who’ve become beasts of burden to losing a young child. Unnecessarily, Meadowland begins with their son's actual disappearance from a gas station only to immediately leap ahead one year after, picking up with married couple Sarah (Olivia Wilde) and Phil's (Luke Wilson) emotional fallout and opposing coping methods. It’s the exact same space to which John Cameron Mitchell's suburban couple belonged, and to be fair, his film eventually does include this scene more or less as well. But it comes at a pivotal point—not just as exposition—and with inspired intent amidst many other potent subtleties connecting that couple to…

reviews.author: Sara Clements
reviews.text: We all know the name Medusa: a being of Greek mythology with venomous snakes in place of hair and whose gaze turns men to stone. Some scholars believe she was born with this appearance and power, while others say she was once a beautiful maiden who was changed into a monster by Athena as punishment for desecrating her temple after being assaulted by Poseidon. But who really is the monster? That's a question pondered in writer-director Anita Rocha da Silveira's latest film, one where the Medusas and Athenas of the world are in constant battle.

reviews.text: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Once & Always comes 30 years after the original series. A series that shaped my childhood (despite being 10 years before my time) and made me fall in love with ever interpretation of the Power Rangers to date. Now, is this special good? No, not exactly, it’s obviously made on a small budget and it shows…but I grew up watching Mighty Morphin Power Rangers so seeing most of them back decades later is a joy and made me incredibly nostalgic for my childhood. I’m biased, yes, but Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Once and Always, unlocked so many memories for me that it’s hard not to love it.

reviews.author: Henry007
reviews.text: In "Mutter muss weg" geht es um den von Bastian Pastewka gespielten Tristan, einen von der dominanten Mutter beherrschten Totalversager. Dem begegnet auf dem Heimweg von einer Therapiesitzung ein netter Mann namens Josip, der kurzerhand anbietet, die Mutter zu töten. Tristan, der seinen wahrsten innersten Wunsch erfüllt sieht, aber selbst zu feige ist jemals etwas gegen seine Mutter zu sagen, geschweige denn etwas zu unternehme willigt ein. Aber die Mutter, gespielt von Judy Winter, überlebt und zeigt sich danach von einer sehr gütigen Seite. Also will Tristan den Mordauftrag zurückziehen. Das aber geht nicht so einfach, denn Josip hat den Job längst weiterverkauft. Was folgt, ist eine turbulente Komödie, die von schrägen Verwicklungen, verblüffenden Momenten und wunderschönen Bildern nur so…

reviews.author: Realkatan
reviews.text: Bei „Mutter muss weg“ haben die Drehbuchschreiber viel gewagt: Schwarze Komödie, Sozialkritik, Mystery, Haken schlagende Story und sogar mehrere kleine Verbeugungen in Richtung des italienischen Giallo aus den 60/70er-Jahren. Nur leider ist das Ergebnis nicht sehr gelungen, was zum Teil an einen völlig überforderten Bastian Pastewka liegt, der mir die Motivation seiner Figur nicht näher bringen kann. Und auch die Story ist eher eine Ansammlung kurzer Geschichten als eine stimmige Erzählung. Da kann auch die stimmgewaltige Judy Winter nichts retten. Es hätte schlimmer kommen können und ist zu kurz um mich richtig ärgerlich zu machen. Und wenn der Regisseur Edward Berger zuerst so etwas abliefern musste, um später „Konklave“ und „im Westen nichts Neues“ auf die Beine zu stellen, bin ich milde gestimmt.

reviews.text: What's particularly fascinating, especially when you're only a couple of hours away from here, is the sense of closeness and relevance it imparts. Monrovia, while seemingly small and typical of many Midwestern towns, much like the one I am from in the region, holds a unique cultural snapshot that might mirror or contrast with your own experiences. The film doesn't shy away from the complexities of small-town life, from the mundane to the profound. The distance between where you live and where the film is set could make you reflect on the familiar and unknown aspects of a nearby place, there's a quiet, almost unexpected intimacy in seeing a documentary on a place so physically close, yet emotionally distant, in terms of your own connection to it.

reviews.author: brendanowicz
reviews.text: Unlike Aspen, where Wiseman’s gaze seemed often contemptuous of his subjects, I think he goes to great lengths not to pass judgment on the people of Monrovia. But the film is scathing in its assessment of the health and outlook of this community. Any doubt about Wiseman’s perspective was removed by the mattress scene: a salesman extolling the virtues of a Tempur-Pedic mattress by holding up a jar filled, he says, with a yellow fluid approximating how much sweat is annually absorbed by inferior mattresses. The sales pitch, crucially, takes place in a gymnasium. This town is too small and cloistered to support a local mattress store, so they wait for a traveling salesman to pitch them on a better way. By their own neglect or some amalgamation of external forces that have left them to stagnate, this town, effectively, is sleeping in its own filth.

reviews.author: Vadim Rizov
reviews.text: "Monrovia is a pure case study in 'fly-over country,' a tiny town whose demographics shifted from 99.2% white in the 2000 census to 97.3% in the 2010 census. In the culture wars we will all be pleased to engage in until our deaths (the way things are going), there are, broadly speaking, two stances on this type of community. There’s the anti-, 'What’s the Matter with Kansas?' case, which isn’t all that new and doesn’t really require much explicating (hotbeds of xenophobia and racism, a lust to impose reactionary mores on the populace). The pro stance is equally familiar, if no less reductive; white small-town America’s seemingly undistinguished nature belies deep values worth fighting for, ones which depraved coastal elites, blinded as they are by cocaine and sodomy, are powerless to recognize."

reviews.author: Wes
reviews.text: There's a fear of sincerity in my country, I've found, and it hurts our horror. Being afraid of something requires an admission of vulnerability, which is alien territory for the archetypically stoic New Zealander. Our horror is usually arch, deadpan, sarcastic - anything to escape discomfort. It's with this in mind that I was overjoyed to find that this film, while by no means humourless, was a genuine crack at a ghost story.

reviews.author: Chris Hormann
reviews.text: A film ripe for rediscovery, that marked the beginning of the remarkable Gaylene Preston's feature film career. It's a seriously good thriller with more than a touch of black humour but also one which has the stamp of the female voice all over it, no more so than in Heather Bolton's chief protagonist Meg. Come for the scares but stay for some beautiful camerawork and lighting and for this Wellington resident, it captures the city before glass towers started to take over though thankfully there is much that remains recognisable.

This adaptation of Elizabeth Jane Howard's ghost story has a cozy and charming dimension, centered as it is around a spirited ginger gal who makes a nicely down-to-earth heroine (yay for redheads!)... but the coziness is somewhat dispelled as the snare of patriarchy (Meg's world having an extensive supply of shitty men) starts to tighten around Meg's throat.

reviews.text: I feel like this film is such a heartwarming letter from a past that truly felt different. There’s a gentleness to it that’s hard to come by now, a sincerity that makes you want to believe in the goodness of people again. National Velvet offers something simple but truly profound, a way of looking at life through kindness, patience, and moral clarity. It’s sweet, unapologetically so, and there’s real comfort in that sentimentality. The film feels like a reminder that believing in people, trusting them, and choosing to care are not naïve acts, but necessary ones. And what National Velvet does best is how it frames ambition without cynicism. It tells a cautionary yet hopeful tale about winning against all…

reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: It's Oscar season, so let's dig into Golden Age nominees, forgotten to generations but still alive on Letterboxd. This one is quintessential Louis B. Mayer-approved MGM family melodrama. Wholesome, romantic, idealized postcards from a pop-up book brought to life; dense colors, denser costumes, even denser art direction. A pandora's box of classic movie star icons, from Mickey Rooney to Donald Crisp to Anne Revere (who actually won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress) to a teenage Angela Lansbury (who as of February 2022 is 96-years-old, god bless her) to the star of the show, a 12-year-old Liz Taylor. She's shocking to look at in this. Liz has a wide-eyed thousand-yard stare to her eyes, like Medusa was a child from Village of the Damned. After puzzling for a while, I concluded that she would have made a terrifying Reagan in The Exorcist circa 1944. Frightening simply to imagine. National Velvet? More like National Nightmare.

reviews.author: Lowbacca
reviews.text: Yes, this largely just is a lot of people talking about their own takes on heroes and villains, at points only feeling somewhat loosely grouped on theme and there's not necessarily a distinct throughline on this. However, where this makes up for that (in my mind) is that there really aren't many people that feel particularly unnecessary. This isn't just what do people think about the villains in DC Comics, or even what do fans think, but it's what a whole lot of people involved in telling those stories think about the nature of villains and their relationships to heroes. With that, this does feel like it's providing real insight as it's not just speculation or analysis but also allows a lot of people to explain exactly why they made the choices they did. That rises it up well above something that wasn't as prominently featuring creators.

I have some rather fundamental disagreements on what makes a villain interesting, fun, or important. These aren't my characters, so I will never say that these interpretations and philosophies here are "wrong," but that they do expose why I have large disconnects with a decent chunk of DC stories. Damn shame, because I think the character designs themselves are some of the best in all of fiction.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This anthology is great fun and a super tribute to HP Lovecraft! Like all anthologies, it hinges on the success of its individual stories; and really it doesn't disappoint in that respect. All three greatly benefit from a thoroughly nihilistic tone and some absolutely wonderful practical special effects. The three stories take influence from various Lovecraft tales; but only the second one really bears a close resemblance to the story it is based on. Still, all the themes featured will be familiar to fans of the great writer. The stories themselves are inventive and really don't hold back on the gore either. The final segment in particular is thoroughly nasty! Despite the fact that the film generally is quite dark,…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Neo Tokyo" is a 1987 anthology anime, assembling the works of three collaborative directors all showcasing a visioned story from the collective works of Japanese science fiction writer Taku Mayumura. As each director is given their piece to present, the assembled order starts with director Rintaro featuring a segment entitled "Labyrinth Labyrinthos", Yoshiaki Kawajiri directing a segment entitled "The Running Man", and finally Katsuhiro Otomo presenting a work entitled "Construction Cancellation Order". Each director who helmed their own unique style really adds a tonal difference in process of animation as well as storytelling difference, as the each of the directors wrote their translations of Mayumura's stories for the screen to fit their respective mold.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Though I am having some difficulty tracking down sources on it at the moment, I have always heard that Federico Fellini signed on to Spirits of the Dead expecting the other segments of the film to be directed by Bunuel and Welles, only to be stuck with Vadim and Malle in the finished work. Simon of the Desert also sprung out of a potential omnibus which would have once again paired Bunuel with Fellini, only for plans to fall apart, leaving the short. It’s a hard balancing act finding directors that can stand as equals, or produce work that won’t cast a shadow over lesser collaborators.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Purging the evil from its digital tool, rewiring it to serve the subjugated and redirecting it against the subjugators. Dogmatism built up over centuries of rule are split by the atom and soon an entirely new array of futures becomes possible. Anti-technological technology; it is not inherent but in how we use them, and where one destroys the earth the other unites despite both wielding the same tool. Would they allow such things to exist if it meant those they subjugate could use them as well? Neptune Frost mines the inherent contradictions born out of colonial exploitation and how such enterprises are built on unspoken hypocrisy.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: “Neptune Frost”—the dense Afrofuturist film from co-directors Saul Williams and Anisia Uzeyman—holds many resplendent identities at once: It’s a musical; it’s an intersex narrative; it’s a technological allegory espousing anticapitalist and anticolonialist views. It’s a collective dream coated in a blue lacquer dancing on the edge of something unrecognizable, something wholly transcendent. And it arrives with an exceptional display of bravura.

reviews.text: From a traditional narrative perspective, Neptune Frost is an incoherent, poorly paced mess. However, one would be unwise to dismiss it out of hand based on that, particularly as the film is not trying to do anything that could reasonably be called "traditional." Its production design and costume work are exceptional, and the whole Afrofuturism aesthetic in general is so neat. Perhaps no surprise given Saul Williams' background, the music is wonderful. Sometimes a film comes along that isn't necessarily "good" by conventional metrics, yet provides something unique that has value in a different manner.

reviews.text: Tempo ist die Devise, bei dieser eher unbekannten neuseeländischen Action-Perle von Geoff Murphy, der uns später in seiner Karriere neben Young Guns 2 auch noch Freejack beschert hat!Der gute Mann hat ein Auge für schweißtreibende Action, und das beweisen schon seine frühen Kiwi-Filme, die er Anfang der 80er Jahre in seinem Heimatland drehte.Im Kern ist Stirb niemals allein eine knapp 90-minütige Verfolgungsjagd quer durch Neuseeland - und das zu Land, in der Luft und mit allem amöglichen Gefährt, dass einem kaum Zeit zum Verschnaufen bleibt. Die Chemie zwischen den beiden Hauptcharaktären, die sich doch eigentlich nur miteinander vergnügen wollen, könnte man als sympathisch naiv, bis hin zu sexuell aufgeladen und lebensmüde bezeichnen. Blech wird tonnenweise verbogen, Flugzeuge und Helikopter werden geschrottet... Unübersehbar, dass der Hauptteil des Budgets für die Action verwendet wurde.Kurzweilges Dauer-Action-Feuerwerk, ohne Hänger, viel Abwechslung und schönen Landschaftsaufnahmen, inszeniert von einem begnadeten Handwerker des Genres! Rumst anständig!

reviews.text: An interesting premise of using a flashlight as the found footage cam that shows some original and fascinating ideas by Scott Beck and Bryan Woods. The film is coated in creepyness and when it flexes it’s muscles it can really play on your brain. It uses an effective lights on/lights off approach that when watched in the ride mood can over some solid scares. The film gets a bit lost in the plot at times and while there is some intriguing themes it just feels there is more of the story to tell that we don’t get too much of a glimpse of. Everyone involved shows promise for sure. The actors play up to their scares well and keep things shouty and disoriented but the real shining lights are the combination of Beck and Woods who show originality, a knack of a good scare and the promise of some future good scripts.

The first half is a bit confusing and sometimes feels kind of silly, but once the tension starts to build, it really picks up and starts messing with Martin's sanity. There are some solid twists that dive into themes of guilt, paranoia, and fear. The film does a great job of creating an unsettling atmosphere, keeping us unsure of what's real—especially since I went in blind, not having seen the trailer. The first act ends with a rocket launcher. George Dzunda jacks Bruce McGill up during the second and gets to deliver silly dialogue like "I want him showered and shaved like it's payday and South Street is filled with ladies who don't know the word 'no'." And the third features a station wagon getting driven through a hyper-stylized French Quarter hotel front. I mean, there are worse ways you could kill 105 minutes of boredom than with this Walter Hill clone.

reviews.author: Romcomrad
reviews.text: My Film Theory is that this was edited down from a ten episode cancelled CW drama that never made it to air. Characters appear and disappear from the plot, or people are introduced only to be killed literally two minutes later. The first half of the film feels like a completely different movie than the second half, and even the moment-to-moment editing it confusing and choppy. I would believe it if you told me the editor was hand-stitching film frames until a big wind blew in and he needed to finish the movie in one hour. Also I am fascinated by the lore of this town. Everyone is extremely blonde and lives in ostentatious mansions with preppy upper class wardrobes, but they're all public school employees or can't afford to go to college. All the locations look extremely gentrified too, with soulless but quirky decor and hipster clientele.

reviews.text: There is a very interesting scene in the film. For context, we have a 15-year old gymnast, exhiled in Switzerland. She is Ukrainian and the film is set in 2013-2014, a pivotal period in Ukrainian modern history. She is working hard to become a great gymnast, while having the thoughts of her home country. In the specific scene, she is facetiming a friend of hers and her friend accuses her of not being in true solidarity with what is going on in Ukraine. She tries to dismiss what her friend said, but the friend ends up resorting to "you're not here, you are in the comfort of a good house" ultimately destroying what Olga is going through as well and increasing her self-doubt and worth as she is not there she is feeling she is not actually helping.

Olivia reunites Bogey Man director Ulli Lommel with its star Suzanna Love for a bizarre tale of a young girl who witnesses the murder of her prostitute mother as a child, before growing up and starting an affair with an American businessman to distract from her loveless marriage. The tone is serenely surreal and hypnotic; moments that never quite make sense overlaid with a dreamy soundtrack. The film also has a strange obsession with London Bridge, with the plot eventually following the bridge from London to its new home in Arizona, neatly making this a film of two halves with various plot threads that mirror…

reviews.text: The question for me is whether it's worth it to spend so much time in the head of Onoda: if we gain something from seeing the world as he saw it, or how the movie imagines he saw it. There are other perspectives to consider, and while I can respect the film's approach and its commitment to limiting the perspective, it doesn't really sit well with me that it's his story that gets the focus, and not the people of Lubang, who spent thirty years being terrorized by a man who as the film portrays him, just willfully rejected reality so as to hold on to what little meaning was in his life.
