reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Lost in greens. A fascinating story told in an engrossing resonating way. It approaches Onoda 30-year war stand in a direct practical manner that avoids reducing it to a symbol, it is neither a heroic resistance act. of alienation or some sign of Japanese military madness, but a tough negotiation with the land. How those men kept living there, the fictional world they create for themselves. Some great landscape work and performance and tight control of time. Those warm external shots have a lot of power that help put Onoda's story into a larger context and director Harari makes a great job at keep each of his narrative sections focused on those daily exchanges that made his survival something worth share.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: The banality of military authority, the madness of fighting a war with the sole purpose of following an order. Very humane conduction by Harari, some really good acting and an engaging storyline to keep its initial motif running. Less about survival than it is about following a fascistic way of thinking while trying to find meaning for your sacrifices. Seems weirdly shorter than its running time, maybe due to our body responding to the long ellipses that the film traverses.

Herzog knows as much, having brought up the topic of Onada in countless interviews, writing an entire novella dramatizing his time in the Lubang brush, and even enthusiastically expressing his desire to adapt that novella into his first animated film.

reviews.text: The true-life story of a Japanese soldier who spent nearly three decades on an island in the Philippines, believing that WWII had never ended. The first two hours of the film feel quite episodic, moving, as it must, through years and years of story time. But it doesn't rush, it's stately and deliberate, and hence won't be to everyone's liking. However, during the third hour, this does achieve a kind of sublime grace, and the fact that it leaves all its questions about war unanswered is a beautiful show of restraint.

reviews.text: Essentially Russian WW2 300, just without the comic stylization. The Spartans are even mentioned, just in case you didn’t get the similarities. If you watch knowing this is action movie mythologizing of propaganda, what’s left is a well-directed, impressively slick war actioner. Panfilov’s 28 takes some time for the siege to begin, but once it does, directors Druzhinin and Shalopa do a stellar job at blending sets, pyrotechnics, practical effects, scale miniatures, and CGI to deliver intense chaotic set-pieces. Repetitive in the sense of being limited to trenches and tanks, but well-paced, immersive, and with no shortage of menacing steel hordes.

Ca. die Hälfte des Budgets wurde vom russischen Staat zur Verfügung gestellt. Wie typisch für Filme der Ära Putin wird das Heldentum der sowjetischen Soldaten hervorgehoben, ohne sich dabei kritisch mit dem Regime des Massenmörders Stalin oder den Verbrechen der Roten Armee auseinanderzusetzen. Entsprechend lächerlich - aber gewissermaßen unterhaltsam - sind die Dialoge. Immer wird das Vaterland und die Heimat beschworen, die Menschlichkeit (lol), und schließlich scheint sogar Gott auf der Seite der Sowjets zu sein.Die deutschen Soldaten sind nur Schießbudenfiguren. Sie laufen den Russen immer willig vor die Gewehre. Auch die zahlreichen Panzer sind verdammt ungefährlich…

I know the story of Panfilov's 28 Men was an urban legend but it doesn't make this any less of a great film. A definite recommend if you're interested in the Eastern Front, or just WW2 in general.

reviews.text: Panfilov's Twenty Eight (2016) is a Russian War Film based on an event that happened on the Eastern Front during WW2. As with most of these David vs. Goliath stories (many are referenced in the film), you know there is going to be a lot of death, destruction and acts of heroism. Doesn't matter what army you fought for, everyone involved has a valid story to tell. Excellent dialogue among doomed soldiers. The CGI mixed in with models of the German tanks was surprisingly flawless and damn the explosions were fierce. Another example why the Europeans make the best war films, they lived it and know how to tell it. F 'O' M 8/10

reviews.author: Владимир Бабенко
reviews.text: Неожиданно хорошо, особенно с учетом того, что Михалков и в какой-то мере Бондарчук уже сформировали мое предвзятое отношение к кино о Великой отечественной войне. Панфиловцы совершенно лишены мнимого романтизма, не измазаны псевдопатриотичностью, не разукрашены компьютерными красивостями и не накручены излишним драматизмом. Достоверность батальных сцен достигает такого уровня, что ты периодически вздрагиваешь от взрывающихся снарядов и выходя из кинотеатра ощущаешь тревогу, будто сам, пусть на какие-то мгновения, но оказался рядом с гибнущими людьми. Конечно у меня есть претензии, главным образом к сценарию. Первая половина фильма скучновата и изобилует странными сценами, в виде пересказов историй о семи самураях, великолепной семерки и трехсот спартанцев, но при этом она умудряется вживить в твою голову ощущение присутствия и документальности происходящего. В общем, получился не очень сбалансированный, но при этом добротный фильм о войне.

Wie er mit Trauer, Tragik, dunklem Humor, der Absurdität, dem Selbsthass, der Hoffnung und unseren Schuldgefühlen jongliert, ist beeindruckend. Seine Mini-Serie oder sein Mammut-Film (Eure Wahl) ist überlegt, unverkrampft und stilistisch bunt inszeniert, ohne dass eines dieser Adjektive aufdringlich oder bemüht wirkt. Das belegt allein die aufwendige Dinnerparty-Plansequenz, die sich in die 3. Stunde schleicht und die ich erst zurückspulen musste, um ihre Finesse völlig zu erfassen. Genauso glorios-präzise sind dann auch die Dialoge. Oder diverse Momente von Leigh, Weaving und Torrens. Doch über allem schwebt, leidet, kämpft, spottet oder suchtet ein beeindruckender Benedict…

reviews.author: Gunther Ramysen
reviews.text: Philbert (Three’s A Crowd) is a sort of pilot for an animated series intended for ABC. The series would combine animation with live action images. The television series would not come to fruition. And the pilot was used as a short film for the cinema. Philbert tells the story of a cartoonist named Griff who draws the comics of the character Philbert. Philbert has the superpower to come to life as a cartoon character. In this pilot, Philbert tries to come between Griff and his girlfriend Angela when he hears that the two want to get married. The pilot was directed by a very young Richard Donner. A piece of TV/film history that I really wanted to see now that I am taking a closer look at Richard Donner’s work. There is not much special about the short film except for the fact that Richard Donner directed it.

They welcome a newcomer—ignoring his overactive perspiration, quick temper, and manic state—with open arms and within hours of his arrival, set this man in his mid-20s up with one of their own tween children and brainstorm ways he can ingratiate himself into the community. reviews.text: I come back to this documentary every couple years. It's not about loving the poems--a lot of them I think are fucking ridiculous but some of them I adore--it's more about the insane passion everyone expresses in this film. The motion named in the title isn't that they are filming poetry recitation but instead that poetry is always evolving, changing. As an artform it is in constant motion, something each poet included discusses, and this doc is an attempt at an egalitarian presentation of an artform that has been caged up and swept away from its roots as a part of how speak to each other and how we synthesize our world.

reviews.text: Mann creates a much better organizing principle and concept for this defense of poetry, featuring a range of performances from spirited recitation to a screaming quartet. From synthesizers to dancers and even full-on rock bands, the poetry on display is rarely dull with even the simplest of presentations bolstered by the uniqueness of its readers or the words themselves. While that may sound like a barrage of ideas and sounds, it's spaced out rather evenly with the poets explaining how important the performance is to their work or the perennial grouch Bukowski taking potshots at the whole concept. I truly wish I could forget his analogy of poetry being like a "hot beer shit", but the other poets make up for it.

reviews.text: Marcia Gay Harden, the woman that you are for this tremendous performance! What struck me about Pollock is how actor-star-director, Ed Harris, takes to task his subject. Showing him as talented, to be sure. But he foregrounds how pathetic, controlling, and lacking in understanding Jackson Pollock was as a human being. That the film is smart enough to contextualize Pollock within the art world at the time and America at large, is simple but so necessary for biopic. (And it’s something that, say, Maestro lacks. Like I left that movie with no further knowledge or understanding of Bernstein which is a grave flaw within a biopic.) This is a bracing, smart work, elevated by its trenchant and tender performances.

The rest of Pollock’s family, who have gathered for a reunion at Pollock and Krasner’s farmhouse, are tired of their hosts’ self-absorption and perhaps a little jealous of — even mystified by — Pollock’s success. One of his brothers’ wives retorts, “Is Picasso more important than your family?” The confused, disappointed look on Harris’ face conveys a complex of emotions, including the alienation…

reviews.text: Dans un paysage saturé de biopics qui confondent admiration et aveuglement, 𝑃𝑜𝑙𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘 avance à contre courant. Le film d’Ed Harris ne cherche jamais à sauver son personnage par son génie. Il accepte au contraire de le laisser apparaître dans toute sa laideur, sa violence et son inconséquence. Jackson Pollock n’y est ni un héros romantique ni une figure tragique sublimée par l’alcool et la souffrance. Il est un homme profondément difficile, égoïste, cruel, et presque toujours incapable de mesurer les dégâts qu’il provoque autour de lui. Et pourtant, le film ne le juge pas. Il le regarde. C’est précisément dans ce refus du confort moral que 𝑃𝑜𝑙𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘 devient un très bon biopic.

As such the battle for the hill had the ingredients for a pretty good anti-war film, because both sides used their soldiers as expendable pawns in a bloody battle that had no strategic importance. However, the film "Pork Chop Hill" isn't clearly conveying an anti-war message like Lewis Milestone's film "All Quiet on the Western Front" did. There's more than a smattering at least of flag waving going on in PCH. But the action is pretty compelling as a company of US soldiers commanded…

The black cowboys remain forgotten, and this film seems to be more or less shunted off to the side as well, sadly. Sadly, because of course, erasing parts of history for the sake of continued racist violence is appalling, and sadly because if it had resuscitated the Western genre, it would have meant an entirely new landscape over the next two decades. Instead of revisionist, we could have had revitalizationist Westerns, Westerns that dispelled myths and reshaped American history into something anyone could be proud of, by remembering those anyone…

As Reggio's editing continues to be his strongest asset, there are still those who will actively choose to dislike this film for doing nothing particularly more with filmic language than Koyaanisqatsi but ultimately when someone's filmic ideas are as consistently interesting as Reggio's, who needs growth? reviews.text: Cornball ethnographic tourism, the sort of depth and tact I’d expect from a Golan/Globus production (which I say with all the love in the world for the legendary “bad news Jews”). It’s not exactly that it’s short on moments that capture the weird magic of the first or even meaningfully iterate on it (the multiple exposure-based sequences here are quite compelling), moments that point towards the media stream addled information overload of the third, gorgeously layered shot compositions and totally singular images (lots of good shit with flickering electric lights), etc... but it seems like all Reggio really wants to say here is “reject modernity, embrace tradition, look at how these poor brown people live,” which is a deeply unsatisfying and somewhat unseemly thing to build a movie off of.

Shot on several continents -- Powaqqatsi creates its own global village, linking it all with the hypnotic repetitions of Philip Glass’ score. It never denounces nor praises technology’s place in the third world, but it lets the viewer come to their own conclusions.

reviews.text: Powaqqatsi is Godfrey Reggio's follow-up to Koyaanisqatsi and the second installment of the Qatsi trilogy. This time around, Reggio points his camera at developing countries and examines how they are able to maintain their culture in the face of encroaching industrialization…or something along that line. The music score from Philip Glass is beautiful and the cinematography is stunning, as virtually every frame from Powaqqatsi could be clipped from the print, blown-up, mounted, and hung in a gallery. Despite the fact that some of the shots presented are longer than they perhaps need to be, the film is, at times, inspirational, sobering, and/or devastating.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Cleans the franchise up after the over busy clunkiness of Shane Black’s entry by reducing the logline (and, in turn, the iconic alien beast) to its pro wrestler essence. “Predator vs. Commando” transformed into “Predator vs. Lethal Weapon” before “Predator Battle Royale”. Now, it’s “Predator vs. Native Warrior”, stripping all pretension away and barely leaving room for anything beyond one properly choreographed and thrillingly gnarly set piece after another, arrows and tomahawks flying and drawing green blood as the ultimate hunter takes his own scalps. There’s a theory that you can use these movies to take the pulse of where action filmmaking currently sits since ‘87, and this one feels fit for the post JOHN WICK era: precise, well photographed chaos that’s more than a little show-offy. What a pleasant surprise.

reviews.text: It’s the kind of police drama that feels like a bruise: dark, aching, and very real. The film dives into the mud of family loyalty versus professional ethics without trying to be sleek or stylized; it’s gritty, sweaty, and carries the emotional weight of a slow-burn tragedy. Norton and Farrell throw sparks at each other in a dynamic that feels genuinely exhausting, reminding us that sometimes honor is a burden far too heavy for the wrong shoulders. It doesn't reinvent the genre, but it inhabits it with an intensity and a visual grain that makes you feel the New York cold in your bones.

reviews.text: Between this and Take Out, I feel like no one was conveying life in NYC as authentically as Sean Baker in the 2000s. The scrappiness here is so beautiful, and perhaps feels sorely lost in Baker’s latest work. Nowadays Baker maintains similar editing and shooting styles, but feels to be forcing what was once his only option. When you have no crew, it’s going to be messy and that’s beautiful. When you instruct a big crew to be messy, the authenticity falters and perhaps some of the intrinsic heart is lost. Nonetheless I haven’t seen a Sean Baker film that I haven’t enjoyed, his early work just feels doubly special to me.

reviews.text: I feel like I just witnessed color in film for the first time. There is a lot to love about Ran. It's way of finding heart and beauty in a story fueled by hatred and tension is one of my favorite aspects, I suppose. But then there's the color. And the editing. And everything else. I'm just really glad this wasn't my first Kurosawa and that I've unintentionally been building my way up to this. Because while it does stand alone as a fantastic piece of filmmaking, there's something really special when putting this in the context of his other work. Ran puts every skill Kurosawa has mastered throughout his career to the test. As a result you get what is easily his best work and an experience that is so good, to call it overwhelming would be an understatement.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Shakespeare within the Japanese mountains. Ran, a relocated retelling of King Lear, is possibly the greatest film adapted from Shakespeare. This is Akira Kurosawa at his most ambitious and most mature, making cinema his tool to tell an epic and deeply human story of greed and deceit. People acted out this tale hundreds of years ago, and Ran maintains a melodramatic and theatrical sensibility, whilst capturing all its moments on film. It is classical storytelling confined by the rules of modern cinema, but if Kurosawa is setting those rules, there's no limit on how creative it can be.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The prevailing emotion in this film is anger. Rage, hatred, loathing. It is such a bitter, angry film that even the clouds in it seem to seethe with it. What we see is the tale of a proud, powerful man whose rule is so absolute he cannot fathom the fall he is about to experience, and what we see is the fall of a man whose past has done nothing but maim, murder, and malign those around him. He has forged his fate a thousand times over in warfare and conquest. When he demands his sons split evenly the kingdom he has created, he naively believes his authority will persist beyond his willingly ceding that authority.

reviews.text: Appropriately massive and serious for a period epic if not particularly exciting. I don't mean to suggest that this is the product of a weakened John Woo; there's plenty of cinematic sweep on display, but his personality bursts through too scarcely. This feels deliberately restrained, the rough ferocity of his action rounded off in favor of (admittedly impressive) scale, and at a lumbering five hours that's close to fatal.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: I'd been avoiding this so maybe my excitement is just that it was so much better than I imagined, but I really loved mostly all 4-and-a-half hours plus of Red Cliff. Due perhaps in part to the length, but also to Woo's chops, I felt like every character and strategy was clearly delineated... not a feeling I'm always used to in these Asian epics. Woo hasn't lost an ounce of skill or imagination in staging action, and here he gets to play around with historical heroes that border on mythological in their battle prowess. When Tony Leung's character plucks an arrow from his chest and with this same arrow stabs the man who fired it at him through the base of the skull, I nearly flipped my lid. Not to be trite, cliche and simple, but this is truly epic and just plain awesome.

reviews.text: With all the current noise around real-world space travel clogging up the news cycle, it feels like the right time to revisit a similar moment - albeit one with a destination a little further afield. In a neat piece of Hollywood-friendly timing, July 4th 1997 saw NASA’s Mars Pathfinder successfully land on the Red Planet, firing the imagination of both audiences and studios alike. Suddenly, 'serious' sci-fi was back in vogue, and by 2000 we were treated to a mini-wave of Mars-set films...most of which proved so commercially toxic they seemed to take the planet’s box office prospects down with them.

reviews.author: DKW_Skidoo
reviews.text: I first saw this way too young, but its campy pretension holds up surprisingly well. Two of the hottest, horniest stars of their generation at each other's throats in a greasy, overcooked slab of southern gothic. So warped and perverse it's actually quite funny, especially since this was released just as Vietnam escalated. Its officer class are repressed headcases, churned up with fear and loathing, while their wives pop pills, self-mutilate, or provoke the help into sniffing their undies. A whole lot of silent screaming expressed in semi-surreal ways. From the start, John Huston always found dark humour in his situations, no matter how bleak things got. Here he appears to have a sick chuckle at the military's expense. A way of life worth whipping until it bleeds. Brando and Taylor give two of their best performances here, but their characters are unlikely to charm their biggest fans.

reviews.text: Quand j’essaie de réfléchir, je me dis que je ne sais pas grand-chose de mon père. Que pensait-il ? Oui, que pensait-il du monde dans lequel il vivait ? De lui-même ? Et des autres ? Comment percevait-il les choses de la vie ? Les choses de sa vie ? Tout ce que avait été mon père. C’est à dire tout ce que j’avais à lui reprocher, tout ce pourquoi je l’avais détesté, avait été façonné par la violence du monde social. La vie de mon père, sa personnalité, sa subjectivité furent déterminés par une double inscription dans un lieu et dans un temps dont la dureté et les contraintes se démultiplièrent en se combinant. La clé de son être, où et quand il est né. reviews.text: Interesting to see so many people take this to task as MAGA cinema (I guess based on its critique of the media and Eastwood's own libertarian leanings?) when a couple bone-headed screenwriting conveniences aside this is one of the more ruthless and heartbreaking depictions of cop worship put to screen. It's there explicitly in the writing but it was Paul Walter Hauser's complex and frankly unbelievable performance that really won me over. I was on the verge of tears more than once watching this unremarkable, good-hearted oaf suffer abuse at the hands of a misplaced idolatry in American institutions and maintain an unassuming courtesy and moral framework even as real systemic injustice of the authority he reveres tramples over him.…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Probably my favorite from the Late-Eastwood Heroism Project, mostly because instead of focusing on the trials of law enforcement or military service or even SULLY's simple grace under fire, this is just about a culture of unending cynicism and mistrust and anger. Everyone's looking to poke holes in Richard, everyone is convinced that he's too dumb, too fat, too fucking polite to be anything other than a shifty weirdo at best, a mass-murderer at worst. Plenty of material for both sides of the Clint divide to chew on here too, including a maybe-problematic portrayal of women, a self-interested and inherently deceptive media landscape, some hypocrisy re: law enforcement, and even the prominent placement of a few Confederate flags, but I submit to you that it's all of a piece given Eastwood's career-long infatuation with subtle gradations of virtue (or lack thereof). Also Paul Walter Hauser is very good here.

Not fully consistent but always interesting and all the three stories have their own merits. Liked the scene where the director and producer are having conversations who are actually the screenwriter and producer of this film while poster of Wei's own film is hanging on the wall in background. Waited a long time for this one and thankfully pretty solid from Wei Shujun again.

reviews.author: Akira_Hitchcock
reviews.text: 應該是今年目前為止看到最棒的「華語」電影，整部電影由三個短篇所組成，講述的一群劇組在永安鎮前製到開鏡的過程，其中顯現出了魏書鈞充沛的創作力。在影史的脈絡中這些關於製作電影的「電影」屢見不鮮，但多數都非常無聊或迷幻難懂，溫德斯所拍的《事物的狀態》就是一個把製作電影拍的迷幻難懂的代表，而其中有趣並且類似於《永安鎮故事集》的電影，我會首推David Mamet所拍攝的《State and Main》同樣是講述一群劇組來到小城鎮拍攝電影，隨著這群劇組、大明星、導演、製片的進駐，整個小城鎮不再安寧，拍攝電影不段產生的意外與不斷改動的劇本最終產生出了一個極為諷刺的電影，Mamet 寫出的台詞向來諷刺且火辣，完全與《永安鎮故事集》的第三段故事有異曲同工之妙。 - 製作電影的電影難拍就在於，多數想拍這些電影的導演，都過分的局限於創作者自身的框架，導演過分卡在自己的困境中難以跳脫，最終拍出的作品也多半曲高和寡，君不見，推薦費里尼偉大的《八部半》終究是這些導演，畢竟一般的市井小民又哪懂了什麼藝術追尋、預設前提呢。故《永安鎮故事集》由永安鎮上一名剛成為母親的女櫃檯為出發點推進故事，講起了大眾對於電影明星的幻想與難以突破的現實與身份，第二段的短篇，接續著第一個短篇的時間軸，講著成名女星時隔二十多年回到故鄉拍片，原本想與多年未見的老友見面，卻發現不只故鄉的一切物是人非，老鄉的阿諛諂媚都是她發現自己幻想中的故鄉與初衷，都早已不服存在。第三段短篇又延續了第二段短篇，這次聚焦在導演與編劇、製片三者在電影開拍前的角力與辯論。-我從來沒想過可以在華語電影中看到這麼有趣的後設製作電影的電影，三段短篇不止時間軸線性，更令三個短篇互相堆砌且有著統一的對於Ripples of Life主題的呼應，第二個女明星回家鄉探尋初衷的故事，因為第一個故事中小顧對於女明星的憧憬更佳具有力道，第三段導演與編劇角力劇本的過程，同樣的也是談論第一段、第二段中提到藝術與生活平衡的拿捏，商業與藝術又該如何取捨，而魏書鈞選擇了一個非常諷刺的角度在第三個短篇中，開了整個產業、甚至關於自身（導演直男癌）所有名導演、影評人一個大玩笑，不只在談話中嬉笑怒罵這個產業的荒謬性，並且直指著創作中的主觀與不主觀根本沒有多少觀眾在意，導演的跋扈、編劇的失意、製片人的豪賭讓《永安鎮故事集》成了一個令人難忘的荒謬喜劇，這樣言之有物有時又有點過頭的段子玩笑，都令我非常喜歡，比起多數沒有什麼話想說，或說出來根本沒什麼料的導演，魏書鈞真的非常多話想說，對於這個世界、對於華語電影、對於戲劇與人生。-對了，第二段結尾那顆畫在玻璃上流淚的眼睛的視覺意象真是太讚了，是整部片的魔幻時刻，第一段故事的結尾也非常棒，那個被摔打再沾板上的魚，就像是小顧所承擔的現實，她的日常僅是這些劇組接近真實的美術場景之一，厲害了這個諷刺力道，第三段冥王星時刻實在太諷刺了，每段導演、編劇、製片的吵架過程我都愛，但硬要我選一段的話，會是導演與編劇探討買追女生買早餐這個行為是否過份媚俗，真是笑死我了。

reviews.author: Jack Russo
reviews.text: On the roles which we play, navigated as the distance between where you are and where you want to be, or rather, the creative difference between circumstance and inspiration. Very funny as a pre-production satire pertaining to the notion of a failed artistic vision in which cast & crew alike are preoccupied with their own subjective sights, but that lack of objective direction slowly depresses into something far more subtly sad when the hierarchy of the film set arises and everyone finds themselves conforming to the social structures that had already been enacted elsewhere; urban developments built across the river; parades marching down the street; screenplays sold off to unseen investors. Often one is made to feel little more than a stand-in while playing the leading role in their own life, to which they may find themselves centre frame for a day, yet merely looking out the window for a lifetime.

reviews.author: Richard Doyle
reviews.text: Beatrice Ring is a model and aspiring actress who meets Japanese student Larry Huckmann at a job modeling for an art class. Although she has a jazzbo boyfriend (Francesco Casale), Huckmann pursues her and she becomes interested in his devotion to her and odd, philosophical outlook on life. They become involved, and their relationship becomes increasingly obsessive, ending in tragedy. Aldo Lado's odd erotic drama is loosely based on the Issei Sagawa case, where a Japanese student studying in Paris murdered and ate one of his classmates. That makes it sound like this is some kind of gore fest, but it's not. It's a slow, slightly erotic artsy drama that is at it's best when it focuses on this couple and Huckmann's philosophizing, and kind of okay when it focuses on Ring trying to find a job. It's kind of like a cheap. Italian version of a Nagisa Ôshima film.

Film after film of delicate human stories that never have much of a plot, contain none of the glamour the big screen is usually reserved for and often show a very real side of humanity many of us like to forget exists, and yet every one manages to deliver a harpoon into the soul of the viewer. Well maybe harpoon isn't the right term, that's too blunt and quick. The Dardennes films take little pick-axes and just dig at your insides until you're consumed by the rawness on screen and left in a blubbering heap on the floor.

Note that even the white woman who sets the horror show in motion by blaming a Black man for her white lover's domestic violence stresses that she was not raped, but immediately those crowded around her begin to whisper of her violation, and even the sheriff to whom she says this immediately begins to shake down local Blacks demanding to know who raped her. There isn't an escalation here so much as a chemical explosion that continues to burn without lessening, and though Singleton never visualizes the most…

That said, I can't stop thinking about Ving Rhames. We all love Marsellus Wallace, but this is his best performance, as commanding and iconic as Mifune and Eastwood, a world-weary Mann with no name the second he arrives onscreen, riding into a tragically true Yojimbo scenario and carrying a literal fistful of dollars. The character is completely fictional, but this otherwise good movie becomes Great anytime he's at the forefront. Quentin Tarantino famously called Django Unchained "a southern." With a few tweaks here and there, Singleton would've beat him to the punch.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Rosewood was the best work in the career of John Singleton (“Boys N the Hood”), a criminally overlooked film. 142 minutes long, but doesn’t feel long. In 1923 Rosewood, Florida, a predominantly black town, Ving Rhames is a prospector unjustifiably sought for rape of a lying white woman. An angry mob of white men pillage, destroy and kill black citizens until the town is obliterated. Vicious and potent – this is what we want in an honest docudrama on this subject. Jon Voight plays one of the few peace-loving white men, Don Cheadle a pacifist black man until he compromises to raise a gun, then Loren Dean, Michael Rooker and Bruce McGill as some very prejudiced and shameless men who go on a torrent of excuses to keep on killing and destroying indiscriminately. A couple of compromised moments, otherwise a tough and admirable film on a horrible chapter in history.

reviews.author: Nick Dauphin
reviews.text: Who would have thought that a hilarious and somewhat poignant film about the negligence of the elderly would come in the form of a sci-fi anime mecha rampage? Roujin Z addresses issues like the lack of consideration to the aging population ("Why does she care about him? He's just an old man!" shouts one of the characters) and the wisdom/passion they have that the public seldom acknowledges (the elderly hackers). Both of these are exaggerated to city destroying comic extremes. However, the animation and visuals range from disappointing to breathtaking levels. Even so, Roujin Z isn't short of thrills and doesn't pull any punches. I can only wonder as to why this isn't cited as an anime classic more often.

reviews.author: Boy Roarbison [fka Nag Champion]
reviews.text: I've envied Bruce Springsteen for many things. But being that close to Roy Orbison is chief among them.Where to start? The legendary backup band? All the celebrities in the audience? The pristine setlist? The fact that, at his age, he was still able to hit every note like it was 1959? This was one night where the godfather of pop music songwriting, and one of the most gifted singers to ever live, showed off his legendary abilities. Shot in black & white, one year before his death in 1988, in front of a star-studded crowd at the Cocoanut Grove in Los Angeles-- and Roy brought his "A" game. The backup band: Bruce Springsteen, Elvis Costello, Tom Waits, Jackson Browne, T-Bone…

reviews.author: Rocky🕵️🎞️
reviews.text: If you asked me who the greatest singer of all time is, I’d probably go back and forth between Roy Orbison and Buddy Holly. But on most days, it’s Roy. And if you ever need proof of why, this concert is all you need. Shot in black and white, the set design, the vibe everything takes you back in time. And Roy’s voice is unreal. He’s not even trying in most parts, yet every note hits straight to the soul.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Just an incredible performance by Roy Orbison. There's so much power to this footage. He's on stage with a lot of people, including Elvis Presley's old band with James Burton, Bruce Springsteen, Tom Waits, Elvis Costello, Jackson Browne and many others, but Roy is like his own planet and seems to step up to the microphone like some mythic presence. His voice never deteriorated and it just soars over everything here. The knockout blow is "In Dreams" which is delivered perfectly. A must see.

reviews.text: Sammy Davis Jr. is Charles Salt. Peter Lawford is Christopher Pepper. (These are the jokes.) They co-own a night club and are constantly in trouble with the law, particularly the uptight Inspector Crabbe (Michael Bates). That situation doesn't improve once a call girl/spy (Jeanne Roland) dies on the rug in Salt's dressing room and Salt has to explain that she was like that when he got there. More corpses start turning up in their night club and suddenly they are involved in a conspiracy to overthrow the British government and establish a new one.

reviews.author: Wade Garrett
reviews.text: While this is pretty silly and stakeless, the breeziness of Sammy Davis, Jr. and Peter Lawford's chemistry makes this pretty fun. While they're not the first absurdly laidback comedy duo, these guys' swinging, horny ids feel closer to early Cheech & Chong than anything else. The whole plot is that a spy who's undercover as a prostitute is stabbed in Lawford's room, but with her dying words he misunderstands her as drunkenly trying to schedule a sexytime rendezvous. It's that type of movie. Could have been funnier and when the plot takes over in the third act, it's not very interesting. But I'm always going to have a soft spot for something this successfully irreverent. Hell, this movie kind of hooked me once I realized Davis was playing "Salt" and Lawford was playing "Pepper" instead of the other way around.

reviews.author: James Patrick
reviews.text: There's nothing special about Salt & Pepper other than Sammy Davis, Jr. and his interplay with Peter Lawford. The duo has no special powers (other than wearing a dashing cravat) and they appear to lack any discernible tact when it comes to being agents of espionage, inadvertent or otherwise. But here's the thing about movies in this late-1960's era of Bond spinoffs and regurgitations -- they're not playing James Bond. Or even capable humans. The "spy" genre became a catalyst for any manner of narrative laziness, and Salt & Pepper displays all the telltale signs of a movie without any real motivation or reason for existing. O que ele faz é mostrar como a violência surge quando uma instituição fica tão grande que deixa de enxergar o valor das pessoas que estão dentro dela. É aí que a comparação com Harakiri, dirigido pelo próprio Kobayashi alguns anos antes, se torna inevitável e muito interessante. Os dois filmes criticam a ordem feudal e os códigos rígidos do Japão antigo, mas cada um segue por um caminho próprio. Harakiri expõe a falsa moral do sistema samurai e desmonta, passo a passo, a ideia de honra que todos repetem sem pensar. É um filme mais pesado, mais crítico. Já Rebelião…

reviews.text: I usually bristle when people describe movies they don't like as evil but Santa Fe Trail is one of those exceptions where that descriptor is unquestionably warranted. This is an utterly despicable movie which posits that fighting to abolish slavery is morally abhorrent and depicts real-life abolitionist John Brown as a megalomaniacal villain. Though the film does not outright endorse slavery, its wishy-washy "who are we to judge" perspective does express a tacit approval. Maybe the enslavement of human beings is wrong, but it's also legal and therefore must be upheld. The film's worldview is the most extreme and dangerous expression of blind centrism, where the violence of the state is approved but violent resistance is denigrated. The slippery moral…

The move from the sepia-toned and monochromatic industry staple to the wonder of Technicolor was like turning on a light bulb in the dark, but it didn't start with The Wizard of Oz (1939), although the impact it had, made it the most influential. But even taking 1939 as a starting point, why wasn't everything in colour from then on? It's a question I…

reviews.text: From today's point of view, 'Santa Fe Trail' is both historically and morally questionable in how it portrays the pre-Civil War era. Making John Brown out to pretty much be a fanatic villain for trying to end slavery while Southern gentlemen like a young General Custer (played by Ronald Reagan) are trying to put an end to his bloodshed sounds completely insane now, but apparently seemed like a passable way to tell the story in 1940, which makes this a bit of a difficult movie to rate.

reviews.author: Kevin_Robbins
reviews.text: I recently rewatched Santa Fe Trail (1940) on Prime. The storyline follows a West Point graduate in Kansas City ensuring things go smoothly for the railroad company as they prepare to lay down their tracks. Meanwhile, tensions are growing over slavery and the ways of the South. The American Civil War is about to begin, and their efforts may get caught in the middle of it.

reviews.author: Grace
reviews.text: Conceptually confusing and a political/moral dumpsterfire. Sides with the confederates, takes a middle-ground on slavery (“who are we to decide who’s right or wrong about slavery”), and sets up abolitionists as terrorists to ‘polite southern society’. The antagonist John Brown slowly becomes a particularly awful version of the white saviour stereotype. Halfway through the film he ‘frees’ a group of slaves from a small town in Kansas and when asked what they should do for food and shelter Brown replies “From now on you must fend for yourselves as other free men do... My work here is done.” This speech is then met with cries of joy from the people.

reviews.text: "Scarred Hearts" is a 2016 film directed by Radu Jude. Based on the original written work by Max Blecher, the film follows a character named Emanuel who spends time within a Romanian sanatorium in the mid to late 30's. Emanuel is basically a conduit of character for Blecher, who himself had similar to exact experiences until his early death at 28 from spinal tuberculosis or "Pott's Disease". In his short lifetime, Blecher was published a few times over, marking for his works holding importance to this day.

reviews.author: Abhishek
reviews.text: Squarely nuanced and impenitently erudite, behaving as a bridge between cinema and literature, Radu's film operates in an anarchic attitude evincing its confounding humor and exuberance in the bleak, transient face of life & happiness. Fulfilling its poetic magnitude through formalism rather than narrative or thematic aspects, this challenging take on mortality, love, and fascism emphasizes static camerawork and subtle blocking in manifesting the key truth of mankind and strikingly engendering emotional undertones, as it should be.

reviews.text: Like The Death of Louis XIV (released the same year), concerns a dying man almost entirely confined to a bed. But this is far from Serra's minimalism or materialism; Jude practically exults in the beach-side sanatorium that Emanuel (M. Blecher's stand-in) is confined to. As played by Lucian Rus, the writer is gaunt and frail-looking, yet also an energetic, voluble presence who seems to "love playing the victim," but sometimes rightly so; he's maybe a misogynist philosopher-poet, but definitely a lothario. "Humour helps you heal!" says the preternaturally confident, wise-cracking doctor, who might seem a bit cruel, though it's really just the times. And humour abounds throughout: wryly morbid lines ("I'll take care of you... with a bullet to the…

reviews.author: Eliecer Gaspar
reviews.text: The body is the inscribed surface of events. Fin de siècles happen twice or three times in a century. But what does it mean to be from one's age when you are perpetually bedridden and you don't live past your 20s? Scarred Hearts represents this situation in a tale inside a larger world of historicism and its oppressive essentialism. It inscribes its occurrences on a perpetually crumbling mass that reinvigorates itself in the act of living. Until the will abandons it and the essence of life is set free. A film’s framing rarely provides this much depth and beautiful muse[um]ification.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: As a cinematographer Jack Cardiff's career is a swath of masterpieces stretching across several decades. As a director, however, his output is limited to mediocrities and outright disasters. This, I'm afraid, is the latter. It's also, oddly enough, badly photographed, Cardiff having farmed out that task to some third-rate hack. The plot (what there is of it) is patchy and uninvolving and the film's travelogue aspect — shot at myriad locations across sunny Spain — fails to carry the heavy load. If you're looking for a stodgy late-50s color fiasco hiding behind gimmicks, like Cinerama and Smell-o-Vision, look no further. Otherwise, drive on.

Converted from plain old 70mm into 3 panel Cinerama, Holiday in Spain is somewhat unique for a 3 panel Cinerama film, given that it has an actual plot and narrative. It is a Hitchcokian-esque comedy starring a young Marcus Brody, Indiana's buddy. He's a mystery writer who basically forces himself into a real life mystery, after being witness to an attempted hit on a beautiful woman. Brody runs around and gets into mishaps, while the film is also showcasing, travelogue style, the beauty of Spain. While the original gimmick was the smell-o-vision, which is…

reviews.text: First, there was SCENT OF MYSTERY, which premiered in Chicago in 1960 with the gimmick of Smell-O-Vision. The brainchild of producer Michael Todd Jr., whose late father had been married to Elizabeth Taylor, Smell-O-Vision sent approximately 30 different odors to theater patrons via plastic tubing attached to theater seats. Tobacco, oranges, coffee, shoe polish, and flowers were among the various smells that were triggered at specific moments to coordinate with on-screen action.

reviews.text: Radu Jude's short film Plastic Semiotic beautifully uses plastic toys to critique modern consumerism and the artificiality of daily life. The film juxtaposes a puerile sense of humor, often seen in scenes where Barbie-like figures are subjected to absurd scenarios, including acts of sex, violence, and self-harm. These scenes initially come across as random and juvenile, akin to children making their toys engage in nonsensical activities. However, as the film progresses, it becomes clear that these acts are a metaphor for the deeper, more troubling aspects of human nature and societal norms.

reviews.text: I often forget how canny John Waters is. Rewatching this, for the first time in over 15 years, what struck me most is the way Waters addressed the American obsession with crime and sensationalized murder with his usual over-the-top aplomb and obvious affection. He lightly satirizes in the midst of pure farce, and yet even as he is saying "this is ridiculous," it's clear that he fucking loves it. I've mentioned before what I love about him is his evident appreciation of the freaks and weirdos that populate his films, but it's even more than that: He's not judging. He's one of us.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: During the peak of the torture porn boom, filmmaker Christopher Smith delivered his own take on the genre, albeit in a sarcastic and comic tone. Craig Zobel followed fourteen years later with his more political version, but after watching both, I prefer this one. While Zobel's vision is occasionally funny, the entire political component is predictably contentious and contrived. Smith, on the other hand, has more leeway in criticising consumerism and companies, particularly those responsible for manufacturing the weapons that take so many lives. This commentary is done in a more jovial and often absurd tone, making it simpler to sit back and appreciate the carnage and the occasional clever kill.

reviews.text: As ironical as a dark comedy can be. The very idea that reading the wrong prayers can invoke death and the fact that it can be thought of, is just perfect as a black comedy. And the brilliant thing is, Jude just lets the contradictions to unfold, without a sense of judgement, which makes the entire thing very natural. You just see a priest, with a blue collar attitude, doing his regular job but still so much elements of black comedy naturally emerges from those very little yet nuanced detailings. By the time Shadow of a Cloud ended, I couldn't believe it was a short film with 30 minutes runtime, such is the depth of the narrative and beholding power this film possesses. It has all the qualities to be a proper feature if Jude ever wants to consider it. Brief but pitch-perfect and extremely relevant piece of work.

reviews.text: Absolutely fantastic making of documentary, the likes of which we just do not get enough of anymore. What makes this one special is how it captures so much on set footage. Instead of just having people talk about the filming, we spend a lot of time going through all portions of the movie and watching it come together in real time. It's just structured so well and it's almost like watching a visual commentary track. Peele is so smart and so passionate, and you can feel how much he inspires others while also truly respecting each and every person contributing to the film. Fell even more in love with both the film and him as a filmmaker.

But by the end of movie, the kid had gotten the hang of the superhero game. He defeated a super-villain, saved Philadelphia, found the birth mother who’d abandoned him as a child, and gave a piece of his powers to his five foster siblings. So what’s left to do in the sequel?

reviews.text: Decided to give this a look after reading the Rialto Report piece on Allison Louise Downe. It can be misguided to automatically read the work of female artists as “feminist”, but there is something to be said for the depiction of the girl gang here, who are sexually liberated and unabashed and supportive of their collective pursuit of carnal pleasure. In fact, the depiction seems like it might be entirely positive until they decide to punish one of their members for her pursuit of monogamous, long term love. So the characters’ rejection of polite society has its dark side, and we are challenged by their embrace of “good times”.

reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: Black magick, statist oppression, non-localized consciousness, catalepsy. A giallo revision of the 70's paranoid thriller, set after the collapse of Prague Spring. It unfolds like a downbeat psychedelic spy novel, with all the flowers not gone but crushed underfoot. In both texture and thematics, Short Night Of Glass Dolls feels like it has either absorbed elements from or evolved parallel to the Czech New Wave. A cold air of inevitable, stale sadism, a ruling class bored with its own decadence but unwilling to let go, a policy of unyielding, reflexive sacrifice.

reviews.text: One of the high points of 1970s paranoid fiction. It is about sinister forces, political and sexual, that the protagonist stumbles upon, but it keeps its focus clear on how helpless he is against actual power. Jean Sorel, half pulp hero, half passive figure, goes through the night looking for a woman and can only find death and things he can't quite understand in a constant reminder that his hotshot American journalist status means nothing. He tells the story from the medical table, not yet dead but unable to respond as the metaphysical weight of his conspiracy seems to have taken over even his own body. reviews.text: A vital slice of cinema from Canada's golden age of tax-free film production. Fits smack dab in the Schrader/Scorsese wheelhouse of men-on-the-edge with a little bit of Safdie-style neurosis for good measure. Our erstwhile protagonist, John Collins, has been the top skip tracer, tracking down & harassing people delinquent on their shady payday loan-style payments, at his company for three years and is trying for a forth. There's a lot to like about John - he's confident, forthcoming, and humorous - but as the film follows his desperate attempt to close his biggest account, we see cracks begin to form in his likeable veneer. There are a few hard curveballs throughout the runtime, and this low budget banger keeps the drama…

Sure, being a celebrity necessarily means you lose some amount of anonymity, but you don't lose the right to privacy, nor the right to not be stalked and harassed. Since the morally void subject of the doc is not worth the film, what you're left with is an appreciation of the photographs he took- and yes he is talented and they are beautiful shots. In watching this doc you become complicit in giving a platform to this tool, which I don't want to do, but now its too late because I'm already watching, so screw this doc!

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Snapshot really took me by surprise. I've been meaning to watch this for years. I had always understood it to be something of an Australian giallo. It's not. It barely dips into the thriller genre until its final act. Instead it is an affecting, somewhat grim coming-of-age story—one in which everyone surrounding our lead character is a predator. Sigrid Thornton is perfect. It's hard to believe she was a last minute replacement. She manages to balance vulnerability, pep, courage, and charisma throughout the film making her plight believable and engaging. The film has a slick look, and, as a Melbournite, it's a blast seeing all the familiar (but very different looking) locations. Snapshot is a bit slow, and it's messy structurally, but I had a damn good time with it.

reviews.text: Snowtown treads carefully in its depiction of real life murders. It demystifies the serial killers at its centre. The film is not about murder, it is about a broken community where evil has emerged. The characters are caught in a whirlwind of anger, getting themselves irate and paranoid about imagined threats of paedophiles within their community, essentially distracting themselves from their real problems. They have no authority figures and feel there is no sense of justice, allowing charismatic evil to fill that void. Snowtown presents a decaying world, of people who live without hope, in filth and blood. Fragile masculinity hangs over the picture, as characters feel they have to stamp out weakness and partake in brutality. Anger, pain, and…

reviews.text: a film after my own heart's desire: a mid-budget gothic horror adaptation of one of robert e. howard's pulp heroes, featuring tons of fun squibs along with an episodic storyline that bounces from slaughter in the middle east to lovecraftian creatures, daemonic barbarians, black magick, decrepit churches, and further adventurous sundries. the action's well-shot and choreographed, it's not afraid to thematically be about a man's genuine reckoning with his faith in god, and there's tons of cool practical effects & decapitations! audiences didn't know how good they had it in 2009; something this fun and un-pretentious would never be made nowadays.

reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: Let’s just get it said right from the top: the writing is absolutely non-existent. Microscopic. Minimized. Replaced or substituted for action and style, which ends up not being a total killer. The underdeveloped writing and character tropes are noticeable to a point of hokey drama, when a less tone-deaf melodrama would work just fine. I would like to think the filmmakers knew what they were sacrificing to focus on a titular-character action-revenge piece, where some of the action and some of the make-up, effects, and blocking work surprisingly well. With that said I can never discredit Pete Postlethwaite, while looking fragilely ill here, is no question the top performer and the saving grace of some well-starved cinematic charisma.

In mant regards, the film is successful: it is quick-paced, fun, and its hodge-podge of story elements is entertaining at the least. Cinematically, it is nicely put together, and its graphic novel/historical amalgam imagery is striking.

reviews.text: A perfect version of its own procedural engine. Propulsive and very contained. Applying Mamet’s usual con games towards widespread conspiracy both serves him rather well as a genre filmmaker and highlights how brain poisoned he already was by 2004. Some great work by Kilmer that goes far beyond making the most of Mamet’s dialogue. Spartan delivers a lot of its force out of how much of a strange object it is, a forgotten late 80s DTV action thriller/paranoid fantasy blown up through huge self-seriousness and unusually high resources, that it is familiar and complete out of place, be it in 2004 or today, a major part of its pleasures.

reviews.author: Cappie
reviews.text: A ripsnorting-ly fast paced thriller with zero hand-holding and a cast fully committed to delivering Mamet's unique writing. Spartan is an underrated gem, one that has sailed under the radar of a lot of film fans and one that should be essential viewing to anybody attempting to make a spy thriller. What makes Spartan so great is that it doesn't treat its audience like an idiot, the plotting is tight and contains not a trace of fat or exposition. It is an impressive effort.

reviews.author: shookone
reviews.text: David Mamet repeatedly strives to tackle rather idiosyncratic material, so that - at least in terms of genre or story - hardly any distinctive style is discernible. The political thriller Spartan, for example, could have been directed by an idiot—at times, one thinks, given the almost ridiculous script constructions and plot twists the film is trying to sell us. And yet, a pull is created—admittedly, greatly enhanced by Mark Isham's magnificent music. This existentialist distance from the characters, which the film imposes on us, becomes a strange moment that makes a film enigmatically fascinating.

reviews.text: A rote cop-triad story somewhat elevated by a serious commitment to operatic melodrama on the part of director Wilson Yip and composer Chan Kwong-wing. Sammo Hung is the gangster, Simon Yam the veteran cop willing to break all the rules to capture him. Donnie Yen is the new guy on the force, plagued with a still-functioning conscience. Rather than explore the intricacies of this scenario, territory which has been covered again and again in Hong Kong cinema post-A Better Tomorrow, Yip simplifies it to the extreme, and then throws us a curveball: it's not really a movie about cops and triads, it's a meditation on fatherhood, and namely what terrible parents all these guys are. Maybe this film could be accused of being too unpolitical, as it doesn't address Nazism at all, but only describes the lives of soldiers serving under its regime. Perhaps it is a bit too much melodrama in parts, especially the scenes with the female German-Russian soldier could have been shortened, but I can live with that.

reviews.text: Star of David: Beauty Hunting aka. Beautiful Girl Hunter is a Nikkatsu Roman Porno that was directed by cult filmmaker Norifumi Suzuki who became famous by making Pinky Violence movies for Toei. So this one is somewhat of a slight departure for him. While his movies rarely lacked sex and violence, this one gave him the opportunity to take it to the extreme. And he sure seized that opportunity. The film is based on a famous erotic manga by Masaaki Sato. With a 100 minutes runtime it is also an unusually long Roman Porno. But the movie has quite the story to tell and a fitting ending that gives the movie an almost philosophical touch.

reviews.text: "The Night Evelyn Came Out of the Grave." Or the Night Nikkatsu...well just came. After watching a lot of unsubtitled Nikkatsu with less than 10 logs, it feels like I'm going above ground by watching this; even though we're stuck in a basement. It blends the early (and underlooked) period of their early 1970s Gothic pink films with the Violent Pink era of Yasuharu Hasebe. It could also fit with their "Zoom Up" giallo-riffs that start with "Zoom Up: Murder Site" (released 2 months before this film). Give our lead a "Hatchet for the Honeymoon" as we follow his crime spree and familial trauma. It's a convergence of influences that parallels the slasher but is far more bizarre and personal.…

There’s enough violence against women imagery here to fill 200 sexist American films of the era, yet the chamber of horrors (complete with holocaust obsession and many annotations about post war Japan’s denials and privileges) packs a disturbing symbolic charge about the eternal return of Japan’s violence. In your face directed by Norifumi Suzuki as if no sleaze corner should be let unturned.

reviews.text: Roland Emmerich's "Stargate" is a film that is both too long and too short for what it may want to be. As action-oriented science fiction adventure, the film is too quiet and lacks the tension needed to propel its thrills. As a science fiction epic, the film is too undeveloped; it offers interesting suggestions of world building and of answers to deep questions, but it never fully answers them. Caught between these two poles, "Stargate" still manages to entertain and is mostly appealing. It is an engaging, if frustrating, piece of work.

reviews.text: Another treatise on feeling lost, lonely, and fragile in a dangerous, collapsing post-colonial world from our foremost master of the intersection between the sensual and political. No other filmmaker is as gifted as Denis at the conflicted ambiguity between desiring the touch of another and having that touch cursed by unseen material, transactional forces. MQ is in the running for the strangest/best physical performance of the year (even the way she simply walks barefoot in the rainy streets is hypnotizing), and I will be sliding the moody, ambient jazz Tindersticks score into my end-of-the-year rotation immediately. Were the Cannes critics shown a different movie?

reviews.text: My understand is that the source novel is very specific. Denis’ movie exists not only in a suspended time, but place as well. It is perhaps because I'm currently in an easy mood to connect to an idea of purgatory, but the entire thing remains very appealing for me. Stars at Noon is pretty much about clinging to another body as the uncertain shadows falls over you, less a romance than longing for one as you die slowly. It certainly makes great use of Denis facility to shift between physical and abstract…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Stunt Rock" is the most literal interpretation of a film's title put into application at face value and applied to the narrative. The 1978 Ozploitation vehicle is literally a film based on the concept of showcasing stunts and then vignettes of rock stage performances. Interestingly enough though, you would assume that something of this subtype would be a documentary style, even in the vein of a potential "Mondo" doc in style and setting, but it isn't formulated in that way. Rather there is quite some informational application on how stunts are performed, but it's all written into the narrative as a formal story instead.

Usually you have to read up on the behind the scenes stuff or watch really closely to see all the compromises made to get a production like this happening, however with Stunt Rock it's right there in front of you. Famously the result of a burst of shower-based inspiration, Brian Trenchard-Smith's pitch of "Famous stuntman meets famous rock group, much stunt and much rock takes place, the kids will go bananas! Eureka!" was, also surprisingly, accepted, but with strict conditions. The Dutch producer Martin Fink put up the $400,000 budget, but only if the movie could be shot in 15 days, be…

reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: An ode by BTS (not that BTS) to the most thankless profession in the business, one that has finally garnered the appreciation it deserves thanks to the overabundance of green screens and digital effects in modern motion pictures. I am of course referring to the stuntman (or stuntwoman). Stunt Rock plays out like the feature length end credits of a Hong Kong action thriller, highlighting the best bits and those which went awry, with only the barest of threads to tie together some semblance of a narrative together. An entire scene could just be a dog wearing a magician's cap eating a plate of spaghetti. These moments are interspersed with rock performances, featuring a group whose musical fortitude couldn't muster up…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Not a ton that isn't remedial for someone who follows the craft but nevertheless a totally overdue story being told here. I particularly enjoyed the aspects involving not just how tough these incredible performers are, how much they have to push past to do the extremely dangerous stuff they do (let alone to be allowed to do what they do), but how much simple preparation and practice is involved. That said, I wish just one of these stunt docs would feature some discussion of how much of all this hard work never gets properly seen because of shoddy editing and direction, because it's just as much a crime as the adversity that actually does get highlighted here.

reviews.text: Had a lot of fun listening to all these recollections from stuntwomen, sharing their own collective experiences working on sets and coordinating with the directors every chance that they have. That's perhaps where this documentary finds itself at its best: because you have stuntwomen of all ages and races sharing their own individual testimonies that are always insightful into a world that's often left in the dusk when many action movie stars often boast about doing their own stunts, but Michelle Rodriguez having a whole lot of love for her stunt team, especially in the way that she narrates this film, makes it all stand out.

reviews.author: Caleb O
reviews.text: If you liked The Fall Guy, check this doco out! A really interesting dive into the world of female stunt performers, dealing with the intense physicality, the sexism of the industry, and the thrill of the action. There’s an excellent mix of women currently working, and those who lead the charge in the 70’s to 90’s, and some great reflections of that time. I won’t lie, for a documentary about female stunt performers, I was surprised every time a man was interviewed—however the director April Wright never allowed them to become dominant, and their segments were always uplifting the stuntwomen. Very interesting watch.

reviews.text: An enjoyable film about a professor who finds himself in time travel shenanigans when he invents a way to send emails into the past. There's nothing here that stands out as anything too special, from Lukas Bossuyt's solid but workmanlike direction to the thoroughly serviceable performances across the board. But the film takes its low-key sci-fi premise and runs with it, with some neat time travel ideas, even if you can always kinda guess where it's going. It's possible that I'm overrating this somewhat (I have a very soft spot for anything time travel, and I'm always happy to add a new movie to my "Movies that feature a time-travelling communication device" list), but I had fun with it.

reviews.text: The same summer as Woodstock 1969 a series of free concerts were held in Harlem's Mount Morris park that featured: Nina Simone, Sly and the Family Stone, BB King, The Staples Singers, Mahalia Jackson, Stevie Wonder, Gladys Knight and The Pips, and David Ruffin among many others and was attended an audience of 300,000 black people. It's astonishing if you go back and watch the Woodstock concert film or Gimme Shelter, just how unlistenable and trash most of the performances were compared to this show of…

reviews.author: Sam Van Hallgren
reviews.text: I'm just going to go ahead and make the claim that this is the best edited concert doc ever. Surely the complete performances - nevermind the complete sets - are excellent and I look forward to the multi-volume extended edition; but Questlove and his music-savvy editing team seem to understand exactly how much music is enough to make the individual case for that performer's electrifying talent and the broader case about what the concerts themselves set out to accomplish. Just an incredible work of craftsmanship in addition to being a vital document.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: The wonderful music makes the argument, the movie around the footage fails to do. So much questionable editing and overuse of bad talking heads (some of it of really questionable music TV doc level). It often seems to be taking a clue from its main argument and just let it all get lost in the noise. Still, Questlove should get plenty of credit for recovering this footage and using his clout to make it available, I just wish he trust it more. In some ways my frustations with Summer of Soul mirrors some of my frustrations with contemporary discourse, it is an act of recovery that seems to believe a huge win is just getting this material and give it the most tepid mainstream hack treatment, like "making it televised" is the win, when it deserves so much more.

reviews.author: Cinematic Underdogs
reviews.text: The sad part about modern times is that there are undoubtedly comparable festivals, but the glut of content dilutes their impact and potential for posterity, making what was once timeless and immemorial now dispensable. In contemporary life, we are simply weighed down by overabundance. Memories of the great spectacles of this age will be largely forgotten, fragmented into tiny niches, filed away into personalized jpeg and wav files, and ultimately destined to survive in catalogues as mere novelties. Today’s great concerts will endure in the shadows, devoid of the mythological grandeur that arose from the mono-cultural scarcity of the late 60s.

reviews.text: I don't entirely disagree with the common complaint that the climax is unnecessarily muddling; who needs a serial killer bad guy when outer space itself is already so hostile? But the villain's Sun God madness is also an example of the competing threads here of pragmatism and spirituality, and there are numerous other instances of the fallible astronauts being simply unable to rationalize or adapt to the inevitable, beautiful, dreadful power confronting them. Typically for Alex Garland these surface ideas in the screenplay don't really resolve, but this is punctuated by enough sublime moments (like the crew huddled together in awe of Mercury as a nickel-sized dot against its star, or Michelle Yeoh's character finding a tiny sprout in the burned-out greenhouse) to maintain a balance between contemplative and exciting. Also I just think tech-heavy space stuff is intrinsically fun.

reviews.text: Rivalling the best and most terrifying works of 1980's body-horror, 'Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story' is also a wise and deeply beautiful tribute to a great artist, whose life was as hemmed-in and torturous as any medieval martyr's. Using Barbie and Ken dolls rather than actors is strategically brilliant, reinforcing how we view our lives and bodies as things to be performed, to be controlled, projections of image, status, wealth, ideology. Karen Carpenter's nightmare was one of perpetually eroded autonomy, near-imprisonment and psychological abuse in the guise of what was 'best for her'. The hunger strike, the limiting of food consumption, these are some of the only forms of self-assertion available to persons in such radically controlled situations, where their…

reviews.author: Kurdt
reviews.text: Pleasant post-mumblecore film revolving around two movie editors and their love lives. At its best when it focuses on the minutia of post-production, such as having to cut a scene you both like that maybe doesn’t add to the plot, or the absurdities of the ADR process. The film could have been genuinely great if it had a little more focus on these intricacies - any film that takes a deep dive into the process of anything is pretty great in my book - but there’s also some relationship stuff to chew on. It’s okay, mostly because Alex Karpovsky is, as always, great in his deadpan, coy-but-honest sort of way. Seeing him as a co-lead here is a lot of fun. There’s also a vague link between he and Tarik Lowe’s editing careers and how they’re essentially trying to edit together their lives to fit their specific preferred vision. Sort of. Just watch it if you like Karpovsky, basically.

Based on the screenplay of Dario Argento’s giallo classic, Guadagnino’s radical new take is less a remake of the original than it is an estranged sibling — the fraternal twin sister who recognized herself as the black sheep of an already twisted family, ran away from home to become a fascist, and has dressed in gray every day since then. reviews.text: Magnus von Horn’s Sweat provides a brief glimpse into the life of a fitness influencer who’s wrestling with the invasive nature of her work and the perpetual noise that surrounds her. Portraying this influencer is Magdalena Kolesnik who is revelatory here, showing someone who, on the surface, is deeply narcissistic in her pursuit of a flawless public image yet, as the film progresses, we find much more nuance beneath that glossy exterior that makes the film feel all the more authentic. reviews.author: Brian Formo
reviews.text: To give a hint at what's special about TÁR you needn't look further than the opening credits. The opening credits start backwards with members of the crew that generally are at the very end of the end credits, like catering and production units and assistant editors. This is a movie about how an ego can grow too big and turn to manipulation when one role gets too much credit in a collaborative field. An orchestra is like a film set, and most collaborators get shoved to the back of a program or the end of the film credits. While this adds to the movie's run time up front, it's a fitting gesture for the movie you're about to watch.

reviews.text: "Tarantula" is simple, formulaic atomic age 50's movie fun. Brought to the screen by director Jack Arnold, who most notably delivered the infamous "Creature from the Black Lagoon" (1954), but also endeavors like "It Came from Outer Space" (1953) and "The Incredible Shrinking Man" (1957), "Tarantula" is a perfect blend of schlocky science fiction kitsch mixed with elements of shock horror in a time when going to the movies was full of pure escapism. Retrospectively, there is actually an elegance to these somewhat "can do mentalitied" post WW2 efforts that are done in repetition for pure enjoyment. They carry with them a weight of opportunity, a unique sense of "we fought the battle and now let's have some fun", leaving…

The misty, moody black-and-white cinematography is gorgeous and atmospheric. On a narrative level however Tetro rings very fake and forced. It is a story of family ties, but also hard to follow or care about. Coppola's 21st Century descent into the international arthouse scene makes for something interesting, though the "deep" dialogue and high art references end up making Tetro seem like an imitation of better movies. In the end it looks great and feels meaningful, but adds up to little. There's tonnes of style and ideas, but mostly I found Tetro long and uninteresting.

reviews.author: Max Coombes
reviews.text: Antonio Canova hired workers to carve marble into sculptures, and then he, the sculptor, polished the surfaces. This is not uncommon in the arts: for centuries the unnamed hands of artist workshops or atelier committed much of the labour to producing artworks, and the artist whose name you know might have offered its final touches- the colour blue, a hand, an eye. Even just the under-sketch: your favourite painter might not have laid their paintbrush on your favourite painting. Often if you know the artist's name it's because they took on a role that we might now associate more with a director, overlooking a coherent vision across the various people involved in the works' production. reviews.text: A 16mm frenzy of industrial body horror that is equal parts Eraserhead (clear inspiration for its uncompromising sound design of scratching/screaming) and Videodrome (plenty of fleshy, lo-fi technophobia FX), combined with Tsukamoto's uniquely jolting, untethered handheld photography and intrusive, borderline unhinged editing style. Steel and steam, sweat and flesh, concrete and rust, oil and blood; all melted together by the scummy black & white film and expressionistic lighting. Completely grotesque in its sexually-repressed, machine-infected, subterranean psychosis. Pure mutilated, open-wound, what-the-fuck cinema. Lost it when the dude's dick was suddenly a giant power drill. Your future is metal, just keep going deeper.

reviews.text: This was Gene Kelly's last screen appearance before his death. The last words we ever got from Gene were from Irving Berlin. "The song is ended but the melody lingers on" as That's Entertainment begins playing. This feels bittersweet, as one of the few of the old guard still alive for this film, it truly marks the end of an era and a career & life so tremendous that it defies description. Each one of these three films is quite special for a different reason, but watching Gene Kelly bid his farewell is perhaps my favorite. It makes me tremendously sad, but it is oh so fitting a farewell that you cannot help but smile through the tears.

reviews.text: Bomani J. Story is a director to truly keep an eye on because oh boy, such a unique directorial vision. The reimagining of Frankenstein allows for room for more empathy and I loved our lead, Vicaria, trying to bend human nature and the state of death in order to bring her brother back. A really memorable film that I hope people check out in the next week once it is out!

reviews.author: Kevflix And Chill
reviews.text: An purely dialogue driven sci-fi film that explores artificial intelligence in a manner similar to a thought experiment. Imagine a scenario where a AI chat is created with a primary directive of keeping children safe by luring and catching online sexual predators. What sorts of moral quandries arise out of utilizing such a tool? What happens 2 years, 10 year 40 years down the road as this AI continues to evolve? I love this kind of thought provoking sci-f that has exceptionally well realized world building, but focuses almost purely on the minutiae of those science fiction concepts. Worthy addition to my Lo-Fi Sci Fi List. Also, inspired casting to have Bishop from Aliens play the counter to our AI in the third act.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A tad too expository, not even in terms of its tech or ideas which comes with the genre territory but emotionally (don't know how badly I needed a robot girl yelling “you gaslit me and gave me your trauma!” to an elderly Lance Henriksen, for example…) but as far as trying to take some of Spielberg and Kubrick's ideas about AI as an allegory for parenting or a reflection of ourselves that inherits our flaws and histories and translating them into an Ex Machina-esque existential chamber play about agents who hunt down pedophiles this is a very solid low-budget indie sci-fi debut. Very good child performance at its center, a good feel for rhythm and negative space, predictable but effective…

reviews.author: Marianna Neal 🇺🇦
reviews.text: I love a good, dialogue-driven, ethics-questioning sci-fi movie, and The Artifice Girl is exactly that. In some ways it reminded me of Her and Ex Machina, though I would say those two are better films, and a grounded discussion of AI development is more relevant than ever at the moment. Lots of interesting ideas to think about in this one, despite the fact that the movie took a pretty standard and predictable route. The actress playing the AI girl is a bit hit or miss, depending on the scene, but the rest of the cast is excellent. Really enjoyed this one, would definitely recommend to sci-fi fans!

Fascinating to see someone whose work I have generally thought of as bitter, cynical, and spiteful (in a clever and entertaining way) confront the way that bitterness, cynicism, and spite isolate and destroy people by deadening the things that kept their kindness afloat. And it’s so funny!! Everyone involved is at the top of their game but I’m particularly impressed by Colin Farrell. I don’t know how or why he looks so different here than he usually does but it accentuates his dopiness and sadness in a way that really makes you pity him, until you’re no longer fully meant to (at which point you sort of see the Farrell we’ve seen for years.)

Julie Maragon is to Buck’s side, detached yet pulled by the unwanted gravity of the situation, while Jim McKay—the new owner of Big Muddy—leans in keenly as fervent peacemaker, from his horse. Julie spouts some words in anger to McKay suddenly, cutting a knife through the blazoned tension of all the land talk between him and Hannassey. Pa perks up and looks at the space between she and McKay. Buck stands imposingly without a word, fulfilling his role in the games of ranch-hands yet he still cannot see. But Pa sees. He now knows. reviews.text: I am blinded by greatness (again), or rather, clearly enlightened. Wyler’s direction is impeccable. While characters are in focus, others linger in the background with astounding body language and glares. I can’t think of another instance this good where the love between two characters grows infinitely without words (or touching!). By the time everyone is at Hannassey’s porch, the physical language is more hard-hitting than any insult previously flung in animus. Simmons, Peck, Ives, and Connors have dialogue in this scene yet what they speak with their eyes and among the negative space between their bodies is all thanks to Wyler. There are a few close-ups that are key to interpreting these developing feelings between McKay and Maragon, and in…

reviews.author: Four Winds Movie Reviews
reviews.text: An 18th century story about the life of an unusual family of an Italian nurse and an orphaned boy and their lives over the years, as it crosses the borders all over Europe from the fall of Marie Antoinette through the Napoleonic Wars. A shadow follows the two until fate interrupts them and what unfolds is a slow and very atypical period drama that takes the unusual step of not focusing on a romance and forbidden love, but on the traditionally insignificant character of the maid whose stories are often left unheard. We follow her and her life rather than the historical events that surround her world. Mostly for fans of this genre.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: All the Dardenne brothers’ films that I’ve seen so far have a central character, but these characters don’t necessarily have a character arc. As my immersion in the siblings’ unique yet remarkably flawless body of work deepens, I find these two storytelling tendencies equally fascinating in the way they convey the real “flavor” of life — living each day without knowing what the next one will bring… a grimmer take on Forrest Gump’s iconic “box of chocolates” metaphor.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Child is a powerful tale about desperate times. It's about bad decisions made by people at the bottom of society, who struggle to do right within the unfair world around them. At the centre of the film is an unwise, selfish decision, and its consequences spiral out to ruin lives. The characters are naïve, making bad choices for inexplicable reasons. Yet they exist in a world of desperation, with no money, no home, and no job. As expected from a film by the Dardenne Brothers, The Child is very sad. The consequences of capitalism means those unable to descend any lower down the economic hierarchy will be doomed by any bad decision. The film is rooted in naturalism and social realism, making its moral complexities seem real rather than abstract. There is a lot of pain and anxiety in the world, and only so much that can be resolved within our current social structures.
