reviews.text: There’s a pretty reassuring review on here that was something I knew before watching this but needed to hear again afterwards where it describes the visuals as “meaning whatever they mean to you.” This film is very personal, and how it is approached depends entirely on how you look at it. I found myself feeling so many different emotions throughout this thing. Excited, irritated, depressed, turned on, uncomfortable, you name it. It’s a film about this man’s life but is also incredibly personal to the viewer, with visuals so abstract yet so specific, you can’t argue that this doesn’t make you feel something. It’s using filmmaking in a way that feels so easy yet so mastered and reminded me how powerful this medium is. I got a very specific experience out of this and what’s so amazing about it is that I guarantee you will too, but it will most likely be completely different.

reviews.text: What a unique experience, an experience where I didn’t just watch a film but began to contemplate it, to feel it. Director Sergei Parajanov created a film that escapes very much the traditional standards, crafting an illuminated manuscript that, instead of pages, offers sacred scenes. Every image seems composed to be eternal, as if it doesn’t belong to the flow of time but to a separate space where symbols speak literally. It's a film in a state of hypnosis, where poetry becomes visible. And when it ends, what remains is the impression of having touched an ancestral secret, a secret that will never be spoken aloud but whispers its truth through color, texture, and silence.

reviews.text: A puzzlingly undervalued film from Peter Glenville and Graham Greene. It is by no means flawless - the pace is somewhat sluggish; Elizabeth Taylor is underwritten, inappropriate and ill-accented; there is evidence of Alec Guinness's part being hacked back when half an hour was removed after the original release - but the location shooting in Africa is resonant and the Greenian themes are enthralling, especially since the benighted country of Haiti has kept plunging into the abyss since this was made nearly 60 years ago.

reviews.author: Richmond Hill
reviews.text: Whilst Graham Greene's 1966 novel set against François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier's creole tyranny in Haiti was his usual cynical satire of local bloody politics and even bloodier international interference, the filming by Peter Glenville a year later suffers from emaciated exposition and temporal bloat. In what plays like the world's first unabridged audiobook (but without the author's inner monologues and outer moral agonies drowned in gin), an acute case of 1960s Roadshow-itis can be diagnosed.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Too-good-to-be-true first time viewing. The Conformist is a quiet character study like Le Samourai but with the content reversed: Marcello is desperate to be as cool as Jef, and in his desperation he constantly reveals how uncool he actually is. His frantic belief in the big Other belies his lack of belief in himself. Through this psychological drama, the film aligns fascism with a kind of impotence and repressed sexuality. The cinematography is also all-time great status (primarily shot composition and color palette, but also the DP's mysterious ability to shoot as if his massive film camera were a weightless nothing he can manipulate as he pleases). I would have immediately rewatched it if not for a prior engagement to see Rebecca on the big screen; but there's always tomorrow.

reviews.author: CJ Probst
reviews.text: Now this is what a beautiful film looks like. As I have been slightly underwhelmed by some of the early cinema I watched for Film School Dropouts, I got from The Conformist that irresistible, nostalgic magnetic pull that I had been seeking because it was so beautiful I just wanted to jump through the screen. Whether it is the period Italian fashions, the old cars or the chic interiors enhanced by some otherworldly cinematography, the entire film felt like a cool breeze flowing in on a warm day or that perfectly brisk weather that comes immediately before a rain. So refreshing and invigorating.

reviews.text: Even though I have no personal connection to the country, beyond my own Eastern European heritage, I've long held a fascination with Romania. Its relative anonymity within Europe cloaks the nation with an air of mystery that extends far past the cob-webbed halls of Dracula's castle. Radu Jude's documentary about Romania's involvement in the Holocaust is one chapter of history that I'm sure many Romanians would like to remain concealed. Reminiscent of Bill Morrison's work, Jude juxtaposes decaying contemporary photos of every day Romanians at play with voice-over lifted from a Jewish doctor's diary, which matter-of-factly chronicled Romania's descent into madness as it occurred. reviews.author: skythesheep
reviews.text: Photography acts as a historical snapshot whose contexts depend upon the objective relations of reality captured and the subjective framing as seen, unseen, and manipulated within. With his 2017 essay feature, a supplementary successor to Scarred Hearts, Jude uses Costică Acsinte's photos from 1937-1946—primarily portraits and still life, though two landscapes act as bookends—as visual references while narrated portions of Jewish author and doctor Emil Dorian and radio broadcasts and propaganda songs from the era are juxtaposed to depict the Romanian Holocaust. These cracked, burnt, and degrading photographs carry a desolate silence as their complicity or, at least, lack of awareness to the changes of Romania and the upsurge of anti-Semitism and fascism. It is the very contrast of these lifeless images to the horrors related only by audio which signify a depth of representation no Holocaust film can except by the nature of this lack, something Jude is wholly aware of in establishing this ascetic aestheticism.

reviews.text: UNDTAGELSEN ("The Exception") has the ingredients to serve one of those truly delicious nineties-like thrillers where thrills and kills, twisty endings, the effects of psychology and killer looks make for one entertaining ride. But in true fashion of Danish cinema we're not too keen on making full genre movies so we apply some of our usual social-realism and stiff acting to keep it grounded in a world of 'realism'. This results in a film that never fulfills it promises of depicting the psychological, and pshycical, effects of a toxic workplace where the notion of being evil becomes both a professional and personal obsession.

reviews.author: Jacob Hinchely
reviews.text: The Exception is a borderline pretentious and dull non-thrilling "psychological thriller" that - besides being pretty to look at - features the most mundane scenario of all time: Power dynamics and paranoia at a freaking library. That's not necessarily bad; the aspects of micro aggressions and being passive-aggressive at the workplace is not totally without merit. But all this is weirdly put alongside cases of PTSD and genocide. I'm not joking. Yes, it's so tonedeaf. It's based on a book, but movie adaptations are always different, and things that might have worked in a book doesn't automatically work when put on a screen. For instance, the setups are just so obviously staged here, and you can spot them coming a…

It’s never really sure if it wants to be brutally realistic or melodramatically sentimental, and this creates a jarring discrepancy in tone, emotion and ultimate impact.

reviews.text: I found The Forgotten Battle to be a gripping and tumultuous depiction of World War II. While it occasionally lost focus due to the multitude of characters, I believe this mirrored the chaotic nature of the war itself. Connecting fully with the characters proved challenging, not due to any shortcomings in their performances; rather, it stemmed from the limited screen time each character received. Despite commendable performances all around, the abundance of lead roles in the movie meant that we only scratched the surface with each one. The film served as an enlightening snapshot of the Netherlands during this tumultuous time, providing me with insights and lessons learned. reviews.text: The Four Feathers is a masterful example of British cinema being able to go toe-to-toe with 1930's Hollywood escapism. It's one of the great adventure films that no one talks about for some reason. I can only suppose that's because watching British imperialism triumph over the "fuzzy wuzzies" in the Sudan isn't everyone's cup of tea. Nevertheless, you've got to appreciate the sheer scale and audacity of the film. Largely filmed in Technicolor in the Sudan shortly before WWII, the location photography is stunning. If you're looking for a desert spectacle along the lines of Lawrence of Arabia, then look no further. In fact, John Clements was intended to play T.E. Lawrence in a film that wouldn't be realized until…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: This is my first Zoltan Korda film, and at the risk of upsetting fans of this very fine film, I preferred Shekhar Kapur's much maligned 2002 effort that starred Heath Ledger in the central role as Harry Faversham. Kapur's film was a $30 million dollar adventure film that looked like they'd spent $100 million dollars on it, and sits proudly inside my Top 100 Films of All-Time List. Korda's film however does look impressive for a 1939 release, shot on location in Sudan, this was a real family affair, with Zoltan directing, his brother Alexander producing, and his other brother Vincent in charge of Production Design. Adapted from A.E.W Mason's novel from 1902, this tale of perceived cowardice and dishonour,…

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: The Four Feathers is one those classic 19th century adventure novels that I devoured as a kid and was surprised how much I enjoyed with I returned to it as an adult. Like The Red Badge of Courage or Lord Jim it’s about cowardice and redemption and resonates with someone like me, raised on tales of bravery and adventure, but who sat out the real thing and wonders how I’d acquit myself.

reviews.author: James
reviews.text: Zoltan Korda's imperialist yarn The Four Feathers is a sweeping action-adventure epic, a technicolour desert spectacular to rival even Lawrence of Arabia in its stunning visual realisation and ambitiously large budget, something that Germany's invasion of Poland a few months after its release essentially halted for the time being, making this the last hurrah of pre-war British cinema.

So whilst impressed with it to a certain degree I have to say that the only character I was really involved with was that of Durrance. With his character becoming blind due to sunstroke. I felt Ralph Richardson gave the best performance in the film and it is no surprise that he is the one name that stands out on…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Director Shekhar Kapur knows how to make a $30 million dollar film look like a $100 million dollar film. The proof can be seen by simply looking at Elizabeth or this film which is as close to an epic as modern films come. Epic storytelling, epic visuals, and battle scenes that would impress Sir David Lean himself. Set in the Sudan during the time of the Mahdi this is a story about the accusation of cowardice, of honor, of duty, of friendship, and unfortunately they don't make them like this any more. With a top notch cast led brilliantly by Heath Ledger and ably backed by the likes of Djimon Hounsou, Wes Bentley, and the impressive Michael Sheen, it's a shame this never found the audience it deserved.

reviews.text: November 24th 1991 was the day that millions of music fans lost one of the greatest showmen the world has ever seen. Regardless of whether you liked or loathed Queen's music, their flamboyant lead singer was hard to ignore. AIDS had taken its biggest showbiz name yet, and the outpouring of grief stretched around the globe. Once again the disease was back in the spotlight and it took great bravery for the remaining members of Queen along with their management to help spread awareness about AIDS by deciding to stage a concert to celebrate the life and legacy that Farrokh Bulsara had left behind him.

reviews.text: Guled, uneducated and illiterate, supports his family’s marginal existence by working as a gravedigger and market porter but, when his wife Nasra falls desperately ill, there is a profound sense that the next grave he digs might be hers. Far from being the condescending, even fetishising, portrait of grinding poverty that has featured prominently among film festival favourites in recent years, particularly when depicting the global south, The Gravedigger’s Wife is a humanist fable of familial love continuing to blossom in the darkest of times. Yes, it is sad and troubling at times, but it is also humorous, charming and even hopeful.

reviews.text: Finnish-based writer/director Khadar Ayderus Ahmed‘s debut feature, the first film from Somalia submitted for an Academy Award (it did not make the final shortlist), is a great example of the kind of small-scale, character-driven, narrative feature (several of them, like this one, supported by the Doha Film Foundation) that I have enjoyed so much this MIFF. Ahmed finished filming in 2019 but Covid delayed post-production and DFF assistance to sign on to a distribution deal. Under its original title, Guled & Nasra, it won four awards, including Best Film and Best Director at the 2022 Africa Movie Academy Awards and screened in the Critics’ Week stream at Cannes last year.

reviews.author: Mike Kennedy
reviews.text: This first narrative feature from writer/director Radu Jude saw him drop into the Romanian New Wave and realise all of the potential he had shown in his earlier short films. Jude co-wrote the screenplay with Augustina Stanciu and it contains a number of elements that would appear in his later films: a very dark sense of humour, rounded central characters who always appear slightly off-kilter, a jaundiced view of the family as the cornerstone of society, and an analogy about the current situation in Romania that does not hit you in the face but burrows away close to the surface.

reviews.text: Swedish sombre intense psychological drama in which an older teen returns to his rural home after spending 2 years in some sort of youth detention centre. Living in an all-male household with his father and brother, and sometimes his ailing grandfather, he returns to the same school he was in when committing his (as yet unknown) crime. It becomes obvious that the locals from his school and their parents are not prepared to forgive and forget.A fine character study of a psychologically complex young man and his seemingly impossible attempts to fit back into his previous life.A fine directorial debut from Magnus von Horn whose recent film 'The Girl with the Needle' is picking up a lot of good reviews.

I liked that the film makes no attempt to give the lead character any degree of likability, and Swedish singer Ulrik Munther has a cold demeanour that fits the part quite well. It does ramble at times, and it's obviously very bleak, but a fairly strong debut from Magnus von Horn.

reviews.author: Ashlea 🖤 🐂
reviews.text: Yes, this directorial debut suffers from the same aimlessness as these three young leads, but the film's pulse is strong, and the cinematography captures the struggle to be young, poor and in a backwards place quite well. The place they live in offers them nothing: and yet they have no choice to go back due to impulsive decisions and a lack of opportunity. It's one of those sad situations where nobody is looking out for their well-being and prospects. First-time director Luàna Bajrami has a story to tell: but isn't quite there yet with her screenwriting skills, and some of the construction of this film felt quite forced. Everyone deserves equal rights, equal opportunity and to live free of abuse.

reviews.author: Leesah Sea
reviews.text: THE HILL WHERE LIONESSES ROAR is quite the feat for a very young writer and director (Luàna Latifi – who is also an actress). This coming-of-age story of three young woman trying to escape their oppressive life in a small town in Kosovo is free-flowing with a loose narrative which feels similar to their aimless lives. They’re not sure where they want to go, what they want to do, they just know that they don’t want to remain where they are. I’d be lying if I didn’t think of The Bling Ring while watching their transformation in the film. This would have been better with a more focused narrative, but this is an impressive debut feature from a new up and coming directing talent.

We then make a jarring switch to broad daylight where we are introduced a young art restorer and the fresco he has been hired to fix. The partly exposed painting depicting a suffering Saint with certain details hidden; teasing a hidden menace always bubbling beneath the surface. The House of the Laughing Windows is not typical for the genre. It's a real slow burn and there's no high body count or gory death scenes. What we do get is an intricately plotted mystery, augmented by an intensely oppressive atmosphere. Pupi Avati makes best use of…

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: When I was a kid, my grandad used to look around at things for sale in the world, and say, "Pshh, I could make that." And sometimes he did. It was an admirable, DIY spirit, though in practice it meant his closet was full of baseball caps featuring misspelled major league team names, their misshapen logos and deformed mascots rendered in felt and hot glued with a sense of pride incommensurate with the quality of the final product. After the release of Star Wars in 1977, it's as if every low budget filmmaker in the world turned into my grandad. "We can make that, they thought." And they most certainly tried.

reviews.text: An Italian Star Wars knock-off directed by Aldo Lado, it is around 10 times more competent than Starcrash, but a third as mad (that said this is mad enough to have a robot dog stand in for R2D2). The Humanoid was a big enough production for the local industry, Enzo Castellari is credited for second unit (and Antonio Margueritti as FX supervisor). The visual design is almost hilarious copycat from Lucas which can be disappointing on spots while the film remains charming low key. Richard Kiel somehow plays Han Solo and Chewbacca rolled into one (while also sounding suspicious like his 007 villain when he is turned into the titular humanoid). Arthur Kennedy hammy performance would be worth a look on itself and Morricone’s score is pretty good as well. Lado just moves things along really well. The Italians have no shame, but they also can do this kind of throw away film with a high spirit few can match.

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: As usual, Chaplin builds the Tramp’s character through the tiniest of gestures. There’s a moment on the ship, after the Tramp has won some cash from playing cards, when he learns that the mother of the Edna Purviance character has lost her money. When Purviance looks the other way, the Tramp slips some bills into her coat pocket. He then pauses, retrieves the wad, takes a dollar or two back, then slips the others back in. As is often the case in Chaplin’s pictures, class and romance are inextricably linked.

reviews.text: A fellow with no money decides to go to a restaurant, as he struggles to pay his bill, hilarity ensures - Chaplin would grow to be a more self-conscious dramatist as time goes on, which isn't a dig, he simply grew as as an artist and would continue to throughout his career, but this is really where the first shades of the mature Chaplin appear. reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: The Immigrant was Chaplin's first full immersion into his own creations, marking the moment when the Tramp ceased to be a vagabond coming from nowhere and going anywhere. From then on, the character would reflect aspects of Chaplin himself. It’s a turning point in Chaplin's body of work, as every film thereafter would echo elements of his own history. Yet, despite its serious undertones, the film remains light-hearted — not to diminish the gravity of its themes, but perhaps because immigration also carried positive associations such as ambition, solidarity, and hope for a brighter future.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: A microcosm of almost everything that is great about Chaplin and the only of his short films that is as great as his later feature-length work: his brave, brutal honesty behind every joke here reaches a seeming mathematical precision - yet the cumulative effects are always impossibly lyrical. It's also the only one of his earlier works where his romantic sensibility seems fully developed. The suspense mechanics near the end where Chaplin struggles to find a way to pay for his meal are also remarkably staged and far more virtuosic than anything Griffith was doing at the time - almost entirely done in a single master shot! Perfectionism never seemed more poetic than this.

reviews.text: Two movies here, surgically and genetically grafted together in a way that is neither natural nor divine. The first is a big-budget studio horror movie, with Stan Winston special effects and a ponderous moral about how the true beast of the world is man. The second is Marlon Brando and Val Kilmer acting flat-out insane while wearing a series of increasingly ridiculous headwear. Unfortunately, the second movie never really stands a chance against the first, and goes to dog heaven once the first movie regresses to its baser impulses - lots of gunfire, blood, and an almost complete lack of dramatic tension or mystery (I guess the assumption was that everyone is familiar with the original story, so why bother with the slow doling out of clues as to what Moreau had been doing on his island? Because it's fun, that's why).

reviews.text: First Laotian film I've seen and it really stuck with me, which something that most recent films don't do. This is a well-executed, if unusual, ghost story that seems confusing to start with, but wraps up sweetly at the end. The film is slow at parts, quite hard to follow, and really demands your full attention but the concept is original and consistently engaging. It definitely brings up questions about consequences and regrets. It uses a simple yet ambitious, unusual storytelling approach and does a brilliant job of mashing genres to make its purpose shine. I love how subtle the changes between two different time periods and the contrast between advanced technology and the surroundings. It's truly effective and genuinely haunting. Because it's so rich I feel like there's a lot of little details that I've missed and it demands a second viewing in order to soak in all of its goodness.

In one story, there's a moving coming-of-age tale about someone trying to process the loss of their friend - another about a lonely soul trying to regain a sense of what it is that she'd lost. reviews.author: Jack Russo
reviews.text: An existential wasteland caught in transitory points; houses are being built in the day; trains are departing in the night; the teenage mind is a dreamed state of words that are unspoken and actions that are undone, feeling its way through a sensory tactility of woods where spectres roam amidst the silence. As suggested by the title this is a voyage, one whose unacquainted outsiders retreat into the isolation of grief inhabited like a shared osmosis of metaphysical mourning imparted through abstract realism. For all their mutual wandering their worlds remain dislocated yet unexplainably knowable, occupying an eerie elliptical nature measured in the ambiguity of the living and the dead, but within that very indiscernibility is a place where fleeting memories attain profound meaning for those who may not have lived them but certainly experienced them as they continue to drift through consciousness and into the beyond.

reviews.author: Mike Kennedy
reviews.text: In yet another case of serendipity entering into my movie choices, the day after watching Richard Misek’s A History of the World According to Getty Images (2022), I got an email alerting me that Radu Jude’s short film (10 minutes) was streaming at dafilms. Misek’s essay film looks at the “ownership” (and attendant monetising) of archival historical footage, the power that comes from withholding access to this historical footage (that is in the public domain) except for a significant fee, and the consequences for an understanding of history that results from these images being held captive behind a paywall. Jude’s documentary comes at these same issues from a slightly different angle.

reviews.author: Morgendämmerung
reviews.text: Radu Jude‘s zehnminütiger Kurzfilm The Marshal‘s Two Executions setzt zwei verschiedene Darstellungen der Hinrichtung von Ion Antonescu, dem faschistischen Führer Rumäniens während des Zweiten Weltkriegs, gegenüber. Der Film kontrastiert das originale Filmmaterial aus dem Jahr 1946 mit einer fiktiven Nachstellung knapp 50 Jahre später. Das originale Filmmaterial wurde vom jungen Kameramann Ovidiu Gologan gedreht und zeigt die Hinrichtung Antonescus und dreier weiterer Nazi-Kollaborateure durch ein Erschießungskommando. Diese Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen sind stumm und vermitteln die rohe und grimmige Realität des Ereignisses. Dem gegenüber steht die Nachstellung von 1994 unter der Regie von Sergiu Nicolaescu in seinem Film "Der Spiegel". Nicolaescus Version wird für ihre melodramatischen und propagandistischen Elemente beurteilt, einschließlich theatralischer Darstellungen und sentimentaler Musik. Jude’s Film hebt Unterschiede zwischen diesen beiden Versionen hervor und zeigt punktgenau, wie hier historische Ereignisse manipuliert und dramatisiert werden.

Jon Voight is actually pretty good here and the story is dry but impactful with some strong moving parts. reviews.author: SpaghettiNoir
reviews.text: This is totally my thing on paper: a '70s paranoid conspiracy thriller involving a cabal of Nazis. Unfortunately, lead Jon Voight is miscast; aside from being completely unbelievable as someone who dislikes Nazis, he's also a bore with a terrible accent (and not a so bad it's good, Anaconda-accent either). The movie could generally use more fun or schlock or sleaze to make watching Voight sneak around secret SS rallies mildly interesting, but Ronald Neame & team choose the gloomiest and most generic approach. And don't get me started on the ending.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: The Odessa File is one of those '70s conspiracy thrillers, but one that seems to warrant much less attention than the rest of the subgenre, and I can kind of see why. It's arguably a bit heavy-handed in parts and a tad too long, but I can't lie, I kind of love the film. However, I am a bit biased since it's a key staple film in my household. It's a pretty sleek and tense thriller that mixes Cold War paranoia of the time with an investigative journalism main plot. It's often tense throughout, and honestly, that's its biggest strength here, along with a pretty solid Jon Voight performance. It probably lacks a bit of punch compared to many, but it's sleek, exploitative fun, and honestly worth a watch!

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: I love a seventies conspiracy thriller. And on paper this one sounded great. In reality it’s…fine. And it’s a shame because post-war nazi organisations and cover-ups (like the real-life operation paperclip) should be fertile ground for creating something fascinating and tense. But this film never quite gets it all right and suffers a bit from some lethargic direction and interesting acting choices where some of the cast are doing accents, some are sustaining them and some aren’t even trying. The dialogue is nothing to write home about either. Everyone involved is lucky that the plot is good enough to carry it all along regardless.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "The Odessa File" is a 1974 thriller directed by Ronald Neame. Starring Jon Voight in the central role as Peter Miller, the film circulates upon one man's accidental journey into elements of conspiracy, particularly pertaining to the aftermath of WWII and the relocation of SS Members of the Nazi's. As Miller, a journalist, comes across a book detailing firsthand observations with concentration camps, his ownership of having the book in his possession draws some heat upon him. This all leads to direct notations of him infiltrating a society of prior SS Members who still exist to expose them in any way he can.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: The mid to late sixties saw a plethora of conspiracy novels that were adapted for the screen by every studio in Hollywood and here in Europe. Whether is was Cold War or espionage and spy novels, they were ripe for an audience still fascinated by WWII and the aftermath of the break-up of Germany and the partitioning of Berlin. Everybody loved a spy novel, from the Harry Palmer books of Len Deighton to Alistair MacLean, Robert Ludlum and this one from Frederick Forsyth.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Conspiracy thrillers were all the rage back in the seventies. Numerous novelists were doing brisk business in the bookshops and in turn many were turned into some great movies. Ronald Neame followed up his disaster film "The Poseidon Adventure" with this thriller starring Jon Voight. Set in 1963, this sees a young German journalist drawn into a deadly game of cat and mouse with a clandestine organisation of ex- Nazis. "Odessa" was a secret society for former SS officers evading war crimes that had embedded themselves in every facet of German life. Policeman, judges,politicians, these men were everywhere, protected by the sinister organisation with powerful connections.The story revolves around Voight's character Peter Miller who stumbles upon a diary of…

reviews.author: Demdike
reviews.text: One of those steadfastly earnest po-faced what i like to call Cold War thrillers which sees journalist John Voight and his search for the commanding officer of the Riga Ghetto concentration camp in Latvia who he believes is alive and residing in Germany. His quest is put in deadly jeopardy by ODESSA - an organisation set up to protect former members of the SS in post-Second World War West Germany.

reviews.author: Daisoujou
reviews.text: For the record, I know nothing about the book this is based on. That being said, it's appropriate that this is based on a book, because this film feels like reading sparknotes, cliffnotes, a wikipedia summary, or whatever you prefer. It's a spy thriller devoid of thrills, just a dry plot going from point A to B. There's not a single hint of style, developed characters, interesting locations, just no spark of imagination to be found anywhere. It stifles every bit of life out of a plot about a secret society hiding nazis, which should be an easy shortcut to being at least SOMEWHAT interesting. I usually ramble a lot longer about movies but I can't bring myself to say…

reviews.text: Ronald Neame's adaptation of Frederick Forsyth's thriller about a reporter who stumbles upon a secret society of former SS officials kept safe. They're now conspiring to destroy Israel and restore Germany to its former glory under Hitler. It has some good moments but is often far-fetched. And suffers from that old conspiracy film trope about a single man undoing an entire movement before it wrecks havoc on the world.

reviews.text: Okay, are we counting this as a Christmas movie then? The film begins briefly in Israel on 23 September 1963, transferring to an already Christmassy Hamburg on 22 November 1963, as Perry Como sings 'A Christmas Dream' through the car radio, only to be interrupted by news of the Kennedy assassination. The story continues on until its conclusion on 9 January 1964. I'm saying yes, it's certainly based around the season of good will.

reviews.text: It's easy to see why The Only Game in Town lasted only sixteen performances on Broadway. Its characters (aging showgirl Fran Walker and bar pianist Joe Grady) are largely opaque, the love story is profoundly unoriginal, and the writing is sometimes very glib, particularly as the story reaches its climax. And the movie (the final one directed by George Stevens) isn't great either — in addition to grappling with the problems faced by the play, at nearly two hours, it runs far too long But, somehow, it manages to make the story compelling, due almost entirely to the performances of and the unlikely, weird chemistry between Warren Beatty and Elizabeth Taylor in the least (and almost only) roles.

reviews.author: Bill Chambers
reviews.text: This is such a deeply strange movie that I'm not sure how to assign it a star rating. Watch as Old Hollywood and New Hollywood collide in a slow-motion trainwreck. Set in Vegas, shot in Paris, yet it takes place almost entirely in a boxy apartment. Even though they were only a few years apart in real life, Liz Taylor and Warren Beatty are so anachronistic together it feels like a time-travel movie where nobody's impressed by modern conveniences. Incidentally, four years after playing Joe Grady in this, Beatty would play Joe Frady in The Parallax View. It's a cookbook!

reviews.text: I'm not sure I'd really call The Orphanage a horror film. It certainly has horror elements—haunted house, ghosts, brief scenes of gruesome gore—and its atmosphere is positively chilling, but the overall emotion that the film inspires isn't one of fear, but one of sadness. The Orphanage is a tragedy, and it's so thoroughly built upon a single utterly fascinating scene that I want to skip right past talking about how beautiful the cinematography is and how exceptional the central performances are and just unpack this one scene.

reviews.text: They ask her why she thinks God hates the English, they ask her why she wears men's clothes, and we see their religious, nationalist, sexist bigotry on full display. We see them twist religion into something ugly and hateful. They accuse her of pride, but she shows only selflessness, and their stubborn disbelief instead reveals their own pride. They say they have pity, but it's the pity of condescension rather than sympathy. She shows only patience, while they show anger and resentment. Her face is always raised upward toward God; their faces are always pointed down. It's clear who the villain is here.

reviews.text: Romanian director Radu Jude’s beautifully filmed political comedy short, in which a persuasive sculptor (Alexandru Dabija) tries to get funding from a cultural bureaucrat (Cristina Draghici) to restore a monument to the sailors from the Battleship Potemkin on the banks of the Danube-Black Sea canal. He explains how the ending to Eisenstein's film was propaganda, and that the sailors had actually had to seek asylum in Romania. During the discussion he realises he'll have to spin the story to fit modern ideology and geopolitical thinking, to have any chance of getting the project funded.Featuring numerous clips from Eisenstein's classic to illustrate his pitch, "the sharp and sardonic discussion touches on Romania’s sufferings under Soviet rule, Russia’s latter-day aggression, and the contentious politics of official commemoration".

reviews.author: MUBI
reviews.text: As sharp as a knife’s blade, Radu Jude’s latest short visually quotes Sergei Eisenstein’s Soviet classic Battleship Potemkin to dissect the paradoxes of the present. Two brothers follow a man who seems to be their father, but he's more like a stranger — a figure slipping between authority and distance, control and silence. His return feels like an intrusion, a presence that neither comforts nor belongs. The emotions that stir within them are tangled and uncertain, Their emotional complexity is honestly the most interesting aspect, and the film’s imagery aligns with this tension. Wide, empty spaces, still waters, and desolate roads reflect their internal unrest. I can’t lie, though, it gets overwhelming at times and stretches longer than it needs to, but overall, it’s an interesting concept that could’ve been executed a bit better.

reviews.text: Being Ti West's first directorial endeavor, I had a slight curiosity how this film would play out. That being said, I'm only lukewarm on the successful nature of the whole "X" (2022) trilogy, scratching my head at times when I see people specifically saying that "X" was amazing when I thought it was loosely fine at best (I won't rule out a rewatch someday). I'll give some flowers in the direction of "Pearl" (2022), but once again "X" and the third film "MaXXXine" (2024) only were partially successful in my mind. reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: The first Ti West film owns all of the auteurist tics he’d go on to refine - deliberate pacing, low lit cinematography, throwback aesthetics, rubbery practical gore SFX - but is still very much the product of a guy with $50K, a 16mm camera, and a bunch of buds willing to commit to his vision in their own backyards (shooting in Kennett Square and Rehoboth Beach made me nostalgic for the East Coast). Adding Tom Noonan as your fictional late night Ghoulardi was also a nice touch. Perhaps my biggest takeaway is that West seems to be a guy who’s pretentious about craft but not the stories he’s applying this handmade quality to. reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: There's a scene early in The Smiling Madame Beudet in which the title character's husband arrives home from work. Madame Beudet is reading in their home's main room, and keeps her eyes on her book as he enters, reacting not at all to his presence. Apart, that is, from taking a careful, very deliberate breath. It's a breath we all recognize, the one you take when you're getting dangerously angry, and you need to ground yourself to stay rational. It's the breath that you release, slowly, through barely open lips, with your eyes closed, a breath that acts as an emotional barrier against a maddening force.

reviews.text: This impressionistic silent film directed by French filmmaker Germaine Dulac is a penetrating and glorious avant-garde assessment of a marriage going through its death throes. Dulac entices a remarkable performance out of Germaine Dermoz, as the protagonist Madame Beudet, and her cinematography displays stunning use of sophisticated special effects for the period. The Smiling Madame Beudet is a beautifully sketched movie that manipulates ordinary props to illustrate confrontations within the marriage.

reviews.text: Written and directed by Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, The Son bristles with its themes while simultaneously simmering with the threat of exploding violence. It observes Olivier (Olivier Gourmet), a carpenter who teaches young teens at a training centre. Olivier is struggling to deal with the loss of his son, who was killed five years earlier, and now separated from his wife, knowingly takes on a new student, Francis Thorion (Morgan Marinne), the murderer of his son. The film trades heavily on the workshop environment being full of tools that Olivier could, at any given moment, potentially use as a lethal weapon. It's a surprising story that is precisely paced and wonderfully acted, and its impact is unhurriedly incremental, right up to its ending. Like most other films by the brothers Dardenne, the story has a small emotional conclusion with no massive cathartic pay-off. Instead, The Son finishes with a wordless scene that is open to multiple interpretations.

Her name is Julie Harte, she’s played by Honor Swinton Byrne with the raw honesty of someone feeling her way through a solar eclipse, and she’s following in Hogg’s uncertain footsteps with the shaky confidence of someone who’s seen “I Know Where I’m Going!” enough times to convince herself that she might. She even lives in an immaculate re-creation of the writer-director’s former apartment, built on a soundstage and surrounded by massive blow-ups of the photos Hogg once snapped through the windows of that flat.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: This is the most ambitious movie ever made in a California garage for $25,000. A Lovecraftian, slow cinema labyrinth that follows cave spelunkers as they encounter a Cthulhu-esque stop motion creature, this movie envelops you like a dreamy fog. From the handmade cave sets to the ominous synth score, THE STRANGENESS rewards patient viewers with a comforting, unearthly experience. Director Melanie Anne Phillips transitioned in the early 1990s and would go on to work with the International Foundation for Gender Education. In 1994, she founded the first online transgender support site. According to script writer Chris Huntley, the monster in THE STRANGENESS was intentionally designed to resemble a penis with a vagina for a face. This detail appears to represent a deeper meaning on Phillips’s behalf, and it makes me appreciate the movie—and her work—even more. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: Lamps in the dark, flares coloring half-seen monsters red, shadows upon shadows, claustrophobic setting, this slow-built horror does with pockets of light and cramped space what most cinematographers / filmmakers / horror masters can't fathom. Tensions between our characters come naturally, even if not every performance does, and they another layer of horror to this skillfully crafted story. The main flaw is that, early on, we're hit with a lot of native mythology-set dressing that we don't need. Something horrible happened in a mine. No need to appropriate from an oppressed nation's culture (even if it's vaguely done). But once we move past that tired cliche and just get to the meat of it--exploring an abandoned mine, and also a monster--it becomes one of the finer horror gems I've stumbled upon.

reviews.author: ButtNugget
reviews.text: When asked which role she feels most proud of, on numerous occasions Kate Beckinsale never fails to mention this movie. Upon seeing it, I can now see why she finds special resonance with the titular attorney of the story. Cate McCall and her many tribulations at both the personal and professional levels make for a gripping character study. Its central tale of personal redemption can leave one in admiration for the character. Fighting inner demons has never looked more fraught. It helps that Beckinsale appears absolutely dedicated to this role. It’s easy to forget, especially after all those Underworld movies, that she possesses quite the formidable acting chops. Until now, I’ve only encountered this level of passion from her during collaborations with Whit Stillman. It’s just rare to see Beckinsale in this light—and for that, this gets a recommendation. A small film but one with a big heart.

reviews.author: Robert Daniels
reviews.text: In Barry Jenkins’ 10-hour historical fantasy miniseries The Underground Railroad, regret is generational, as easily passed down in a family as eye color or hair texture. The Underground Railroad, adapted by the Moonlight director from Colson Whitehead’s Pulitzer Prize-winning 2016 novel, takes place in antebellum Georgia. Yet it’d be a mistake to call the series a slave narrative. There’s only pain and suffering in a genre originally constructed to end slavery by explaining the horrors of plantation life to Northern white readers.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: A monumental reimagining of American history, Barry Jenkins’s adaptation of Colson Whitehead’s Pulitzer Prize–winning 2016 novel is a harrowing and rhapsodic journey through a still-echoing past. Weaving together historical fiction with moments of magical realism, The Underground Railroad is a full sensory immersion into the world of Cora (Thuso Mbedu), who, fleeing slavery, embarks on a treacherous quest for freedom—and is menaced by violence, supported by a clandestine community fighting for liberation, and haunted by the people she loses along the way. With images of searing power and stirring poetry, Jenkins delivers an epic saga of survival and resilience that pushes the limited-series format to new heights of cinematic transcendence.

reviews.author: Jack
reviews.text: Barry Jenkins brings to life the achingly beautiful words of Colson Whitehead in this staggering and sublime cinematic odyssey. It’s ten masterfully crafted hours where you can find so much love and passion behind every frame: from James Laxton’s vivid, poetic images to the enchanting soundscape of singing cicadas and rustling leaves—only elevated by Nicholas Britell’s soul-stirring score. Jenkins unifies all of these elements to craft a series so heart-wrenching in its depiction of the atrocities of American slavery, but one that, instead of reveling in constant violence and trauma, chooses to embrace the fantastical grandeur of its epic narrative and create true cinematic poetry. Barry Jenkins has made a genuinely astounding ode to his ancestors. Essential viewing.

The central performance is terrific, but the real winner is the structure, which follows a sort of neo-noir/gumshoe pattern, but keeps it personal and intimate.

reviews.text: The premise here is a really interesting one: the notion that the smallest decision, no matter how trivial it might seem, can have the most drastic, and in this case tragic, repercussions. Here it is applied to the unfortunate choice that the film’s lead—a young doctor named Jenny—makes to ignore the door buzzer to her clinic when it is pressed late one night outside of working hours. It’s soon revealed that the person at the door was a young immigrant girl looking for refuge, who died shortly after in suspicious circumstances, and who the police are unable to identify. The news leaves Jenny wracked with guilt at her decision to not answer her door, and so she sets out determined…

reviews.text: I am a fan of Lee Scratch Perry's art, but have always found him somewhat enigmatic as a person. Part of it is that I wondered if his eccentricity was a put-on or simply an honest expression of his creativity. I also wondered if he might have an undiagnosed mental illness along the lines of schizophrenia. This movie doesn't offer much insight into these questions, and does his legacy a disservice by presenting so much of his self-mythologizing in an uncritical fashion. I was hoping for a more impartial discussion of his art and life. That said there are parts of this that are fascinating as a warts-and-all glimpse into the man's creative process. I just feel like he's still a total mystery as a person, but maybe that's what he wanted to be.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Holocaust cinema has so implicitly existed in the shadow of a single question that it would no longer seem worth asking if not for the fact that it’s never been answered: How do you depict an atrocity? The most urgent and indelible examples of the form offer equally simple yet perfectly contradictory responses. Documentaries like “Shoah” and Alain Resnais’ “Night and Fog” suggest that you don’t, while historical epics like “Schindler’s List” insist that you must. If the latter argues that seeing is believing, the former maintains that seeing wouldn’t help — that some things are too unfathomable for the human eye to comprehend from a distance, and can only hope to be understood by their absence. A tsunami might…

reviews.text: A chilling directorial achievement with some of the most purposeful sound design I've ever heard. And yet, I couldn't help but feel that the film was very one-note; deliberately so, I'm sure. Even so, the banality of evil can only sustain a horrific on-screen atmosphere for so long. I was chilled to the bone during the first half of the film and only felt that same sensation in fleeting moments during the second half (the piano scene, when the boy locks his brother in the greenhouse, etc.) I appreciate what the film was going for but I can't say it remained effective for me personally the entire way through.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: You could hear a pin drop in a packed house. As soon as it was over, I sat in quiet, absolutely distraught. It made me feel genuinely sick. Nothing could have prepared me for this. We begin in darkness and end in total emotional torment. In a decade full with important films, I believe this is one of the most significant, if not the most. The reluctance to follow a conventional story is admirable; each sequence develops and builds until it bursts at the end and broke me. So relentless and strong, yet full of creative flair and distinct direction. The best sound design in quite some time, dedicated to providing a permanent, horrific experience. Glazer succeeds on all fronts…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: It’s been less than a year since “Free Solo” directors E. Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin debuted the “The Rescue,” a remarkable documentary about the international effort to safely extract 12 young boys and their soccer coach from deep within a flooded Thailand cave system in the summer of 2018. Filled with impeccable recreations that were performed by the actual divers involved, the film was (and remains) so heart-in-your-throat harrowing that it seemed destined to endure as the definitive telling of this story. As I wrote in my review at the time: “‘The Rescue’ is intense enough that even Michael Bay and Peter Berg should recognize that no mega-budget dramatization could match up to it.”

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: Thunderheart is a perfect example of a film elevated by the talents of its director, Micheal Apted. The script is a boilerplate “whodunit?” narrative with buddy cop trappings sprinkled in, often utilized for comedy relief. With Apted at the helm, he’s able to utilize his documentarian background to anchor his film, imbuing it with a strong sense of verisimilitude not typically seen in your run of the mill, early-90’s thriller. Most of Thunderheart is shot on location, its story set on a South Dakota reservation, allowing Apted to submerge the viewer in the culture of Sioux – their political strife, their poverty, and their beautiful traditions. Its not often to get a realistic, studio backed film* interested in exploring the…

Thunderheart is a terrific mystery/thriller that knows how to tell a proper story, reveal elements, create character, shoot action and also be "about" something. Michael Apted was a good one that was lost last year. RIP.

reviews.text: A well done crime thriller with dramatic notes,"Thunderheart" is easily a bit of a gem hiding below the radar of things more talked about. The film is loosely based on the "Wounded Knee Occupation of 1973" but takes far more of crime noir approach than a direct historical biographic position. From this standpoint, the viewer gets a portion of the political and historical brevity of the situation inviting them to do further research should they choose to do so, but also giving a general enticing narrative that stands in its own accessible element.

reviews.text: The first time I watched Tokyo Story its emotional core didn't really get to me, but this time around the final act seemed so devastatingly perfect. Yasujirō Ozu's sequence of static compositions manages to find a calmness in the world. He eschews melodrama and is still able to evoke a deeply emotional response in the viewer. Tokyo Story is a fairly standard film for Ozu, using some of his favourite actors (notably Chishū Ryū and Setsuko Hara) and breaking the same rules of cinema that he always does (not showing key events, ignoring the 180 degrees rule, using long pillow shots), but it's executed so beautifully here. Ozu brings up his usual themes - family, change, the struggle between the traditional…

reviews.author: DBC
reviews.text: “This is about all the bad days in the world. I used to have some little bad days, and I kept them in a little box. And one day, I threw them out into the yard. 'Oh, it's just a couple little innocent bad days.' Well, we had a big rain. I don't know what it was growing in but I think we used to put eggshells out there and coffee grounds, too. Don't plant your bad days. They grow into weeks. The weeks grow into months. Before you know it you got yourself a bad year. Take it from me. Choke those little bad days. Choke 'em down to nothin'. reviews.author: TheGreenLama
reviews.text: 1942, Aug 13-16 Short, fast-paced wartime prop film about a British commando who is sent into occupied France on a mission to elicit local help in pinpointing the location of a munitions factory prior to a scheduled RAF night bombing raid (on the 16th). Low-budget studio work that's better than average, but timing is messed up. Entire film says late summer harvest in northern France, except for a few words in the beginning about Americans in N Africa. My guess is that, because Op Torch (Nov 8-16, '42) occurred during filming, Hollywood execs reworked one scene to make film more timely; it probably also altered title used for film. AFI says there were production retakes Dec 14, '42.

reviews.author: CinemaSerf

What now ensues is sometimes quite a potent look at just how the French were living under the rule of their conquerors. "Odette" (Annabella) and her father "Bonnard" (Lee J. Cobb) have him living with them, and must tread a very fine line between staying alive and keeping their family safe whilst helping the Briton ensure the destruction of the plant. Let's just say they don't agree on the best strategy and in desperation the jeopardy gets distinctly more real…

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: The main point of reference for Topkapi always seems to be its director Jules Dassin’s earlier heist film Rafifi. That’s understandable. Rififi is a defining film of its subgenre, so seeing how Dassin varies his approach to similar material is inherently interesting, especially if you’re susceptible to the auteur theory. The difference is like night and day. Quite literally. Rififi is a black-and-white film noir, whereas Topkapi is a colorful (in every sense of that word) international adventure. Counterfeit artist Melina Mercouri persuades her former lover, professional thief Maximilian Schell, to help her steal a jewel-encrusted dagger from the titular Istanbul museum. Schell recruits a gang of experts from several different countries, as well as patsy (and stateless person) Peter…

reviews.author: Wes Edwards
reviews.text: Director Jules Dassin was ridden out of Hollywood in 1949 on charges he was a Communist. The ‘red’ tag, applied because of his anti-fascist politics, was enough to end his employability in US studio projects. His last studio work, made in London through the engineering of producer Daryl F. Zanuck, was the noir classic Night and the City.

reviews.text: This movie has so much going on but is all so much playful fun. It winks and plays coquettish with the audience all the while giving you the drama and intrigue of a solid caper. This thing really delivers on a lot of strong plot devices like team building, location and action. So many great performances from the great Peter Ustinov, Maximilian Schell, but I just love Melina Mercouri's portrayal as Elizabeth Lipp. Honestly I find this movie has so many smart moments in it that the faults I do see are probably clever articulations left to make you ruminate and unfurl in further viewing making it an even better movie. Mr. Dassin is a great director worthy of more accolades.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: A film with more a/k/a's than it has ideas. Whether it's called LOLA, TWINKY or LONDON AFFAIR, the least one should expect from a movie about a 38 year old writer who marries a 16 year old schoolgirl is that it be salacious. This is just stodgy. The first half takes place in London and is shot in the already out-of-date style of those Swinging London pictures. It just comes off as desperate. Once we get to New York, however, this starts to take itself seriously and turns into a deadly dull problem picture. Susan George, as the girl, is never anything but annoying and Charles Bronson, as the "author", is too lumpen to manage comedy.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: You can't extinguish the irrepressibility of wonderful Susan George but Twinky really is a dreadful film. The subject matter - literal dirty old man (porn novelist) marries 16-year-old schoolgirl - is objectionable enough but it is dealt with in a fashion utterly devoid of insight or sensitivity. Richard Donner gives us lots of modish rapid-cutting which is as vacuous as the content and Charles Bronson gives us a performance that redefines sleepwalking. Add in an even dirtier old man in the shape of Trevor Howard and you end up with an embarrassment that is a blot on the careers of all concerned.

Чья-то личная история превратилась в гротеск, первый час прикидываясь комедией, а к финалу переобувшись невыносимой теленовеллой. Чудовищный мискаст Чарльза Бронсона, который никого не убивает, а только бесконечно болтает, периодически гоняя и прописывая леща своей малолетней жене. Малолетка же регулярно забывает, что ей шестнадцать, а не шесть, играет с куклами и канючит, чем постоянно увеличивает уровень дискомфорта и кринжа. При этом запоминающихся сцен совсем немного и для меня самой яркой стала та, в которой посреди очередного унылого разговора Бронсона с каким-то мужиком в кадр зашла собака и смачно нассала.

reviews.text: You'd think an EC Comics horror anthology focusing on westerns, war, and crime would be a hit. Unfortunately, this feature-length pilot flopped. A bizarre result based on the talent involved, alone: produced by Walter Hill, Joel Silver, Robert Zemeckis, and Richard Donner; segments directed by Donner, Zemeckis, and Tom Holland; the Donner directed segment written by Frank Darabont; including the actors David Morse, William Sadler, Brad Pitt, Kirk Douglas, Dan Aykroyd, Lance Henrikson, and Jack Kehler. Even though it's nothing special - shocking based on the names - you'd think this would, at the very least, be better known. I wasn't wow'd by any of the segments, but I wasn't bored by any of them. If this were a tv series, I definitely would've been watching weekly or I'd buy the DVDs if I came across them at a used store.

reviews.text: Solid enough attempt by the crypt crew to bring to life another EC comic. This made for TV movie never transformed into a regular series, which were the film makers intentions. Donner’s first part plays out far too much like a TFTC episode where a gunslinger in the Wild West finds out the harsh truth about his existence. The second about a drag race between the young and the old was a little better, which was directed by Tom Holland. The longest of the three is the last story about a gutless lieutenant in the army that faces death head on. This one directed by Zemeckis is by far the best of the show, and captures best what the comic was all about. And finally as much as I love William Sadler as an actor, he ain’t no cryptkeeper.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: A well above average noirish crime programmer. The story is about Tony Reagan, once a low-level mob associate but now just out of the military and trying to go straight. Almost immediately, he’s framed for the murder of the boss for whom he used to work, so part of the movie is a procedural, as Tony and his little crew of supporters trying to find the real killer. The other part, though, is a well-lit noir, full of double crosses and a little femme fatale action. An incredible amount is packed into about 70 minutes, but it never feels rushed — no surprise, given that the director is none other than William Castle, the king of efficient b-pictures.

reviews.author: Chris Browning
reviews.text: It’s easy to forget that for every great hard boiled/ pulp writer like Chandler or Hammett or Woolrich, there were acres of fine but not spectacular writers who would regularly churn out the tough crime stories to fill out Black Mask and Dime Mystery and their like. And it’s the same with noir as a genre: for every classic there’s the sort of workaday thrillers that came out as b-pictures. And honestly, on this evidence, Castle was far better with these than he ever was with horror. Economy and pace favour the crime story and however conventional the narrative here is (you can spot it a mile off), it’s efficient and pacy and enjoyable. Not half bad at all

reviews.author: CerealAtMidnite
reviews.text: This cracking little noir film is directed by schlockmeister William Castle, but there are no gimmicks here. Instead, we have a pure and simple noir plot involving a returning military man who happens to be the perfect patsy for a frame-up job. Character actors will enjoy seeing Scott Brady (JOHNNY GUITAR, later the sheriff in GREMLINS), Dorothy Hart (1948's THE NAKED CITY), Peggy Dow, soon to appear in Joseph Pevney's exceptional noir SHAKEDOWN), John Russell (PALE RIDER, THE OUTLAW JOSEY WALES), and even a fresh-faced Rock Hudson in a blink-and-you'll-miss-it role. Universal International cranked out scores of these cheap noir and noir-adjacent films during the late 1940s and throughout the 1950s. Some are more memorable than others, but all of them exhibit a basic competency due to the efficiency of the studio production system. There's little to set Undertow aside from so many other movies that are just like it, but it sure is fun while it lasts.

This one largely holds me conflicted but to be totally fair I largely think this is directly a piece that someone more connected with Romania history will resonate with. Technically serving as a documentary, the film bounces back and forth between archival footage and then more modern day narrative as presented by actors talking directly at the camera. The aesthetic and creative elements to this film is wildly original and is what kept me somewhat in tune with what was going on.…

It begins with some comedic overtones but becomes a troubling thesis about the period under totalitarian Communist leader Nicolae Ceausescu.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Uppercase Print, the second documentary feature from Romanian filmmaker Radu Jude, is a clinical glimpse at the distances a government will go in staving off dissent. It delves into the tragic persecution of sixteen-year-old Mugur Calinescuof, a rebellious and disillusioned teenager who penned graffiti slogans, written in blue or white chalk uppercase, of revolt against the authoritarian regime of Nicolae Ceausescu.

reviews.text: Varda intentionally sets this amongst abundance. She takes a character she knows is going to be seen as unsympathetic by so many eyes, and she frames her from everyone else's point of view, letting other voices slowly build a picture for us that may or may not be accurate. What we get from the titular character is just another perspective, and by her own admission, she does not always tell people the whole truth. The insights derived from this are the humanizing of those scorned and unsettled and an understanding of the disaffection that the rote, monolithic normal world can instill.

Mona’s life of freedom allows Varda’s fourth-wall breaking, documentary-style moments of self-reflexivity to hold more weight; characters say she was a friend, but how much of that friendship came from genuine affection and how much derived from subconscious superiority and feeling self-congratulatory over helping a homeless person? One claims Mona had “no wishes, no wants” as a criticism, but does Mona’s presence and her life outside of societal norms make people more aware of their dreams failing, actually clamouring to live a life like hers with no pressure to be or do anything? Varda continually walks this line,…

Oh, and none of the wit, if Kevin Williamson’s involvement as producer got your hopes up. Still, some of the set pieces are inspired, one of which is reminiscent of Razorback of all movies. All in all, a fun, jaw-droppingly atmospheric voodoo slasher that I’ll be watching again.

reviews.author: Wilson
reviews.text: Vincent Ward's Vigil is a really interesting, almost other-wordly, effort. A coming-of-age film, about stresses and difficulties of change (bodily, emotionally, intellectually) becalmed by glorious photography, of greens and of every shade of mud. At times I thought of it as a plot-less folk horror; it isn't horror per se, but it is intrinsically unsettling. It opens with animals and death, a sex scenes climaxes, strange occurrences occur, and the whole 90 minutes lingers in your mind uncomfortably. It has no real plot, but plenty happens, as Ward envisions a world on screen, what happens in that world does not mean as much as the world itself.

reviews.author: ratbastard
reviews.text: Atmospheric drama from Vincent Ward. Adolescent 'Toss' lives on a remote farm in New Zealand with her family. Toss is forced to deal with the aftermath of her beloved father's death, and the introduction of farm hand 'Ethan'. A strange, absorbing and eerie piece - there’s certainly a folk horror vibe to this. A study of maturity / coming-of-age and grief - we see how the loss of the patriarch affects the family dynamics and the farm business. Beautifully presented, boasting some stunning and colourful New Zealand landscape shots - all tinged with a tangible, otherworldly quality and punctuated by a fairly off-beat score. Very light on plot. Certainly more of a moody, character-driven ride - the various interactions become the general focus of the film. The performances are good across the board - with Kay and Kerr perhaps the stand outs. An enjoyable, unique and lo-fi gem.

reviews.author: Ben Buckingham
reviews.text: Ravenous, carnivorous cinema; of dark & mouldering spaces where the fruiting bodies sprout but never die, just crumple & grow, over & over in a tangle of a place where time always sits & waits for your return. A filmic capsule of a memory that might have been your whole life, or just a moment, but the mud & brambles stick forever. No need for water to wash it clean; these textures are of the soul, if you grew up green, climbing, hiding, digging. If you grew up strange, dangerous, outside, then perhaps you dreamt you'd already seen this film. I think it's dreaming us.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Vinyl Nation" is a fun documentary with full depth and meaning. It seems to balance every aspect of the medium itself, from the contextual origin of the record, the technical aspects of how a record works to produce sound and the process that goes into making them. The film does this to balanced precision, but most importantly talks about the heart that goes into it all. The film easily picks up this pitch and plays to that tune through the duration of the film for an earnest heart felt ride. The film touches on the collecting aspects as it naturally should, but really it touches more connectively why people cherish the items in self and historical preservation, than the crueler…

reviews.text: easy to write this off as regurgitating other vinyl docs but the focus on diversity in the record collecting (and selling) community and the approach of passing down a love (or obsession) for analog media to our children (and grandchildren) does more than just fetishize nostalgia, it embraces the future -- which I'd like to see more docs about this type of topic doing

reviews.author: Jake Boston
reviews.text: I love collecting physical media in all shapes and sizes because there is no better feeling in the world than holding a piece of media that you love in your hands and fall in love with that title even before you play it. This doc does a great job showing that passion off in multiple ways and I had a great time watching it. From seeing a vinyl being pressed to the excitement of participating in Record Store Day to the history of the medium there was just so much to learn and dig into… kind of like a bin of records in a sense. ⭐️⭐️⭐️ 1/2 Out Of 5.

reviews.author: Quinn
reviews.text: Around ten years ago, I purchased a beat-up old book from an antique store titled Steal This Book (yes, reiterating that I paid seven bucks for it) written by counterculture kook Abbie Hoffman. Among chapters on such topics as guerrilla radio broadcasting, free medical care, political asylum, and making Molotov cocktails, there's a section on shoplifting. In it, Hoffman suggests that one can steal a vinyl record by sliding it into a pizza box. I remember being tickled by this advice, because it seemed so dated to me that there used to be places where you could buy both a pizza and a record. Fast-forward to last Thursday; I, in my pandemic-appropriate mask and gloves, am in the checkout line…

reviews.author: The Great Owl
reviews.text: Up until a few years ago, I had been a devoted compact disc listener for decades and I did not even have a record player. I owned a few vinyl records, but I mainly had them in my home for decorative purposes as collector's items (tour-only record editions that I bought from merch stands at concerts, etc.). One of my prized possessions was, and still is, an original UK seven-inch 45rpm single pressing of my all-time favorite song, “A Forest” by The Cure, that I bought on eBay back in the early 2000s, although I had no way to listen to it. I just thought that it would be cool to own my all-time favorite song on vinyl.

For three decades I have purchased and loved records with all my black heart.... about a decade back I stopped going to record fairs, I stopped attempting to converse with people in record shops... why? Well the people on this doco are the answer as to why. With only a couple of exceptions, these people are not my people. Not even slightly. Not at all. It was cool to see the pressing plants, those peeps were awright. But the pack of other ‘talking heads’ left a LOT to be desired....

reviews.text: This is undoubtedly one of the best behind-the-scenes looks at Disney animation ever made; it’s so candid and honest in its depiction of Disney’s internal corporate drama, their financial and critical failures, and the messy artistic process that I can’t believe it’s on Disney Plus. If you’ve read the book DisneyWar, this covers much of the same ground in the Eisner/Katzenberg era, but with some exceptionally revealing BTS footage and home video from the animators. It’s simultaneously saddening (ie: making these movies was not a walk in the park and people got hurt along the way) and also somehow uplifting (ie: despite the messiness of the human condition, we still got these works of art that will inspire people for generations to come.)

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: I pressed play because I had a nostalgic itch that needed scratching. While it certainly did the trick, Waking Sleeping Beauty also quickly proved to be one of the all-time great films about filmmaking. It's rich with illuminating material about the Disney Renaissance and its animators, but more than that, it is nothing short of staggering to learn how much drama and tumult was taking place behind the scenes of some of the most joyful movies ever made. An essential documentary.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Focusing on the decade-long corporate and creative tug of war between the powers-that-were at Disney between 1984 and 1994, "Waking Sleeping Beauty" is an intriguing, moving, and satisfying documentary. Assembled by producer, Don Hahn, the film eschews talking heads for archival and fresh interviews, behind-the-scenes footage, and caricatures that tell the story of what would become Disney animation's second golden age.

reviews.text: I’m glad they focused as much as they did on the business side of things, which is the part of the story I know much less about. For that reason I enjoyed it. It was good enough for Al Gore.

reviews.text: The literal and spiritual emasculation is pretty bluntly an analog here for an entire community's disenfranchisement, but that doesn't make this any less powerfully angry or feverishly weird. Fanaka takes great pains to depict a vibrant culture peeking in through the margins of this picture, one barred from economic opportunity and systematically institutionalized -- from within and without -- and by both means deliberately dismantled.

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: A decade removed from the Watts riots, Jamaa Fanaka returns to the scene to lob a molotov at a culture where black men are literally and metaphorically emasculated, locked up, and treated as animals. I’m always in awe of how Fanaka was able to use the trappings of genre to smuggle big, barely cloaked political messages into films that are both hugely entertaining and singularly weird. He doesn’t just use those genre elements and those insane hooks (without getting into spoilers, this film has a BIG one) for cheap pops, though — he fully integrates them into his messages in a way where the two are inseparable. Welcome Home, Brother Charles is predicated on an act of revenge, but the…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A very intimate, gritty, street-level drama about black trauma and community survival in the face of institutional violence until suddenly in the final reel its an absurd revenge exploitation movie that cathartically expresses and weaponizes white emasculation fears of black men through genre filmmaking via the titular Brother Charles' attempted castration at the hands of racist cops resulting in a 12-foot long.... magic snake penis.... that he uses to strangle them to death. Tagging this as spoilers because I had no fucking clue about this insane twist and the shot where it's revealed is so incredible and realized with low-budget real skill behind the camera so I hope others experience it that way too. Even more impressive is that despite…

reviews.author: HalloweenH
reviews.text: I was not prepared for this powerful film. I was expecting a "run of the mill, revenge flick" what I got was much more thought provoking. More like Eddie Bunker's No Beast So Fierce (73) than JD's Revenge (76) I thought the prison sequences, were expertly done. No spoilers, but there's a scene in this flick, that HAS to be seen to be believed. One of my stops, when my time machine is finished is to go back and watch this with an audience. I'm sure it was BEDLAM during that scene. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: Jack Often
reviews.text: What magic was at work that led me to hear about this film and seek it out without the infamous second half being spoiled? Really pleased about that. Jamaa Fanaka turned out this astonishing work on weekends while holding down a job and going to UCLA, where he and a new wave of other Black film students were subject to a lot of discrimination. They put up with it for the freedom to create, which access to the school's equipment provided. That's an even more impressive feat to me than John Waters holding it together weekend after weekend to create his early films. Not to mention that Fanaka scored this himself, as sparely and effectively as John Carpenter might have.…

reviews.text: J. Fanaka #1 --- This movie is mostly known for one scene (which I won't spoil here). But it's so much more than that. And I wouldn't even call it exploitation. It's a drama about a man who has society against him. Racism plays a big part in the story and it doesn't hold back on that part. Those encounters are hard to watch and make you appreciate the wholesome moments even more. The main character is likable and you can feel his struggle. He's gotten out of jail and wants to go straight but finds no job due to his past. The title of the movie "Welcome Home" is more ironic than anything. Most people don't welcome him with open arms but instead, degrade him. Watts and Compton serve as authentic locations to the story. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: mrbalihai
reviews.text: One of the pitfalls of making a docudrama about the L.A punk scene of the late '70s is that most of us who were present when it actually happened are still around to provide a reality check if you get it wrong, and I'm here to tell you that Rodger Grossman's pathetic attempt to capture the rise and fall of The Germs is so far off the mark, it's laughable. Horribly miscast, badly acted, and incredibly loose with the facts, he might as well have been making a movie about The Cowsills in safety pins and mohawks.

He looks the part, but that unhinged quality about Crash is missing. If I were you, stick to the records and to Spheeris's legendary doc The Decline of Western Civilization, which remains about the only filmed document of Darby Crash and the Germs. (Personal trivia: I have a vinyl copy of (GI) from the personal collection of the Riverside, California poet Drew Blood -- aka Drew Bailey -- who was Crash's lover!)

Quem descobriu isto foi um tal Tomás de Aquino e, como era napolitano, sabia do que falava. Quando alguém nos diz: ”A forma é tudo, a ideia não conta”, é pura covardia, não é verdade, tem de se ver bem as coisas: a ideia existe! Depois, há uma matéria e depois, uma forma. The plot focuses on a child killer in Venice and subsequent investigation by a father whose daughter has become the latest victim. The subject material is handled sensitively - it is not an overly graphic film - but this is made up for thanks to Ennio Morricone's eerie score, which mainly consists of children singing, and a killer POV shot shown through a veil. These elements give the film a real skin crawling edge. The film takes its time to reveal the characters and situation in the first half,…

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Who Saw Her Die? is more focused on tone and establishing a mood than the slicing and dicing so often found in its genre contemporaries. The story focuses on a series of child murders that take place in and around Venice. A misty, frigid atmosphere and guilt-ridden sex maniacs are littered throughout, along with a high dose of red herrings and plot twists.

For example, a series of jump cut shots of pigeons swarming a priest in St. Mark's plaza is infinitely more exciting than a two-shot of George Lazenby talking to an old man in order to gain some exposition.
