reviews.text: Something like the Dr. Strangelove of paranoid ‘70s conspiracy thrillers. Obviously, Richert doesn’t have a fraction of Kubrick’s mastery of form, and the convoluted production probably didn’t help. But he still a finds ways to make every scene and character uniquely ridiculous while advancing a Kennedy assassination plot that could have been played straight. Would actually go so far as to say that this is less silly than Stone's JFK, because it has nothing but contempt for the Kennedys and understands that the world is run by clowns.

reviews.author: DallasFrance
reviews.text: One of the ultimate “Only in the 70s” films, with an absolutely stacked cast, and an absolutely bonkers script. A comedy-thriller based on the conspiracy to kill President Kennedy, Winter Kills features John Huston doing Chinatown level scene-chewing, and Jeff Bridges wandering around looking baffled for ninety minutes.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: This is an absurdly honest depiction of the capitalist class and its motivations, so no wonder it had a notoriously troubled production, messy execution, and pathetic box office showing. Lies, obfuscations, anti-communism, blame-shifting, ties to the mafia, owning the police and military, and literally parasitic, continual betrayals, the capitalists in this are the realistic in their cartoonish villainy. Even a cursory glance at their actual actions* would show you that they're even more ridiculous and monstrous than this. As an exploration of the Kennedy assassination conspiracy, it's surprisingly accurate in both tone (in that it's veers from silly to serious constantly) and detail (gathering the kind of symbolic imagery that feeds the theories and just kinda stating the obvious motivations clearly).

reviews.text: A satirical conspiracy thriller with an all-star cast, Winter Kills is the sort of thing I should enjoy more than I do. The problem is that William Richert is a better screenwriter than a director. Wild Bill, as he has been called, uses too many closeups, lets some scenes run too long, especially Dorothy Malone’s pathos, and moves the crazy proceedings sluggishly from scene to scene.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: All conspiracy movies from Parallax View to JFK are inherently cartoonish to some extent, but Winter Kills is an almost transgressive farce. After an intriguing milieu involving a president's assassination, a secret gunman, and murder, John Huston's character makes his appearance riding in a golf cart sandwiched between two gorgeous women, a blanket over their laps. "What do you think those women are doing under that blanket?" he asks his son (Jeff Bridges). "Do you think they're playing with my nuts?" And so goes the odd tonal shifts in Winter Kills. Thankfully, it's more fascinating than off-putting, in no small part due to John Huston's mega performance (and Sterling Hayden's Amish beard). There's definitely a cynicism buried beneath the humor and surrealism. (I was inspired to go on a JFK assassination kick after reading this Adam Curtis essay on a Texas oilman who found himself caught up in assassination conspiracy)

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Like a brain damaged telephone game take on JFK conspiracy thriller fan fiction crossed with the most bombastic daytime soap imaginable, this movie is just so much MOVIE that's it's really hard to take 100% seriously. Every acting Titan is in their own world (scratch that: John Huston is in his own UNIVERSE), while Vilmos Zsigmond paints every scene with his usual elegant eye that this sort of hothouse potboiler trash probably doesn't deserve. Takes on an almost farcically surrealist tone near the end, when we're walked through the Illuminati computer systems (which, naturally, are manned by Anthony Perkins). Just the damndest thing, really.

reviews.author: Jamelle Bouie
reviews.text: I highly recommend watching the short documentary on the making of this very strange JFK conspiracy film. Everyone involved seems proud of the film, but I find it to be a bit tonally confused, unsure of whether it is a farce or a dark conspiracy picture. If it’s the former, it’s like The Parallax View but considerably stupider. If it’s the latter, then it is like The Parallax View but considerably less competent.

reviews.author: Nick Newman
reviews.text: Much as The Eiger Sanction found Clint Eastwood struggling to adapt a Bond parody he didn't find funny, this is any of the decade's Pakula thrillers with every scene gradually, invariably infected by ZAZ's lopsided, bad-taste gags. It's great on both ends: way sharper, more plausible JFK-conspiracy movie than JFK (unless you'd take Costner I-say-I-say-I-saying Stone's fiction over young Jeff Bridges getting confronted by Sterling Hayden in a tank, which, okay), only a touch less formally distinct than Klute, and the closest we'll get to Anthony Perkins as a Bond villain.

reviews.text: "Winter Kills" is a 1979 conspiracy thriller directed by William Richert. Set up within fictional surroundings that are used the JFK assassination as something of a template, the film follows Jeff Bridges character of Nick Kegan as he unravels a mystery surrounding his older brother. His other brother, as the narrative displays, is that of former U.S. President Timothy Kegan who was assassinated. The other interesting thing of note was that Nick's involvement of unraveling this mystery arrives almost two decades after the event while one of the gunmen on their deathbed confesses. Now without Nick realizing it, he is pulled into a sprawling mystery that not only involves major political figure heads but also the affluent Kegan family which…

Passionately performed ones at times maybe, just unfortunately in a way can't help but feel like it's been jerry-rigged backward from the nomination clips it didn't even end up getting. Makes for a strange viewing experience that doesn't leave you a whole lot to engage with other than the baffling Ben Wishaw sitting-his-ass-down-and-listening male ally role/performance and truly hideous shooting style/color grade that actually prompted me to look up the tech specs to see how it was even possible to achieve.

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: An exceptionally vivid and sleazy tabloid tale combined with a Rashomon-style story structure, Wonderland makes an entertaining B side to PTA’s more accomplished Boogie Nights. As John Holmes, the porn actor/drug addict/scumbag extraordinaire, Val Kilmer gives one of his last great leading man performances, working hard to twist the audience around his little finger by weaponizing his unique brand of magnetism, much like he did in Oliver Stone’s The Doors. The supporting cast is absolutely stacked with a who’s who of popular character actors*, but sadly, most have limited screen time and unable to make much of an impression. Eric Bogosian and Josh Lucas** fair the best, generating enough seedy, drug-addled menace to stand out from the pack.

reviews.author: B E R T
reviews.text: This is a simple story that’s made unnecessarily confusing an muddling for no reason. It’s an alright movie as it is, however, there’s so much potential for a great movie here if it just streamlined the characters and plot details. The cast are all really good in their roles, Kate Bosworth and Val Kilmer are very good and Christina Applegate in her small role leaves a good impression. I just can’t help but wonder what could’ve been though if it were just a touch simpler. This case of the Wonderland Murders would make a great season of Ryan Murphy’s American Crime Story, fleshing out all the character details the way this movie tries to do would make more sense and be more effective in a series. Also, I wish we had a straight John Holmes biopic, someone needs to get on that.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Like a lot of pop cultural forensic dissections, this makes as many frustrating and far-fetched conclusions as it does salient observations. The white male angst on free display in the footage is grist for a number of breakdowns of how the collapse of grunge and the brief wave of progressive male rock stars and women rockers had given way to a backlash against the burgeoning teen pop boom of the late-'90s. Jewel, of all people, perhaps sums up the whole thing best when she describes Woodstock '99 as the culmination of Generation X's rebellion against nothing, of feeling dissatisfaction but lacking the visible, unifying element of a Vietnam or whatever to rally against.

reviews.text: Wyrm is a quirky, dystopian coming-of-age comedy about a socially awkward teen living in a future where emotional milestones are tracked, and he’s trying to figure out where he fits in. It has this offbeat vibe that really reminded me of Napoleon Dynamite. The cast is fun, especially the kid who plays the titular character, who’s pretty endearing, and Lulu Wilson and Sosie Bacon bring some great energy. The oddball humor mostly works, though the tone shifts a bit to the dramatic parts. I wasn’t totally on board with the drama—it felt underexplained at times—and the family dynamic was a little confusing. That said, the moments I did get were sweet. It’s a cute, silly film that’s definitely worth a watch for something off the beaten path.

reviews.text: The X-15 was an experimental aircraft that set altitude records in the 60s, reaching the edge of outer space, with pilots being retroactively given astronaut status in 2005. This 1961 film is a fictionalized account of the program, marrying exciting flight footage with less compelling melodrama of the pilot's romantic entanglements. The X-15 in operation, narrated by James Stewart, lends itself to a documentary feel - but the project started life as a Bell X-2 vehicle, so despite the distinguished returns of this plane, for the personal lives any aircraft would do. reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Every line of dialogue is laced with venom. Arrogant misogyny drips from Michael Caine's Robert, cold, disdainful, malicious, full of jealous rages, with no one to counter his callous drive for his own pleasures. The latter would be fine if it weren't at the expense of others; his empty promises leave psychic wreckage. Elizabeth Taylor dominates the film, as expected, but Caine and Susannah York provide their own great performances to form a toxic triangle that is compelling and repulsive. The ending is the kind of delicious vengeance I could not have predicted but would not want changed one bit (well... unless they wanted to make it more explicit).

reviews.text: For some reason, I expected this to be one of those high-camp disasters that Ms. Taylor was churning out at the time, hand over fist. Should have realized from the screenwriting credit that it would be anything but. Taylor's teased-out wigs, York's hair-don't, Leighton's pink mop all compete with any number of groovy, overdone interiors for attention, but Edna O'Brien's screenplay (the only one credited to the acclaimed Irish author) grounds the whole thing in something like truth. It's drunk, but sobering; excessive, brittle, harrowing. And Stanley Myer's score is tremendous.

reviews.author: Schratzi
reviews.text: You can tell me anything…anytime…provided I listen!Wonderfully campy melodrama that was critically lambasted on release and still seems to be sadly underappreciated even among fans of eccentric cinema. I find it a highly entertaining oddity from Elizabeth Taylor’s much maligned late 60s/early 70s experimental phase, which actually encompasses an endlessly fascinating collection of offbeat, daring projects, most of them well worth rescuing from undeserved oblivion. Among all the scandal-sheet hyperbole and gossip-mongering that’s still associated with her name, it’s often forgotten how good an actress Liz Taylor really was. She was also one of the last classic, old-style Hollywood divas and had a particularly hard time adjusting to the swinging, youth-obsessed 60s and 70s, a real woman in an…

reviews.text: The day is Sunday. I met Bill Pullman, by random chance, at a work event the Wednesday night prior to this. reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Sherlock Holmes is one of those characters that's been around for so long that he's ascended into a kind of archetype-hood, with very little new territory being covered in the myriad (perfectly entertaining and worthwhile, of course) versions of the character. Instead, it's more like a Shakespeare play or something, with every actor doing his own variation on a cemented set of themes. What's great about Zero Effect is that even though it's an unmistakable "modern day Sherlock Holmes" movie, it revels in the differences between Daryl Zero and the canonical Holmes mythos, finding moral wrinkles and biographical detail that would never work in a proper Sherlock Holmes movie but feel fun and exciting here.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: For most people, the late capitalistic demand for employees to go full automaton at the start of every shift — to smother their own humanity under a membrane of cheap uniforms, fake smiles, and heartless corporate jargon — is something of a turnoff. For Cassandre (Adèle Exarchopoulos), the stone-faced heroine of Julie Lecoustre and Emmanuel Marre’s fly-by-night travelogue “Zero Fucks Given,” the requirement to gate-check her emotions is the entire reason she decided to become a Wing Airlines flight attendant in the first place.

reviews.author: Ashlea 🖤 🐂
reviews.text: When capitalism and grief are kicking your ass simultaneously: what lies behind the smile of the air hostess? Detaching from human relationships to survive, wondering whether she has a life or merely an existence, starving off her loneliness with cigarettes and parties, and then serving you with a smile. I love the casual, effortless way this film unpacks this young woman's disenchantment and how Adèle Exarchopoulos carries her flattened character's malaise and exhaustion: making a living to what end. It is all told and shot in a natural way that evokes the modern human condition. Her insignificance in the universe and loneliness in a crowd at the end brought up a lot of emotions.
